(p-٢٣٥)Surat Al 'Imran

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif-Lam-Mim.﴾ ﴿Allah.﴾ The mim was given a vowel (ḥurrikat al-mīm) because of iltiqā' al-sākinayn (the meeting of two unvowelled letters), namely its own sukūn (vowellessness) and the sukūn of the lām of Allah. It was given a fatḥa (the "a" vowel) because the fatḥa is light, and it was not given a kasra (the "i" vowel), in order to avoid a succession of kasras, because of the yā' that follows and the kasra of the mīm before it. The fatḥa on the mīm is not due to its being unvowelled with a yā' before it, for if that were the case, the fatḥa would have been required in "Ḥā-Mīm" as well. Nor is it correct to say that the fatḥa on the mīm is the fatḥa of the hamza of Allah transferred to the mīm, because that hamza is a hamzat waṣl (the hamza of connection) which falls away in continuous speech, and its vowel falls away with it. Had it been permissible to transfer its vowel, it would have been permissible to retain the hamza, and retaining it is not permissible. Yazīd and al-A'shā made the mīm unvowelled and pronounced the hamza, while the rest read with the hamza of connection and a fatḥa on the mīm. Allah is the subject (mubtada') and ﴿there is no god but He﴾ is its predicate (khabar). The predicate of "lā" (there is no) is implied; the estimate is: there is no god in existence except "He". "Huwa" (He) is in a nominative position as a substitute (badal) for the position of "lā" and its noun.

﴿The Ever-Living, the Sustainer﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: He is the Ever-Living; or it is a substitute for "huwa". Al-Qayyūm is a fa'yūl form derived from qāma (to stand), and it means the one who stands by justice and the one who stands over every soul in what it has earned.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 3:

﴿Nazzala﴾ means: He (Huwa) sent down (nazzala).

﴿upon you the Book﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿with truth﴾: this is a circumstantial phrase (hal), meaning: He sent it down as a truth that is firmly established.

﴿confirming what is before it﴾, meaning what came before it, ﴿and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel﴾. Both are non-Arabic proper names (ism a'jamiyy). Deriving them from al-waraa (creation) and al-najl (offspring) is a forced etymology (takalluf). Their measure (wazn) as tafʿila and ifʿil is valid only after they are considered Arabic, and it is said: "nuzul al-kitab" [the descent of the Book]. ﴿And He sent down the Torah and the Gospel﴾ because the Qur'an was sent down in installments (munajjaman), whereas the two Books were sent down all at once (jumla).

﴿مِن قَبْلُ﴾ meaning "before" [this], i.e., before the Qur'an, ﴿هُدًى لِلنّاسِ﴾ meaning "a guidance for mankind": for the people of Moses and Jesus, or for all of mankind.

﴿وَأنْـزَلَ الفُرْقانَ﴾ meaning "and He sent down the Criterion." That is, the genus of books, because every one of them distinguishes between truth and falsehood. Or it refers to the Psalms (al-Zabur). Or it repeats the mention of the Qur'an, describing it with a qualifier (نَعْتٌ, na't) to magnify its status.

﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا بِآياتِ اللهِ﴾ meaning "Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of God," from His revealed books and others.

﴿لَهم عَذابٌ شَدِيدٌ واللهُ عَزِيزٌ ذُو انْتِقامٍ﴾ meaning "for them is a severe punishment, and God is Mighty, Lord of retribution." Dhu 'uqubah shadidah (one who inflicts severe punishment), such that no avenger can match it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 5:

﴿Indeed, nothing is hidden from Allah, neither on the earth nor in the heaven﴾. That is, in the world; He expressed it by "the heaven and the earth." That is, He is aware of the disbelief of the one who disbelieves and the faith of the one who believes, and He will recompense them for it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 6:

﴿He it is Who fashions you in the wombs however He wills.﴾ (in the various forms) ﴿There is no god but He, the Mighty⁠—﴾ in His dominion ﴿the Wise⁠—﴾ in His governance.

It is narrated that when the delegation of the Banu Najran came⁠—and they were sixty riders, their chief being al-'Aqib, their leader (ʿumdah) being al-Sayyid, and their bishop and scholar (ḥabr) being Abu Harithah⁠—they disputed about whether, if ʿIsa was not a son of Allah, then who was his father? The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do you not know that no child is born except that it resembles its father?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Do you not know that Allah the Exalted is Living and does not die, whereas ʿIsa dies; and that our Lord is Overseer over the servants, guarding them and providing for them, whereas ʿIsa is not able to do that; and that nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Him, whereas ʿIsa knows only what He has taught him; and that He fashioned ʿIsa in the womb however He willed, so his mother carried him, bore him, nursed him, and he ate and excreted; and our Lord is exalted above all of that?" Thereupon they were silenced, and the opening of Surat Al 'Imran was revealed concerning them, up to some eighty-odd verses.

He it is who sent down to you the Book, ﴿the Qur'an﴾. Some of it, ﴿of the Book﴾, consists of ﴿clear verses﴾ (muhkamat), whose wording has been made firm, being protected from ambiguity and confusion. ﴿They are the mother of the Book﴾, meaning the foundation of the Book, to which the ambiguous verses are referred and by which they are interpreted.

﴿And others﴾, and other verses, are ﴿ambiguous﴾ (mutashabihat), meaning unclear and open to more than one meaning. An example of this is ﴿The Most Merciful sat firmly on the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha 5]. The word "istiwa'" can mean sitting, and it can also mean power and dominion. The first meaning is impermissible for God Most High, on the basis of the clear verse: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura 11]. Alternatively, the clear verses are those in which God commands what He has commanded in every Book He sent down, such as His saying: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you﴾ [al-An'am 151], and so on, and His saying: ﴿Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ [al-Isra' 23], and so on. The ambiguous verses are those whose meaning lies beyond what is apparent, or which admit only one aspect, or which admit several aspects. Some are those whose interpretation (ta'wil) is known, and some are those whose interpretation is not known. Alternatively, the abrogating (nasikh) verse is the one that is acted upon, and the abrogated (mansukh) verse is the one that is not acted upon. The Qur'an was not entirely clear, because the ambiguous verses contain a trial and a means of distinguishing between those who stand firm upon the truth and those who waver in it. Also, because scholars' disputation over them, their exertion of their intellects in extracting their meanings, and their referral of them to the clear verses bring great benefits, abundant knowledge, and the attainment of high ranks with God Most High.

﴿As for those in whose hearts there is deviation﴾ (zaygh), meaning inclination away from the truth, these are the people of innovation (bid'a).

﴿They follow what is ambiguous﴾, meaning they cling to the ambiguous verse which admits of what the innovator adopts, though it does not accord with the clear verse, and which also admits of what accords with the statement of the people of truth. ﴿Seeking discord﴾, meaning seeking to tempt people away from their religion and mislead them, ﴿and seeking its interpretation﴾, meaning seeking to interpret it according to the interpretation they desire.

﴿None knows its interpretation except God﴾, meaning that no one can be guided to its true interpretation, which must be adopted, except God. ﴿And those firmly rooted in knowledge﴾, those who are rooted, meaning who are established in it, who are settled in it, and who have grasped it with a firm bite. This is a new sentence according to the majority. Their pause is at His saying, "except God," and they explain the ambiguous as that which God has kept to Himself. According to them, "those firmly rooted" is the subject, and the predicate is: ﴿They say, "We believe in it"﴾. This is praise from Him, Exalted, upon them for their faith through submission and belief in its truth without specifying its modality. The benefit of sending down the ambiguous verses is believing in them, holding that what God intended by them is true, and recognising the limitation of human understanding in reaching what He has not made accessible to them. This is reinforced by the reading of Ubayy: "and those firmly rooted say," and the reading of ʿAbd Allah: "Its interpretation is only with God." Some do not pause at that point and say that those firmly rooted in knowledge know the ambiguous, and "they say" is a new sentence clarifying the state of those firmly rooted, meaning: these scholars of interpretation say, "We believe in it," that is, in the ambiguous or in the Book.

﴿All﴾ of it, both its ambiguous and its clear verses, ﴿is from our Lord﴾, from God the Wise, whose speech is not self-contradictory.

﴿And none takes heed﴾, meaning none is admonished. Its origin is "yatadhakkaru" (takes heed).

﴿except the people of understanding﴾, meaning the people of intellects. This is praise for those firmly rooted, for their concentration of mind and good reflection. It has also been said that "they say" is a circumstantial clause describing those firmly rooted.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 8:

﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us﴾: do not turn them away from the truth by creating inclination (mayl) in the hearts. ﴿After You have guided us﴾: to act upon the clear (muhkam) verses and to submit to the ambiguous (mutashabih) ones. ﴿And grant us from Yourself mercy﴾: from Your presence, a bounty through success (tawfiq) and steadfastness (tathbit).

﴿Indeed, You are the Bestower﴾: abundant in giving (hibah). The verse is part of the speech of those firmly grounded in knowledge (al-rasikhun), and it is possible that it begins a new sentence (istinaf), meaning: say it, and likewise the one after it, which is:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 9:

﴿Our Lord, You are indeed the Gatherer of mankind for a Day⦆ — that is, You gather them for the reckoning of a Day, or for the recompense of a Day.

﴿There is no doubt about it﴾ — there is no doubt about its occurrence. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not fail in the promise﴾ — the appointment (al-mi'ad, meaning the promised time). The meaning is that divinity (al-ilahiyya) is incompatible with failing to keep a promise, like your saying: "Indeed, the generous one does not disappoint the one who asks him," that is, he does not fail to fulfil what he has promised the Muslims and the disbelievers of reward and punishment.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 10:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ in the Messenger of Allah, ﴿will never avail them﴾, i.e., benefit or avert, ﴿against Allah﴾, i.e., against His punishment, ﴿anything from their wealth or their children.﴾ ﴿Anything﴾ of availing. ﴿And they are the fuel of the Fire﴾, its firewood.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 11:

﴿As the case was with the family of Pharaoh and those before them﴾ al-Da'b (habit, custom, or persistent way) is a verbal noun from da'aba fi al-'amal, meaning he strove and exerted himself in the work. It is used in the sense of the condition and circumstance that a person is in. The kaf (ka, "as") is in the nominative position, its implied sense being: the habit of these disbelievers in denying the truth is like the habit of those before them, the family of Pharaoh and others. Alternatively, it is in the accusative position, governed by lan tughni (will not avail), meaning: will not avail them, like the manner in which it did not avail those (before them). (Ka-dabi) without a hamza wherever it occurs, is from Abu 'Amr.

﴿They denied Our signs﴾ This is an explanation of their habit, of what they did or what was done to them, presented as an answer to an implied question about their condition. It may also be a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: they had indeed denied.

﴿So Allah seized them for their sins﴾ Because of their sins. It is said: akhadhtuhu bi-kadha, meaning I requited him for it.

﴿And Allah is severe in punishment﴾ His punishment is severe. The genitive construction here is not a pure (mahda) one.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 12:

﴿Say to those who disbelieve﴾ They are the polytheists of Mecca.

﴿You will be overcome﴾ on the Day of Badr, ﴿and gathered to Hell﴾ — jahannam (Hell), which is a deep pit. Ḥamza and ʿAlī read both verbs with the ya' (i.e., yughlabūna and yuḥsharūna, in the third person).

﴿And wretched is the resting place﴾ — the place of settling, which is Hell.

﴿There has indeed been a sign for you﴾. The address is to the idolaters of Quraysh. ﴿In two hosts that met﴾ on the Day of Badr. ﴿One host fighting in the way of Allah﴾, and they were the believers. ﴿And another﴾, another host, ﴿disbelieving, seeing them as twice their own number﴾. The idolaters saw the Muslims as twice the number of the idolaters, that is 2,000, or twice the number of the Muslims, that is 600 and some more. Allah showed them the Muslims, despite their small number, as many times their number, so that the idolaters would be awed by them and would shrink from fighting them. (ترونهم) is the reading of Nafi' (Nafi', one of the canonical Qur'an readers), meaning: O idolaters of Quraysh, you see the Muslims as twice your disbelieving host, or as twice their own number. This is not contradicted by what He said in Surat al-Anfal: ﴿and He makes you appear few in their eyes﴾ (al-Anfal 8:44), because they were first made to appear few in their eyes, until they became bold against them. When they joined together, they appeared many in their eyes, until they were defeated. Thus the making few and the making many occurred in two different situations. A parallel to this, among what is interpreted as relating to differing circumstances, is ﴿So on that Day, no one will be questioned about his sin, man or jinn﴾ (al-Rahman 55:39) and ﴿Stop them, for they are to be questioned﴾ (al-Saffat 37:24). Their being made to appear few to them at one time and many at another in their eyes is more eloquent regarding power and the manifestation of the sign. مثليهم is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (نصب على الحال, naṣb ʿala al-ḥāl, the accusative of circumstance), because it comes from sight by the eye itself, as evidenced by His saying ﴿a sight with the eye﴾ (ra'y al-ʿayn), meaning a manifest and clear sight with no confusion in it. ﴿And Allah strengthens with His help whom He wills﴾, as He strengthened the people of Badr by making them appear numerous in the eyes of the enemy. ﴿Indeed in that﴾, in the making of the few appear many, ﴿is a lesson﴾, an admonition ﴿for those who have vision﴾, for those possessing insight.

**﴿Beautified for people﴾**: The one who beautifies is Allah, according to the majority (al-Jumhur) of scholars, for the purpose of testing, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have made what is on the earth an adornment for it, that We may test them﴾ [al-Kahf: 7]. Its evidence is the reading of Mujahid (Mujahid ibn Jabr), "zayyana lil-nas" (with the verb in the active voice, naming the agent). It is also reported from al-Hasan (al-Hasan al-Basri) that the one who beautifies is Satan.

**﴿the love of desires﴾**: Shahwa (desire) is the yearning of the soul for a thing. He called the items he mentioned "desires" to emphasise that they are desired, or as if He intended to belittle them by calling them desires, since desire is considered base by the wise, and whoever follows it is blameworthy, bearing witness against himself to his animality.

**﴿of women﴾**: And female slaves (al-ima') are included in this.

**﴿and sons﴾**: Plural of ibn (son). It may be used in other places for both males and females, but here males are intended, for they are the ones desired by nature and prepared for defence.

**﴿and heaped-up treasures﴾**: Plural of qintar (a great quantity of wealth). It is said: the amount that fills the hide of a bull, or one hundred thousand dinars. Indeed, when Islam came, there were one hundred men in Makkah who had amassed qanatir (heaped wealth).

**﴿of gold and silver﴾**: Gold (dhahab) was so named for the speed (sur'a) with which it departs (dhahab) through spending, and silver (fidda) because it scatters (tatafarraq) through spending. Fadd means scattering.

**﴿and horses﴾**: They were so named because of their proud gait (ikhtiyal).

**﴿branded﴾**: Marked (al-mu'allama), from al-sawma, which is the mark; or pastured (al-mar'iyya), from asama al-dabba and sawwamaha (he let the animal graze freely).

**﴿and cattle﴾**: They are the eight pairs.

**﴿and tilth﴾**: Crops (al-zar').

**﴿That﴾**: The aforementioned.

**﴿is the enjoyment of the worldly life﴾**: One enjoys it in this world.

**﴿and with Allah is the best return﴾**: The place of return (al-marji').

(p. 241)

Then He made them renounce the world, saying: ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something better than that?﴾ — than what has been mentioned before. ﴿For those who are mindful of God, with their Lord are gardens﴾ — this is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), which indicates the explanation of what is better than that. So "gardens" (jannat) is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿for those who are mindful of God﴾ is its predicate (khabar).

﴿Beneath which rivers flow﴾ — this is a qualifier (sifah) of "gardens." It is also permissible for the preposition "for" (li) to be connected with "better" (khayr), and the mindful are singled out because they are the ones who benefit from it. "Gardens" may be in the nominative case, meaning "they are gardens." The reading of those who read "gardens" in the genitive (jarr) supports this, as an apposition (badal) to "better."

﴿Abiding therein forever, and purified spouses, and approval from God﴾ — that is, the approval (ridwan) of God.

﴿And God is Seeing of the servants﴾ — Knowing of their deeds, so that He will recompense them for them; or Seeing of those who are mindful of God and of their conditions, which is why He prepared the gardens for them.

Al-Sabirin ('alā al-ṭā'āt wa al-maṣā'ib) — "the patient," in acts of obedience and in calamities. It is in the accusative (naṣb) by way of praise (madh).

Al-Ṣādiqin qawlan bi-ikhbār al-ḥaqq, wa fi'lan bi-iḥkām al-'amal, wa niyyatan bi-imḍā' al-'azm — "the truthful," in speech by reporting what is true, in deed by perfecting action, and in intention by carrying through resolve.

Al-Qānitin — "the devoted," meaning those who call (to God), or those who obey.

Al-Munfiqin — "the spenders," meaning those who give charity.

Al-Mustaghfirin bi-al-asḥār — "those who seek forgiveness at dawn," meaning those who pray, or who ask for forgiveness. He specified the pre-dawn hours (al-asḥār) because it is the time when supplication is answered, and because it is the time of solitude. Luqman said to his son: "O my son, let not the rooster be more intelligent than you: it calls out at dawn while you are asleep."

The conjunction wa (and) placed between the attributes indicates their perfection in each one of them, and signals that each attribute is independently worthy of praise.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on Surah 3, verse 18:

﴿شَهِدَ اللهُ﴾ means: decreed, or said.

﴿أنَّهُ﴾ means: that.

﴿لا إلَهَ إلا هو والمَلائِكَةُ﴾ means: ﴿There is no deity except Him, and the angels﴾, through what they witnessed of His great power.

﴿وَأُولُو العِلْمِ﴾ means: that is, the prophets and the scholars.

﴿قائِمًا بِالقِسْطِ﴾ means: ﴿upholding justice﴾, establishing justice in what He apportions of provisions and lifespans, in His rewarding and punishing, and in what He commands His servants of giving one another their due and dealing equitably among themselves. Its accusative form (انتصابه) is that it is a emphatic circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl mu'akkidah, حال مؤكدة) of the Name of God, the Exalted, or of the pronoun "هو". The qualifier (حال) is singled out in the accusative without the two conjoined nouns to which it refers, because if you said, "Zayd and ʿAmr came riding," it would not be permissible, due to the absence of ambiguity (عدم الإلباس). However, if you said, "Zayd and Hind came to me riding," it would be permissible, since it is distinguished by masculinity (بالذكورة), or it is in the sense of praise (على المدح). He repeated ﴿لا إلَهَ إلا هُوَ﴾ for emphasis.

﴿العَزِيزُ الحَكِيمُ﴾ is in the nominative as a resumptive new sentence (استئناف), meaning: He is the Mighty. It is not an adjective of "هو", because a pronoun cannot be described by an adjective. The meaning is: He is the Mighty who cannot be overcome, the Wise who never deviates from the truth.

**(p-243)**

﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*jumla mustaʼnafa*). It is also recited as *أنَّ الدِينَ* (*anna al-dīna*, with the particle *anna* read as the opening of the clause), in apposition (*badal*) to His words ﴿that there is no god but Him﴾. The meaning is: Allah bears witness that the religion with Allah is Islam.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites the verse at the time of his sleep, Allah creates from it seventy thousand creatures who will seek forgiveness for him until the Day of Resurrection. And whoever says after it: 'I bear witness to what Allah has borne witness to, and I entrust Allah with this testimony, and it is a deposit [with Allah] for me,' Allah, exalted is He, will say on the Day of Resurrection: 'Indeed, My servant has a covenant with Me, and I am the most worthy of those who fulfil a covenant. Admit My servant into Paradise.'"

﴿And those who were given the Scripture did not differ﴾, that is, the People of the Book, from the Jews and the Christians. Their difference was that they abandoned Islam, which is monotheism (*tawḥīd*). So the Christians professed a Trinity, and the Jews said: "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah."

﴿Except after knowledge had come to them﴾ that it is the truth from which there is no turning away.

﴿Out of envy among themselves﴾, that is, that difference arose only from envy among them and from their desire for leadership and worldly advantages, and from each group drawing people after it. There is no doubt about Islam. It is said that it refers to their disagreement about the prophethood of Muḥammad (ﷺ), where some believed in him and some disbelieved in him. It is also said that it refers to the Christians and their disagreement about the matter of ʿIsā, after knowledge had come to them that he was the servant of Allah and His messenger.

﴿And whoever disbelieves in the signs of Allah﴾, that is, His proofs and evidences.

﴿Then indeed Allah is swift in reckoning﴾, that is, swift in requital.

﴿فَإنْ حاجُّوكَ﴾ If they dispute with you (fa-in ḥājjūka) about the matter that the religion of God is Islam. The intended people are, according to the majority (al-Jumhur), the delegation of Banu Najran.

﴿فَقُلْ أسْلَمْتُ وجْهِيَ لِلَّهِ﴾ Say: "I have submitted my face (wajhī) to God." That is: I have devoted myself and my whole being to God alone. I have not made for Him a partner in it by worshipping another or calling upon another god alongside Him. That is, my religion is the religion of tawhid (monotheism), which is the upright religion (al-dīn al-qayyim) whose soundness has been established for you, as it has been established for me. I have not brought anything novel that you should dispute with me about it. A similar statement is: ﴿قُلْ يا أهْلَ الكِتابِ تَعالَوْا إلى كَلِمَةٍ سَواءٍ بَيْنَنا وبَيْنَكم ألا نَعْبُدَ إلا اللهَ ولا نُشْرِكَ بِهِ شَيْئًا﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 64]. This is a rejection of the disputation, since what he (the Prophet) is upon, and those believers with him, is the certainty about which there is no doubt, so what meaning is there in disputing about it?! (وَجْهِيَ) is read by Madani, Shami, Ḥafṣ, al-Aʿshā, and al-Barjamī.

﴿وَمَنِ اتَّبَعَنِ﴾ This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the tā' in ﴿أسْلَمْتُ﴾, (p-٢٤٤) that is: I have submitted, and whoever follows me has submitted. It is permissible because of the separation (li-l-fāṣil). It is also permissible for the waw to mean "with" (maʿa), in which case it is a maf'ūl maʿahu (object of accompaniment). (وَمَنِ اتَّبَعَنِي) in both cases is read with ya' by Sahl and Yaʿqūb, and Abū ʿAmr agreed with them in continuous recitation (waṣl).

﴿وَقُلْ لِلَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الكِتابَ﴾ To those given the Book, from among the Jews and the Christians.

﴿والأُمِّيِّينَ﴾ And the unlettered, those who have no book, from among the polytheists of the Arabs.

﴿أأسْلَمْتُمْ﴾ With two hamzas, read by Kufan (Kūfī). That is: there has come to you from the clear proofs (al-bayyināt) what necessitates the attainment of Islam. So have you submitted, or are you still upon your disbelief? It has been said: its wording is that of a question, but its meaning is a command, that is: "Submit!", like His saying: ﴿فَهَلْ أنْتُمْ مُنْتَهُونَ﴾ [al-Mā'ida: 91], meaning: "Desist!"

﴿فَإنْ أسْلَمُوا فَقَدِ اهْتَدَوْا﴾ Then if they submit, they have been guided, for they have attained right guidance, since they have left misguidance for guidance.

﴿وَإنْ تَوَلَّوْا فَإنَّما عَلَيْكَ البَلاغُ﴾ That is: they have not harmed you, for you are a messenger who gives warning; your only duty is to convey the message and to point out the path of guidance.

﴿واللهُ بَصِيرٌ بِالعِبادِ﴾ So He will recompense them for their submission and their disbelief.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 21:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets﴾ are the People of the Book, who were content with the killing of their forefathers, the prophets.

﴿without right﴾ is a confirmatory circumstantial clause (ḥāl), because the killing of a prophet can never be rightful.

﴿and kill those who enjoin justice﴾ — Ḥamzah reads (wa-yuqātilūna) "and fight".

﴿with justice﴾ means with equity.

﴿from among the people﴾ meaning: other than the prophets. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The Children of Israel killed forty-three prophets at the beginning of one day, and then one hundred and twelve men from among the worshippers of the Children of Israel stood up, and they enjoined their killers to do what is good and forbade them from what is evil, and they were all killed at the end of that same day."

﴿So give them the tidings of a painful punishment﴾ The fāʾ (fa, "so") has entered the predicate of inna (indeed), because its subject (ism) implicitly carries the meaning of a conditional (jazāʾ). It is as if it were said: "Those who disbelieve, so give them tidings," meaning: "whoever disbelieves, so give them tidings." This is because inna does not change the meaning of the inceptive (ibtidāʾ); it is for emphasis (taḥqīq), so its entry is as though it were not an entry at all. Had its place been taken by layta (would that) or laʿalla (perhaps), the entry of the fāʾ would have been impermissible.

﴿Those are the ones whose deeds have become void﴾, meaning they were lost.

﴿In this world and the Hereafter﴾. So for them is the curse and disgrace in this world, and the punishment in the Hereafter.

﴿And they have no helpers﴾. The plural is used for the pause at the end of the verse (ru'us al-ay, the verse-endings), and otherwise the indefinite singular (nakira, indefinite noun) in a negation is general ('amm, all-encompassing).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 23:

﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book?﴾ He means the rabbis (aḥbār) of the Jews, and that they had obtained a considerable portion of the Torah (al-Tawrāh). The "min" (مِن) here is either for partitive (tab'īḍ) meaning, or for explanation (bayān).

﴿They are being called﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring back to "those who".

﴿to the Book of Allah﴾ That is, the Torah or the Qur'an.

﴿so that He may judge between them﴾ The Book is made the judge inasmuch as it was the cause of judgment; or the meaning is that the Prophet (ﷺ) would judge between them. It is narrated that he (ﷺ) entered their schools (madāris) and invited them, and Nu'aym ibn 'Amr and al-Ḥārith ibn Zayd said to him: "Upon which religion are you?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Upon the creed (millah) of Ibrahim." They said: "Ibrahim was a Jew." He said to them: "Between us and you is the Torah, so come to it." But they refused.

﴿Then a faction of them turns away﴾ This is an expression of astonishment (istibʿād); turning away remains their habitual custom (daydan).

That is: this turning away and aversion is due to their making light for themselves of the matter of punishment, and their hope of coming out of the Fire after a few days, namely forty days, or seven days. "Dhalika" is the subject (mubtada'), and "bi-annahum" is its predicate (khabar). ﴿And their fabrication in their religion has deceived them, what they used to invent.﴾ That is: their own fabricating against Allah deceived them, which is their saying: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved ones, so He will not punish us for our sins except for a brief period."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 25:

﴿So how will it be when We gather them for a Day about which there is no doubt?﴾ That is, how will their condition be at that time? ﴿About which there is no doubt﴾ — that is, there is no suspicion regarding it. ﴿And every soul will be paid in full what it earned﴾ — as recompense for what it earned. ﴿And they﴾ refers, according to the sense, to ﴿every soul﴾, because it carries the meaning of "all people."

﴿And they will not be wronged﴾ — by an increase in their evil deeds, or a decrease in their good deeds.

﴿قُلِ اللهُمَّ﴾ ﴿Say: "O Allah"﴾. The مِيم (mīm) in اللهُمَّ is a substitute (عِوَض) for the particle يا (yā, "O"), which is why the two cannot be combined. This is one of the distinctive features of this name: it takes the letter تاء (tā') in oaths (in the phrase تَاللهِ), it may be preceded by the vocative particle of address (حَرْفُ النِّدَاء), it contains the definite article لام التعريف (lām al-ta'rīf), its hamza is elided in يا اللهُ, and it is pronounced with emphatic articulation (بِالتَّفْخِيم).

﴿مَالِكَ المُلْكِ﴾ ﴿Owner of sovereignty﴾: you possess the whole category of sovereignty, so you dispose of it as owners dispose of what they own. This is a second vocative, meaning "O Owner of sovereignty."

﴿تُؤْتِي المُلْكَ مَن تَشَاءُ﴾ ﴿You give sovereignty to whom You will﴾: You give to whomever You will the share of sovereignty that You have apportioned to him.

﴿وَتَنْـزِعُ المُلْكَ مِمَّنْ تَشَاءُ﴾ ﴿and You take sovereignty from whom You will﴾: i.e., You remove it. The first مُلْك (mulk) is general, while the other two instances are specific, each being a part of the whole. It is narrated that when the Prophet (ﷺ) conquered Makkah, he promised his community the sovereignty of Persia and Rome. The Jews and the hypocrites said: "Far-fetched! Far-fetched! How could Muhammad obtain the sovereignty of Persia and Rome? Are they not mightier and more secure than that?!" Then the verse was revealed: ﴿وَتُعِزُّ مَن تَشَاءُ﴾ ﴿and You honor whom You will﴾ with sovereignty, ﴿وَتُذِلُّ مَن تَشَاءُ﴾ ﴿and You humble whom You will﴾ by removing it from him. ﴿بِيَدِكَ الخَيْرُ﴾ ﴿In Your hand is all good﴾: i.e., the good and the evil. He mentioned only one of the two opposites and left out the other; alternatively, because the discourse concerns the good that He brings to the believers, which the disbelievers denied, He said: ﴿بِيَدِكَ الخَيْرُ﴾, You give it to Your allies in spite of Your enemies. ﴿إِنَّكَ عَلَى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ﴾ ﴿Indeed You are over all things Competent﴾: no one other than You is able to do anything except by Your empowerment.

It has also been said that the مُلْك (sovereignty) meant here is the sovereignty of well-being (مُلْكُ العَافِيَة), or the sovereignty of contentment (مُلْكُ القَنَاعَة). The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The kings of Paradise from among my community are those who are content with food one day at a time." Or it is the sovereignty of night prayer (مُلْكُ قِيَامِ اللَّيْل). And from al-Shiblī: it is independence from everything except the Originator, being sufficient with the One who brings into existence rather than with the two worlds. "تَعِزُّ" (you honor) is by means of knowledge (بِالمَعْرِفَة), or by being sufficient with the Originator, or by contentment; and "تُذِلُّ" (you humble) is by their opposites.

Then He mentioned His overwhelming power by referring to the state of the night and the day in their alternation, and the state of the living and the dead in bringing one out of the other, and He joined to this His provision without reckoning, in His saying:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 3, verse 27:

﴿You cause the night to enter into the day and You cause the day to enter into the night﴾. *Al-iylaj* (إيلاج) means causing one thing to enter into another. It is used here in a figurative sense (*majaz*), meaning: You reduce the hours of the night and add them to the day, and You reduce the hours of the day and add them to the night.

﴿And You bring the living out of the dead﴾: an animal from a drop of semen, or a chick from an egg, or a believer from an unbeliever.

﴿And You bring the dead out of the living﴾: semen from a human being, or eggs from a hen, or an unbeliever from a believer.

﴿And You provide for whom You will without account﴾: creation does not know its number and quantity, though it is known to God. This shows that the One who is able to perform those great acts that bewilder minds, and then is able to provide without account for whomever He wills among His servants, is able to strip the kingdom from the non-Arabs (*'ajam*) and humble them, and to give it to the Arabs and honour them. In some books it is said: "I am God, King of kings; the hearts of kings and their foreheads are in My hands. If My servants obey Me, I make the rulers a mercy upon them; if My servants disobey Me, I make the rulers a punishment upon them. So do not occupy yourselves with the affairs of kings, but turn to Me in repentance, and I will incline them towards you." This is the meaning of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "As you are, so will you be ruled over."

*(al-hayy mina al-mayyit)* and *(al-mayyit min al-hayy)*: read with the doubled letter (tashdid) wherever it occurs, by Madani and Kufi readers, except Abu Bakr.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 28:

﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies﴾ They were forbidden to befriend the disbelievers because of a kinship between them, (p-248) or a friendship before Islam, or for other reasons. This has been established in the Qur'an. Love for the sake of God and hatred for the sake of God is a great gate of faith (īmān).

﴿rather than the believers﴾ meaning: for you, allegiance to the believers is a substitute (mandūḥah) for allegiance to the disbelievers, so do not prefer them over the believers.

﴿And whoever does that has nothing to do with God﴾ That is: whoever allies with the disbelievers has no share in the alliance of God, because allegiance to an ally (walī) and allegiance to his enemy are mutually exclusive.

﴿Except when you fear a danger from them﴾ Except that you fear from them something whose guarding against is obligatory. That is: except when the disbeliever has power over you and you fear for your self and your property, in which case it is permissible for you to show allegiance outwardly and to set aside enmity.

﴿And God warns you of Himself﴾ That is: of His essence, so do not expose yourselves to His wrath by allying with His enemies. This is a severe warning.

﴿And to God is the final return﴾ That is: your return is to Him, and the punishment is prepared before Him. This is another warning.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 29:

﴿Say: Whether you conceal what is in your breasts or reveal it﴾ concerning the allegiance to the disbelievers, or other matters, which do not please Allah.

﴿Allah will know it﴾, and it is not hidden from Him, and this is the most emphatic threat.

﴿And He knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), and it is not conjoined to the response of the conditional (jawab al-shart). That is: He is the One who knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth, so your secret and your open affairs are not hidden from Him.

﴿And Allah is over all things competent﴾, so He is able to punish you.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 30:

﴿On the Day every soul will find whatever good it has done present, and whatever evil it has done, it will wish that between itself and that were a great distance.﴾ "On the Day" (yawma): it is in the accusative, governed by "tawaddu" (it wishes). The pronoun in "baynahu" (between it and that) refers to the Day, meaning: the Day of Resurrection, when every soul finds its good and its evil present, it wishes that between itself and that Day, which is his, there were a great distance, i.e., a long span. Or it is governed by "udhkur" (remember). It applies to "ma 'amilat" alone. "Wa ma 'amilat" (and whatever it has done) is in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'), and "tawaddu" is its predicate, meaning: and that which it has done of evil, it wishes that between itself and it there were a great distance. It is not valid for "ma" to be a conditional particle, because of the nominative "tawaddu". Indeed, the nominative is permissible when the condition is in the past tense, but the jussive is the more common (p-249), and it is reported from al-Mubarrad that the nominative is anomalous (shadhdh). He repeated His saying: ﴿And Allah warns you of Himself﴾ so that it would be in their minds, and they would not be heedless of it.

﴿And Allah is Kind to the servants.﴾ Among His kindness toward them is that He warned them of Himself so that they would not expose themselves to His wrath. It is also possible that He means that, while He is to be feared because of the perfection of His power, He is also to be hoped for because of the vastness of His mercy, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed your Lord is the possessor of forgiveness and the possessor of painful punishment﴾ [Fussilat: 43].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 31:

It was revealed when the Jews said: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved ones."

﴿Say: If you truly love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you﴾. The love of the servant for Allah is preferring His obedience over anything else, and Allah's love for the servant is that He is pleased with him and approves of his actions. It is reported from al-Hasan: Groups of people in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) claimed that they loved Allah, so He wanted to make their words be confirmed by action. Whoever claims His love but opposes the Sunnah of His Messenger is a liar, and the Book of Allah refutes him. It has been said: The love of Allah is knowing Him, continual fear of Him, the heart's continual occupation with Him and with His remembrance, and continual intimacy with Him. It has also been said: it is following the Prophet (ﷺ) in his sayings, actions and states, except what is specific to him. It has been said: The sign of love is that a person is constantly reflective, very much in seclusion, constantly silent, does not see when he looks, does not hear when he is called, does not grieve when he is afflicted, does not rejoice when he gains, and fears no one and hopes in no one.

﴿And Allah will forgive you your sins, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 32:

﴿Say: Obey Allah and the Messenger﴾. It is said: this is the sign of love (for Allah).

﴿But if they turn away﴾: they turn away from accepting obedience. It is also possible that the verb is in the present tense (muda'ari'), meaning: "If you (plural) turn away" (fa-in tatawallaw), with one of the two taa' dropped.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not love the disbelievers﴾: i.e., He does not love them.

God chose (اصطفى) Adam, the father of mankind, and Noah, the shaykh of the messengers, and the family of Abraham, namely Isma'il and Isaac and their offspring, and the family of 'Imran, namely Musa and Harun, who are the two sons of 'Imran ibn Yashhar. It is also said: 'Isa and Maryam daughter of 'Imran ibn Matan. Between the two 'Imrans there were eighteen hundred years.

﴿over the worlds﴾: over the worlds of their own times.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 34:

﴿Descendants﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "the family of Abraham" and "the family of 'Imran." ﴿One of them is from the other﴾ is a mubtada' (subject), and its khabar (predicate), which is in the place of nasb, is an attribute (sifah) of "descendants." That is, the two families are one continuous line of descent, some of whom branch off from others: Musa and Harun are from 'Imran, 'Imran is from Yasahar, Yasahar is from Qahath, Qahath is from Lawi, Lawi is from Ya'qub, and Ya'qub is from Ishaq. Likewise, 'Isa ibn Maryam, daughter of 'Imran ibn Mathan, is connected to Yahudha ibn Ya'qub ibn Ishaq. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) also entered the family of Abraham. It has been said: "one of them is from the other" in religion.

﴿And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾: He knows who is fit for being chosen, or He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing of the statement of the wife of 'Imran and her intention.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 35:

﴿When the wife of ʿImran said﴾. The "idh" (when) is governed by the verb in it (i.e., "qalat"), or by an implied verb "udhkur" (remember).

﴿the wife of ʿImran﴾: she was the wife of ʿImran ibn Mathan, the mother of Maryam, the grandmother of ʿIsa (ʿalayhi al-salam). Her name was Hannah daughter of Faqudha.

﴿My Lord, I have vowed to You﴾ (i.e., I have dedicated, made binding upon myself) ﴿what is in my womb as one dedicated (muharraran)﴾. "Muharraran" is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from "ma", and "ma" here is in the sense of "alladhi" (that which). The meaning: freed for the service of Bayt al-Maqdis (the Holy House, Jerusalem), with no control of mine over it, and I will not put it to service. This kind of vow was prescribed among them, or [it means] devoted exclusively to worship. It is said: "tin hurr," meaning pure, unmixed clay.

﴿So accept from me﴾: "minni" (from me) is read by Madani and Abu ʿAmr. Taqabbul means taking something with approval and acceptance.

﴿Indeed You, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 36:**

﴿When she gave birth to her﴾: the pronoun refers to ﴿what is in my womb﴾, and it is feminine in agreement with the meaning of "pregnancy" (al-hablah), or "soul" (al-nafs), or "being" (al-nasamah).

﴿She said: My Lord, I have given birth to her as a female﴾: ﴿as a female﴾ (unthā) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) referring to the pronoun in ﴿I have given birth to her﴾. That is, she gave birth to the pregnancy, or the soul, or the being, as a female. She said this because dedication (taḥrīr) was only for boys, so she made an excuse for what she had vowed, and she complained to her Lord in sorrow. Because she said this in a manner of grief and regret, God said: ﴿And God knows best what she gave birth to﴾, glorifying what she bore. That is, God knows best the thing she gave birth to and what purposes were attached to it of firm resolutions. (Wa-ḍa'at) is read by Ibn ʿĀmir al-Shāmī and Abū Bakr, with the meaning: "Perhaps God has in it a secret (sirr) (p-251) and wisdom (ḥikmah)." According to this reading, it is part of her speech. According to the first reading, one stops at her words ﴿as a female﴾, and God's words ﴿And God knows best what she gave birth to﴾ begin as a statement from God, Exalted.

﴿And the male﴾ whom she sought ﴿is not like the female﴾ whom she was given. The definite article in both is for prior reference (ʿahd).

﴿And I have named her Mary﴾ is conjoined to ﴿I have given birth to her as a female﴾, and the two clauses in between are parenthetical (muʿtariḍatān). Hannah's naming her Mary was mentioned to her Lord because Mary, in their language, means "the worshipper." So she intended by this to draw near to Him and to ask Him to protect her, so that her actions would match her name, and that He would confirm her hope regarding her. Do you not see how she followed this with a request for His protection for her and her offspring from Satan, in His words: (And I) is Medinan, ﴿I seek refuge for her in You﴾, meaning I grant her protection, ﴿and her offspring﴾, meaning her children, ﴿from the accursed Satan﴾, meaning the one cursed.

In the hadith: "Every child that is born is touched by Satan when it is born, so it cries out loudly from the touch of Satan, except Mary and her son."

**﴿So her Lord accepted her﴾**: God accepted Mary and was pleased with her in the vow, in place of a male.

**﴿with a good acceptance﴾**: It has been said: *al-qabul* (qabūl) is the name of that by which a thing is accepted, like *al-sa'ut* (sa'ūt, a medicine administered by snuffing) is that by which something is snuffed. It means His singling her out for taking the place of a male in the vow, and no female was accepted before her in that regard. Or it means that her mother handed her over immediately after birth, before she grew up and became fit for the service (*al-sadana*, the custodianship of the sanctuary). It is related that when Hannah gave birth to Mary, she wrapped her in a cloth, carried her to the mosque, and placed her with the rabbis, the sons of Aaron, who were in Bayt al-Maqdis, like the guardians (*al-hajaba*) of the Ka'bah. She said to them: "Take this consecrated offering (*al-nadhirah*)." They competed for her, because she was the daughter of their leader and the master of their sacrifices, and the Banu Mathan were the chiefs and rabbis of the Children of Israel. Zechariah said to them: "I have more right to her, for her aunt is with me." They said: "No, until we draw lots over her." So they set off, and they were twenty-seven, to a river, and cast their pens into it. Zechariah's pen rose above the water, while their pens sank, and so he took charge of her. It has also been said that *qabul* is a verbal noun (*masdar*), with an omitted modifier, meaning: "She was accepted with a good acceptance," i.e., with a matter of good acceptance, namely the singling out.

**﴿and made her grow with a good growth﴾**: This is a metaphor for good upbringing. Ibn 'Ata' said: "Whatever tree bears fruit like 'Isa, that is the best of plants." *Nabatan* (nabātan) is a verbal noun of an unusual pattern (*'ala khilaf al-sadr*), or the sense is: "so she grew a growth."

**﴿And he made Zechariah her guardian﴾**: He accepted her, or undertook the responsibility for her affairs. *Wa-kaffalaha* (wa-kaffalahā) is read by the Kufans, meaning that God made Zechariah her guardian, that is, He made him her custodian and the guarantor of her welfare. *Zakariyya* (Zakariyyā) with a short vowel (*al-qasr*) is read by the Kufans, except Abu Bakr, throughout the Qur'an. Abu Bakr reads it here with the long vowel (*al-madd*) and the accusative case. The others read it with the long vowel and the nominative case, as in the second and third instances. Its meaning in Hebrew is "constantly mindful of God and glorifying Him."

**﴿Whenever Zechariah entered upon her in the sanctuary (mihrab)﴾**: It has been said that Zechariah built for her a *mihrab* in the mosque, that is, a chamber which she climbed to by a ladder. It has also been said that the *mihrab* is the noblest and foremost of assemblies, as though she had been placed in the most honoured position in Bayt al-Maqdis. It has also been said that their mosques were called *al-mahareb*. No one entered upon her except him alone. **﴿he found with her provision﴾**: Her provision would descend upon her from Paradise. She never suckled at a breast, and so he would find with her winter fruit in summer and summer fruit in winter.

**﴿He said: "O Mary, from where is this for you?"﴾**: From where does this provision come to you, which does not resemble the provisions of this world and comes out of its season?!

**﴿She said: "It is from God."﴾**: So do not find it strange. It has been said that she spoke while still young, just as 'Isa spoke while in the cradle.

**﴿Indeed God provides for whom He wills﴾**: This is part of Mary's speech, or part of the words of the Lord of the worlds.

**﴿without reckoning﴾**: Without measure, because of its abundance, or bestowed as a favour without being called to account and without recompense for any deed.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 38:

﴿Hunalika﴾ (there, in that place) in that place where he was sitting beside Maryam in the sanctuary (mihrab), or at that time. The words hunā (here), ḥaythu (where) and thamma (there) may be used figuratively for time. When he saw Maryam's state of honour with Allah and her rank, he desired that he should have from Him a child like the child of her mother Ḥannah in honour with Allah, even though she was barren and aged, for her mother was also like that. It has also been said: when he saw the fruit out of its season, he became aware of the permissibility of a barren woman giving birth. ﴿Da'a Zakariyya rabbahu qala Rabbi hab li min ladunka dhurriyyatan﴾ (Zakariyya called upon his Lord, saying: "My Lord, grant me from Yourself offspring") meaning a child; and dhurriyyah applies to both the singular and the plural. ﴿Tayyibah﴾ (good) meaning blessed. The feminine form is because of the word dhurriyyah. ﴿Innaka sami'u al-du'a'﴾ (Indeed, You are the Hearer of supplication), meaning the One who answers it.

﴿Then the angels called him﴾. It was said: it was Jibril (Jibreel), peace be upon him, who called him. The plural "the angels" is used because the meaning is that the call came from this category of beings, as in the saying of people, "So-and-so rides horses." (فَنادِيهُ) with the ya' and imalah (vowel inclination toward i) is read by Hamza and Ali.

﴿while he was standing in prayer in the sanctuary﴾. This is evidence that needs are sought through prayers, and that in prayers supplications are answered and needs are fulfilled. Ibn 'Ata' (Ibn ʿAṭāʾ) said: Allah does not bestow an exalted state upon a servant except through following the commands, sincerity in acts of obedience, and constancy in the prayer niches (al-maḥārīb).

(إنَّ اللهَ) with a kasra on the alif is read by al-Shami and Hamza, on the basis of an implied "saying" (idmār al-qawl), or because the call is itself a speech. The rest read it with a fatha, meaning: "that Allah ﴿gives you good news﴾." (يُبَشِّرُكَ) is read by Hamza and Ali as (يَبْشُرُكَ), and what follows it likewise. It derives from (bashshara/basara), and the light and heavy forms are two dialects.

﴿of Yahya﴾. This name is diptote (ghayr munṣarif, not taking nunation and some case endings). If it is non-Arabic (ʿajamī, foreign), which is the apparent view, then the reason is definiteness and foreignness, as with Musa and ʿIsa. If it is Arabic, then the reason is definiteness and conformity to the pattern of the verb (wazn al-fiʿl), as with Yaʿmur.

﴿confirming﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from him. ﴿a word from Allah﴾, meaning: confirming ʿIsa, believing in him. So he was the first to believe in him. ʿIsa was called "a word of Allah" because his coming into being was by the command "Be" without a father. Alternatively, it means confirming a word from Allah, believing in a book from Him.

﴿and a master﴾ is one who rules (yasūdu) his people, that is, who surpasses them in nobility. Yahya was superior to his people because he never committed a sin at all. How great a mastery that is! al-Junayd said: he is the one who gave both worlds in exchange for the Creator (al-mukawwin).

﴿and chaste﴾ is one who does not approach women although he is able to, restraining himself, that is, preventing himself from the desires.

﴿and a prophet among the righteous﴾, meaning: one who arose from the righteous, because he came from the loins of (p-٢٥٤) the prophets, or one who is among the totality of the righteous.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 40:

﴿He said: "My Lord, how can I have a boy,﴾ an expression of astonishment from the standpoint of custom, and of magnifying (Allah's) power, not of doubt,

﴿and old age has already overtaken me﴾, like their saying: "old age has overtaken him," meaning: old age has affected me and weakened me. He was ninety-nine years old, and his wife was ninety-eight,

﴿and my wife is barren﴾, she does not bear children. ﴿He said: "So it is; Allah does what He wills"﴾, of wondrous acts.

﴿He said: "My Lord, appoint for me a sign."﴾ (Madani, and Abu 'Amr read ﴿āyatan﴾), a sign (ʿalāma) by which I may know the pregnancy, so that I may receive the blessing with thankfulness when it comes. ﴿He said: "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people"﴾, i.e., you will not be able to speak to people, ﴿for three days, except by gesture (ramzan)﴾, except by signalling with a hand, or the head, or the eye, or the eyebrow. Its root meaning is movement; it is said: irtamaza, when he moved. He made the gesture an exception although it is not of the kind of speech, because when it performed the function of speech and conveyed what speech conveys, it was called speech; or the exception is disconnected (istithnaʾ munqaṭiʿ). He specified speaking to people so that it would be known that he was restraining his tongue from the ability to speak to them in particular, while his ability to speak by mentioning God remained intact; hence He said: ﴿And remember your Lord much, and glorify [Him] in the evening and the morning﴾, i.e., during the days of your inability to speak to people. This is among the manifest signs and clear proofs. He restrained his tongue from speaking to people so that he would devote the period to the remembrance of God, not occupying his tongue with anything else. It is as if, when he asked for a sign for the sake of thankfulness, it was said to him: "Your sign is that you restrain your tongue from everything except thankfulness." The best answer is that which is drawn from the question itself. Al-ʿAshiyy (the evening) is from the time of the decline of the sun to sunset, and al-Ibkar (the morning) is from the break of dawn to the time of ḍuḥā (forenoon).

"And when" is a conjunction linked to "when the wife of 'Imran said" (in the preceding verse), or the sense is: "And remember when" ﴿the angels said: "O Maryam"﴾. It is narrated that they spoke to her directly, face to face. ﴿Indeed, Allah has chosen you﴾ first, when He accepted you from your mother, raised you, and singled you out with a noble honour; ﴿and purified you﴾ from what is considered foul of (p-255) deeds; ﴿and chosen you﴾ last ﴿above the women of the worlds﴾, by granting you 'Isa without a father, which was not granted to any other woman.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 43:

﴿O Mary, be devoutly obedient to your Lord﴾: persist in obedience, or lengthen your standing in prayer. ﴿And prostrate yourself﴾. It was said: she was commanded to perform prayer by mentioning qunut (devout obedience) and prostration, because they are among the forms (hay'at) of prayer. Then it was said to her: ﴿And bow with those who bow﴾, meaning: let your prayer be with those who pray, that is, in congregation; or, join yourself to the body of those who pray, be among their number, and do not be among the number of others.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 44:**

﴿That﴾ refers to what has preceded of the story of Hanna, Zakariyya, Yahya, and Maryam. ﴿It is among the news of the unseen which We reveal to you.﴾ That is, this is among the unseen matters that you could not have known except through revelation.

﴿And you were not with them when they cast their pens﴾ *azlamahum* (their arrows), which are their lots (*qidah*) that they threw into the river as a casting of lots. Or they are the pens with which they used to write the Torah, which they chose for the drawing of lots, seeking blessing through them. ﴿Which of them would take charge of Maryam﴾ The phrase *ayyuhum* is dependent (*mutaʿallaq*) on an elided (*mahdhuf*) element indicated by *yulqun* (they cast). It is as if it were said: "They cast them, looking to see which of them would take charge of Maryam," or "in order that they might know," or "they say."

﴿And you were not with them when they disputed﴾ concerning her, each competing for the responsibility of caring for her.

﴿When the angels said﴾: that is, remember. ﴿O Mary, indeed God gives you good news of a word from Him﴾: that is, of Jesus. ﴿From Him﴾ is in a position of jarr (genitive), as a qualifier (ṣifah) of ﴿a word﴾. ﴿His name﴾ (اسمه, ismuhu) is a mubtada' (subject), and the pronoun referring to ﴿the word﴾ is masculine because the one named by it is masculine. ﴿The Messiah﴾ (المسيح, al-Masih) is its khabar (predicate). The whole sentence is in a position of jarr as a qualifier of ﴿a word﴾.

Al-Masih is an honorific title (laqab) from the noble titles, like al-Siddiq and al-Faruq. Its origin is mashiha in Hebrew, and its meaning is "the blessed," as in His saying: ﴿And He made me blessed wherever I am﴾ [Maryam: 31]. It is also said that he was called Masih because he would not pass his hand over one afflicted with a defect without him being healed, or because he would traverse the earth wandering, not settling in any one place.

﴿Jesus﴾ (عيسى, 'Isa) is a badal (appositive) of ﴿the Messiah son of Mary﴾, or a khabar of an omitted mubtada', meaning: he is the son of Mary. It is not permissible for it to be a ṣifah of ʿIsa, because his name is ʿIsa alone, and his name is not "ʿIsa son of Mary." He said ﴿son of Mary﴾ only to inform her that he would be born without a father, so he is not attributed to anyone but his mother.

﴿Honored (wajihan)﴾: possessing standing and rank ﴿in this world﴾ through prophethood and obedience, ﴿and the Hereafter﴾ through the elevation of his rank and intercession. ﴿And among those brought near﴾: He will raise him up to the heavens. His saying ﴿wajihan﴾ is a hal (circumstantial accusative) of ﴿a word﴾, because it is described (as qualified). Likewise ﴿and among those brought near﴾, meaning: and established among those brought near.

(p-256)

And [He will] speak to the people (﴿وَيُكَلِّمُ الناسَ﴾), i.e., and [he will be] one who speaks to the people, ﴿in the cradle﴾ — a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from the pronoun in yukallimu, meaning: established in the cradle. The mahd is what is prepared for the infant as his place of lying down; it is named with the verbal noun (maṣdar). ﴿And in maturity﴾ (wa-kahlan) is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon it, meaning: he will speak to the people as an infant and as a grown man. That is, he speaks to the people in these two states with the speech of the prophets, without any difference between the state of childhood and the state of maturity (kuhūla), in which the intellect is firmly established and in which prophets receive prophethood. ﴿And among the righteous﴾ is also a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl), and the sense is: he gives you glad tidings of him as one described by these attributes.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 47:

﴿She said: "My Lord, how can I have a child when no human has touched me?" He said: "Thus Allah creates what He wills. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is."﴾ That is: when He determines that something should come into being, He brings it into being without delay. However, He expressed it with His saying "Be" to inform of how swiftly things come into being by His bringing them into existence.

(48) "And He will teach him" — Madani and ʿĀṣim read it with the yāʾ (يُعَلِّمُهُ), and its position is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) conjoined to "wajīhan" (distinguished). The rest read it with the nūn (وَنُعَلِّمُهُ), on the basis that it is an independent new statement.

﴿The Book﴾: that is, writing (al-kitābah). He was the best of people in handwriting in his time. It is also said: the books of God.

﴿And wisdom﴾: the explanation of what is lawful and unlawful. Or, al-kitāb means writing by hand, and al-ḥikmah means clarification by the tongue.

﴿And the Torah and the Gospel.﴾

and a messenger to the Children of Israel, [saying]: "Indeed I have come to you with a sign from your Lord, [namely] that I create for you from clay [something] like the form of a bird, then I breathe into it and it becomes a bird by God's permission. And I heal the one born blind and the leper, and I bring the dead to life by God's permission." He repeated "by God's permission" to dispel the illusion of one who might imagine divinity in him. It is reported that he brought Sam, the son of Noah, peace be upon him, back to life while they were looking at him, and they said, "This is clear magic. Show us a sign." So he said, "O so-and-so, you ate such-and-such, and O so-and-so, such-and-such was hidden for you." This is His saying: ﴿And I inform you of what you eat and what you store up in your houses﴾. The "mā" in both places means "that which" or is a verbal (infinitive) particle.

﴿Indeed in that is a sign for you, if you are believers﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 50:

﴿And confirming what was before me of the Torah﴾ i.e., I have come to you with a sign, and I have come to you confirming (the Torah). ﴿And to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you﴾ is a reply to his words: ﴿with a sign from your Lord﴾, i.e., I have come to you with a sign from your Lord, and (I have come) to make lawful for you what Allah had forbidden them in the law of Musa, peace be upon him: fats, the flesh of camels, fish, and every animal with claws. So ʿIsa made lawful for them some of that. ﴿And I have come to you with a sign from your Lord﴾: he repeated it for emphasis. ﴿So fear Allah﴾ regarding my denial and opposition ﴿and obey me﴾ in my command.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 51:

﴿Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord﴾ — an affirmation of servanthood, and a negation of lordship (rubūbiyyah) from Himself, (p-258) unlike what the Christians claim. ﴿So worship Him﴾ apart from Me. ﴿This is a straight path﴾ that leads its follower to everlasting bliss.

﴿When Jesus perceived disbelief from them﴾ he knew from the Jews disbelief, with knowledge free of any doubt, like the knowledge of what is perceived by the senses. (He said, "Who are my helpers?") Madani (the reading of the people of Medina) has it as "Who are my helpers?" It is the plural of *nasir* (helper), like *ashab* (companions) is the plural of *sahib*, or the plural of *nasir* as *ashraf* (nobles). ﴿to Allah﴾ is connected to an omitted element and is a *hal* (circumstantial qualifier) of the *ya'* (the first-person suffix). That is: "Who are my helpers going to Allah, taking refuge in Him?"

﴿The disciples said﴾ *Hawariyyun* (the disciples, the closest followers) of a man: his chosen ones and his intimate companions.

﴿We are the helpers of Allah﴾, the supporters of His religion.

﴿We believe in Allah, and bear witness﴾, O Jesus, ﴿that we are Muslims﴾. They only sought his testimony to their submission as a confirmation of their faith, because the messengers will bear witness on the Day of Resurrection for their peoples and against them. In this is evidence that faith (*iman*) and submission (*islam*) are one and the same.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 53:

﴿Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down, and we have followed the Messenger﴾, i.e., Your Messenger, Jesus,

﴿so inscribe us among the witnesses﴾ — among the prophets who bear witness for their nations; or among those who bear witness to You of Your oneness; or among the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), because they are witnesses over the people.

"And they plotted" — that is, the disbelievers of the Children of Israel, whom Jesus perceived to be disbelieving when they wanted to kill him and crucify him. "And Allah plotted" — that is, He requited them for their plotting by raising Jesus up to the heaven and casting his likeness upon the one who sought to assassinate him, so that he was killed. It is not permissible to attribute plotting (makr) to Allah, the Exalted, except in the sense of recompense, because it is blameworthy among creatures; and on this basis (are to be understood) deception (khida') and mockery (istihza'), as stated in Sharh al-Ta'wilat. "And Allah is the best of plotters" — the most powerful of those who requite, and the most capable of punishing them in a way the one being punished does not perceive.

﴿When God said﴾ is a temporal clause (ẓarf) governed by ﴿the plotting of God﴾. ﴿O ʿĪsā, I am going to take you in death (mutawaffīka)﴾. That is, I am bringing your term to its fulfilment (mustawfin ajalaka). Its meaning is: I will protect you from the unbelievers killing you, and I will cause you to die a natural death (ḥatf anfih), not a killing at their hands.

﴿And I will raise you to Me﴾, to My heaven and the abode of My angels.

﴿And I will purify you from those who disbelieve﴾, from the evil of their company and the corruption of their fellowship. It has also been said: mutawaffīka means "one who takes you" from the earth, from the expression "I took my due from so-and-so" (tawaffaytu mālī ʿalā fulān) when you receive it in full. Or it means: I will cause you to die at your appointed time after you descend from heaven, and I will raise you now, since the particle al-wāw (the conjunction "and") does not necessitate sequence.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "ʿĪsā will descend as a caliph over my community. He will break the cross, kill the swine, remain forty years, marry, have children, and then die. How could a community perish when I am at its beginning, ʿĪsā is at its end, and al-Mahdī, from my family, is in its middle?"

Or it means: "one who causes you to die (mutawaffī nafsika)" by sleep, and "one who raises you" while you are asleep, so that no fear reaches you, and you awaken while you are in heaven, safe and brought near.

﴿And I will make those who follow you﴾, that is, the Muslims (because they follow him in the fundamentals of Islam, even though the sacred laws differ), superior to ﴿those who disbelieved﴾ in you, ﴿until the Day of Resurrection﴾, those who denied him and lied about him from among the Jews and Christians. They will make them know the proof, and in most cases they will enforce it with the sword. ﴿Then to Me is your return﴾ in the Hereafter, ﴿and I will judge between you concerning that wherein you used to differ﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 56–57:

﴿As for those who disbelieve, I will punish them with a severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have no helpers.﴾ ﴿And as for those who believe and do righteous deeds, He will give them their rewards in full, and Allah does not love the wrongdoers.﴾ The explanation of the ruling (al-hukm) is these two verses. (fa-yuwaffihim) is [the reading of] Hafs.

(p-260)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 56–57:

﴿As for those who disbelieve, I will punish them with a severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have no helpers.﴾ ﴿And as for those who believe and do righteous deeds, He will give them their rewards in full, and Allah does not love the wrongdoers.﴾ The explanation of the ruling (al-hukm) is these two verses. (fa-yuwaffihim) is [the reading of] Hafs.

(p-260)

Translation:

﴿That﴾ is a demonstrative referring to what has preceded of the account of Jesus and others, and it is the subject (mubtada'). ﴿We recite it to you﴾ is its predicate (khabar). ﴿Of the signs﴾ is a predicate following a predicate, or it is the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada' mahdhuf). ﴿And the wise reminder﴾ — the Qur'an. That is, the muhkam (firmly established, precise), or it is as if it speaks with wisdom because of the abundance of its wise judgments.

Revealed when the delegation of Najran said: "Have you seen a child without a father?" ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus before Allah is like the likeness of Adam﴾, meaning: the matter of Jesus and his strange condition is like the matter of Adam, peace be upon him. ﴿He created him from dust﴾, that is, He determined him to be a body of clay. This clause explains the state of likeness between Jesus and Adam, and it has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis). That is: He created Adam from dust, and there was neither father nor mother; so likewise was the condition of Jesus. Yet existence without a father and a mother is stranger, and a greater breach of custom, than existence without a father. Thus He likened the strange to the more strange, so that it would be more decisive against the opponent and would cut off the root of his doubt when he considers what is stranger than what he found strange.

It is related from some scholars that he was taken captive by the Romans, and they said to him: "Why do you worship Jesus?" They said: "Because he has no father." He said: "Then Adam is more worthy, for he had no parents." They said: "He used to revive the dead." He said: "Then Ezekiel (Hizqil) is more worthy, for Jesus revived four men, and Ezekiel revived eight thousand." They said: "He used to heal the blind and the leper." He said: "Then Jirjis (George) is more worthy, for he was boiled and burned, then rose up unharmed."

﴿Then He said to him: Be﴾, that is, He brought him into being as a human, ﴿and he was﴾, that is, so he was. This is a narration of a past state, and "then" (thumma) indicates the sequence of the report upon the report, not the sequence of the thing reported.

The truth is from your Lord (﴿الحَقُّ مِن رَبِّكَ﴾). It is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "it is the truth" (هو الحَقُّ). ﴿So do not be among those who doubt﴾ (﴿فَلا تَكُنْ مِنَ المُمْتَرِينَ﴾), O listener, [i.e., those] who are skeptical (الشاكِّينَ). It is also possible that the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and that it is in the manner of stirring up (التَهْيِيجِ) for the sake of increasing steadfastness (الثَباتِ), because he (ﷺ) is protected (مَعْصُومٌ) from doubting (الِامْتِراءِ).

﴿Whoever argues with you﴾ from among the Christians ﴿concerning him﴾, concerning Jesus, ﴿after the knowledge has come to you﴾ of the clear proofs that necessitate knowledge. The "mā" here is in the sense of "alladhī" (who/which). ﴿Then say: "Come"﴾ (ta'ālaw), meaning "come forward" (halummū). What is intended is coming with determination and considered opinion, as when you say, "Come, let us reflect on this matter." (p. 261) ﴿Let us call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, and ourselves and yourselves﴾, that is, each of us and you calls his sons, his women, and himself to mubahalah (mutual invocation of divine curse). ﴿Then let us earnestly invoke﴾, then let us invoke one another by saying: "May the curse of God (bahlat Allāh) be upon the liar among us and among you." Al-bahlah, with a fatha or a ḍamma, means curse. Bahalahu Allāh means "God cursed him and removed him far from His mercy." The root meaning of ibtihāl is this, and then it is used for any supplication made with earnestness, even if it is not a mutual curse.

It is related that when he (ﷺ) invited them to mubahalah, they said: "Let us wait and look into it." Then al-ʿĀqib, who was their leader in opinion, said: "By God, you have known, O assembly of Christians, that Muhammad is a prophet sent by God. No people ever invoked a curse upon a prophet and then their elder lived, nor did their young ones grow up. If you do it, you will surely perish. If you refuse except to hold to your religion, then make peace with the man and return to your lands." So they came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he had gone out embracing al-Ḥusayn, holding the hand of al-Ḥasan, with Fāṭimah walking behind him and ʿAlī behind her, and he was saying: "When I supplicate, say āmīn." Then the bishop of Najrān said: "O assembly of Christians, I see faces that, if they asked God to remove a mountain from its place, He would remove it by them. So do not invoke a curse, lest you perish and no Christian remain on the face of the earth." They said: "O Abū al-Qāsim, we have decided not to invoke a curse upon you." So the Prophet made peace with them for a thousand garments each year. Then he (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, destruction had hung over the people of Najrān. Had they invoked a curse, they would have been transformed into monkeys and swine."

He gathered the sons and women, although mubahalah is specific to him and to the one who opposes him, because that is more emphatic in indicating his confidence in his own condition and his certainty of his truthfulness, since he ventured to expose his dearest ones and the fruits of his heart to this, and did not limit himself to exposing only himself, and his confidence in the falsehood of his opponent, such that if the mubahalah were completed, his opponent would perish together with his beloved ones and dearest ones. He specified the sons and women because they are the dearest of the family and the closest to the hearts. He mentioned them before the selves to draw attention to their nearness and their rank. In this is a clear proof of the soundness of the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ), because none of those who agreed with him or opposed him has narrated that they accepted this (p. 262). ﴿Then we shall lay the curse of God upon the liars﴾ among us and among you concerning the matter of Jesus. "Nabtahil" and "naj'al" are both conjoined to "nadʿu" (let us call).

Verse 62: "Indeed, this is the true narrative" (in Arabic, ﴿إنَّ هَذا﴾ refers to what has been related to you of the account of ʿĪsā).

﴿Indeed, this is the true narrative﴾ — "huwa" here is a separator (faṣl, a pronoun of separation between the subject of inna and its predicate), or it is a mubtada' (subject), and "al-qaṣaṣ al-ḥaqq" (the true narrative) is its predicate, and the whole clause is the predicate of inna. The lām (of emphasis) is permitted to enter upon the separator, because if it is permitted to enter upon the predicate, its entry upon the separator is even more permissible, since the separator is closer to the subject than the predicate is. Its original place is to enter upon the subject.

As for "min" in ﴿And there is no god except Allah﴾, it has the same function as the construction on fatḥ in "lā ilāha illā Allāh" (there is no god but Allah) in conveying the meaning of comprehensive negation (istighrāq). The intended purpose is the refutation of the Christians in their doctrine of the Trinity.

﴿And indeed Allah, He is the All-Mighty﴾ — in exacting retribution;

﴿the All-Wise﴾ — in the governance of rulings.

﴿فَإنْ تَوَلَّوْا﴾ means "But if they turn away": they turned away and did not accept.

﴿فَإنَّ اللهَ عَلِيمٌ بِالمُفْسِدِينَ﴾ means "then indeed Allah is All-Knowing of the corrupters." This is a warning to them of the punishment mentioned in His saying: ﴿زِدْناهم عَذابًا فَوْقَ العَذابِ بِما كانُوا يُفْسِدُونَ﴾ ["We will add to their punishment torment upon torment because they used to spread corruption"] [An-Nahl: 88].

Say, "O People of the Book, come to a word that is equitable between us and you: that we worship none but Allah, and that we associate nothing with Him, and that some of us do not take others as lords besides Allah" (﴿قُلْ يا أهْلَ الكِتابِ﴾ ... ﴿تَعالَوْا إلى كَلِمَةٍ سَواءٍ بَيْنَنا وبَيْنَكُمْ﴾).

"O People of the Book" (ahl al-kitab): they are the People of the Two Books (the Jews and the Christians), or the delegation of Najran, or the Jews of Madinah.

"Come to a word" (ta'alaw ila kalimah): "Come."

"Equitable" (sawa'): that is, equal, even.

"Between us and you": the Qur'an, the Torah and the Gospel do not differ concerning it. The explanation of the "word" is His saying: ﴿Not to worship except Allah, and not to associate anything with Him, and that some of us do not take others as lords besides Allah﴾. That is, "Come to it, so that we do not say, 'Uzayr is the son of Allah,' nor 'the Messiah is the son of Allah,' because each of them is a human being like us. And that we do not obey our rabbis in what they have innovated of prohibition and permission without returning to what Allah has legislated."

From 'Adi ibn Hatim: "We did not worship them, O Messenger of Allah." He (ﷺ) said: "Did they not make lawful for you and make unlawful, and you followed their word?" He said: "Yes." He said: "That is it."

﴿Then if they turn away﴾ from the monotheism, ﴿then say: "Bear witness that we are Muslims"﴾. That is: the proof has been established against you, so it is obligatory upon you to acknowledge and submit that we are Muslims, not you. This is like the victor saying to the vanquished in a dispute or a contest: "Acknowledge that I am the victor, and surrender the victory to me."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 65:

﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you argue about Abraham, when the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him? Do you not then reason?﴾ Each group among the Jews and the Christians claimed that Abraham was one of them, and they disputed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers concerning him. So it was said: Judaism only came into being after the revelation of the Torah, and Christianity after the revelation of the Gospel. Between Abraham and Moses there were a thousand years, and between him and Jesus there were two thousand. How, then, could Abraham be upon a religion that did not come into existence until long after his time? ﴿Do you not then reason?﴾ So that you would not argue with such impossible argumentation.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 66:

﴿Ha, you are these people﴾: "Ha" is for alerting (tanbih), "antum" is the subject (mubtada'), and "ha'ulaa'" is its predicate (khabar).

﴿You argued﴾: this is a resumed clause (jumla mustaʼnafa) explaining the first clause. The meaning is: you are these foolish persons, and the proof of your foolishness and the smallness of your intellects is that you argued ﴿about what you have knowledge of﴾ from what the Torah and the Gospel speak of, ﴿so why do you argue about what you have no knowledge of﴾, and there is no mention of it in your two scriptures, concerning the religion of Ibrahim. It has also been said: "ha'ulaa'" is in the sense of "alladhina" (those who), and "hajajtum" is its relative clause (sila). The reading of "ha antum" with the madd and without hamza wherever it occurs is that of Madani and Abu 'Amr.

﴿And Allah knows﴾ the knowledge of what you argue about, ﴿and you do not know﴾, and you are ignorant of it. Then He informed them that He is free of their religion, so He said:

(p-264) ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was an upright monotheist (ḥanīf), a Muslim, and he was not one of the polytheists.﴾ It is as if He intended by "the polytheists" the Jews and the Christians, because of their associating with Him 'Uzayr (Ezra) and the Messiah. Or the meaning is: he was not of the polytheists, just as he was not of them (the Jews and the Christians).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 68:
