﴿Indeed, the closest of people to Abraham﴾ means: indeed, the ones most specially connected to him and nearest to him, from al-wali (the close relation), which is nearness,

﴿are those who followed him﴾ in his time and after him, ﴿and this Prophet﴾ specifically, singled out for mention because of his particular excellence, and the intended one is Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿and those who believe﴾ from his community, ﴿and Allah is the Guardian (wali) of the believers﴾, meaning their Helper.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 69:

﴿A group of the People of the Book wish they could lead you astray﴾. They are the Jews, who invited Hudhayfah, ʿAmmar and Muʿadh to Judaism.

﴿But they lead astray none except themselves﴾. The burden of misguidance returns only upon them, because their punishment is multiplied for their own misguidance and their leading others astray.

﴿And they do not perceive﴾ that.

O People of the Book, why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah (﴿يا أهْلَ الكِتابِ لِمَ تَكْفُرُونَ بِآياتِ اللهِ﴾), namely the Torah and the Gospel? Their disbelief in them is that they do not believe in what they declare of the truth of the Prophethood of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and other matters.

﴿وَأنْتُمْ تَشْهَدُونَ﴾ (while you bear witness): you acknowledge that they are the signs of Allah; or, you disbelieve in the Qur'an and the proofs of the Messenger's prophethood while you bear witness to his description in the two Books; or, you disbelieve in all the signs of Allah while you know that they are true.

﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you mix the truth with falsehood﴾: you mix belief in Musa and Isa with disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ),

﴿and conceal the truth﴾: the description of Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿while you know﴾ that it is true.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 72:

﴿And a group among the People of the Book said﴾ among themselves, ﴿"Believe in what has been revealed to those who believe" (i.e., the Qur'an)﴾,

﴿at the beginning of the day﴾ is an adverbial expression (zarf), meaning its first part. That is: show belief in what has been revealed to the Muslims at the beginning of the day,

﴿and reject it at its end﴾, meaning: and reject it at its end,

﴿so that they may return﴾, meaning: so that perhaps the Muslims will say, "They would not have turned back, being People of the Book and knowledge, except for a matter that has become clear to them," and so they will return along with your returning.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 73:**

﴿And do not believe except in one who follows your religion. Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God.﴾ "Do not believe" (wa-la tu'minu) is connected to his saying: ﴿that anyone be given the like of what you were given﴾, and what lies between them is an *i'tiraḍ* (a parenthetical interjection). The meaning is: Do not display your belief that anyone be given the like of what you were given, except to the people of your religion, and not to others. They intended: Keep secret your affirmation that the Muslims have been given from the Books of God the like of what you have been given, and do not divulge it except to your own partisans alone, not to the Muslims, lest it increase them in steadfastness, and not to the polytheists, lest it invite them to Islam. ﴿Or that they argue with you before your Lord﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) with "that he be given" (an yu'tā), and the pronoun in "yuḥājjūkum" (they argue with you) refers to "anyone" (aḥad), because it carries the sense of the plural. The meaning is: Do not believe, for anyone other than your own followers, that the Muslims will argue against you on the Day of Resurrection with the truth, and overcome you before God with proof. The sense of the interjection is that guidance is the guidance of God: whomever He wills, He guides, so that he accepts Islam or remains steadfast in Islam, and that happens, and your scheming, your stratagems, and your repelling (*dhabb*) of your affirmation away from the Muslims and the polytheists will not avail. Likewise His saying: ﴿Say: Indeed, bounty is in the hand of God; He gives it to whomever He wills﴾ means guidance and success. Or the speech is complete at His saying: ﴿except in one who follows your religion﴾, meaning: ﴿And do not believe﴾ this apparent belief, which is their belief at the beginning of the day, ﴿except in one who follows your religion﴾, except for those among you who were followers of your religion and who had embraced Islam, because their return (to you) was more hopeful in their estimation than the return of others. The meaning of His saying ﴿that he be given﴾ is: because anyone be given ﴿the like of what you were given﴾. You said that and plotted it, and not for any other reason. That is: the envy and insolence that are in you ﴿that anyone be given the like of what you were given﴾ of the knowledge and the Book has prompted you to say what you said. This is indicated by the recitation of Ibn Kathir (*ān*) with a long vowel and as an interrogative, meaning: Is it because anyone is given the like of what you were given of the Book that you envy them? His saying ﴿or that they argue with you﴾ according to this has the meaning: You have plotted what you plotted because anyone is given the like of what you were given, or because of what is connected to it, namely, your disbelief in it, of their arguing with you before your Lord. ﴿And God is Vast﴾, that is, vast in mercy, ﴿Knowing﴾ of what is best.

Translation:

﴿He singles out for His mercy﴾ with prophethood, or with Islam, ﴿whomever He wills. And God is the Possessor of Great Bounty﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 75:

﴿Among the People of the Book is one who, if you entrust him with a qintar, will return it to you.﴾ This is 'Abdullah ibn Salam. A man from Quraysh entrusted him with a thousand and two hundred ounces of gold, and he returned it to him. ﴿And among them is one who, if you entrust him with a dinar, will not return it to you.﴾ This is Finhas ibn 'Azura'. A man from Quraysh entrusted him with a dinar, and he denied it and betrayed him. It was also said: the trustworthy ones regarding large amounts are the Christians, because trustworthiness predominates among them, and the treacherous ones regarding small amounts are the Jews, because treachery predominates among them.

﴿Except while you stand over him.﴾ That is, except for the duration of your remaining over him, O holder of the right, standing at his head and persisting with him. (يؤده) and (لا يؤده) with a kasra on the ha' and with the vowel lengthened (mushba'a) are read by Makki, Shami, Nafi', 'Ali and Hafs. Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of others, read it with ikhtilas (a brief, abbreviated pronunciation of the vowel) and with the ha' sukun.

﴿That﴾ refers to the abandonment of repayment that is indicated by (لا يؤده).

﴿Because they say: "There is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered."﴾ That is, their abandonment of the rights is due to their saying: ﴿"There is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered"﴾, meaning: no sin or reproach attaches to us concerning the unlettered, by whom they mean those who are not of the People of the Book, and what we did to them of withholding their wealth and harming them, because they are not upon our religion. They used to consider it lawful to wrong whoever opposed them, and they used to say: "No sanctity has been ordained for them in our Book." It was also said: the Jews dealt with men of Quraysh, and when they embraced Islam, the Jews demanded payment from them, saying: "You have no right over us since you have abandoned your religion," and they claimed that they had found this in their book (p-267). ﴿And they speak falsehood against God﴾ by claiming that this is in their book, ﴿while they know﴾ that they are lying.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 76:

﴿Balā﴾ (Yes, indeed) is an affirmation of what they denied, namely the existence of a way (sabil, here meaning a path of blame or liability) against them regarding the Gentiles (al-ummiyyin). That is: yes, there is a way against them concerning them. His saying, ﴿Whoever fulfils his covenant and fears God﴾, is a resumed sentence (jumla mustanaffa), confirming the sentence which balā has taken the place of. The pronoun in ﴿his covenant﴾ refers to God Most High; that is: whoever fulfils the covenant of God and fears Him. ﴿Then God loves the God-fearing﴾, that is: He loves them. He placed the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun, and the generality of "the God-fearing" stands in the place of the pronoun returning from the predicate to "whoever." This includes faith and other righteous deeds, and what is obligatory to guard against of disbelief and evil deeds. It is said: it was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and the like of him among the Muslims of the People of the Book. It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to "whoever fulfils," that is: whoever fulfils what he covenanted with God regarding, and fears God by abstaining from betrayal and treachery, then God loves him.

It was revealed concerning those who distorted the Torah and altered its description of him (ﷺ) among the Jews, and who took bribes for that: ﴿Indeed, those who sell﴾ exchange ﴿the covenant of Allah﴾ — that which they had covenanted with Him concerning belief in the Messenger confirming what is with them ﴿and their oaths﴾ — and what they swore by, such as their saying: "By Allah, we will surely believe in him and surely support him" ﴿for a small price﴾ — the enjoyments of this world, such as leadership, bribery and the like. His saying ﴿the covenant of Allah﴾ strengthens the reading that the pronoun in "bi-ahdihi" (in His covenant) refers to Allah. ﴿Those will have no portion (khalaq) in the Hereafter﴾ — i.e., no share. ﴿Allah will not speak to them﴾ in a way that would gladden them, ﴿nor look at them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ with a look of mercy, ﴿nor purify them﴾ — nor praise them. ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾ — afflicting.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 78:

﴿And indeed among them﴾ [among the People of the Book] ﴿is surely a group﴾ [who are] Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Malik ibn al-Sayf, Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and others.

﴿who distort their tongues with the Book﴾ they twist them, by reciting it, from the correct to the altered. Al-layy (twisting, ليّ) is the act of turning, which is diversion. The intent is their distortion, such as the verse of stoning, the description of Muhammad (ﷺ), and similar things.

﴿so that you may think it﴾ The pronoun refers to what is indicated by ﴿who distort their tongues with the Book﴾, which is the altered text. It is also permissible that it means they bend their tongues with something resembling the Book, so that you would suppose that resemblance to be ﴿from the Book﴾, i.e., the Torah.

﴿and it is not from the Book﴾ and it is not from the Torah. ﴿And they say, it is from Allah﴾ This is an emphasis of His statement ﴿and it is not from the Book﴾, and an added censure of them.

﴿And it is not from Allah, and they speak lies against Allah while they know﴾ that they are liars.

That it should not be for a human that Allah give him the Book, the judgment (ḥukm), the wisdom (ḥikmah), and prophethood, and then he say to the people, "Be worshippers of me rather than of Allah," but rather, "Be rabbāniyyīn" (those devoted to the Lord). This is a refutation of whoever believes in the worship of Jesus, peace be upon him.

It is said: A man said, "O Messenger of Allah, we greet you as some of us greet one another. Shall we not prostrate to you?" He said, "It is not fitting that prostration be made to anyone other than Allah. But honour your Prophet, and recognise the rights of those who deserve them."

"The judgment" (al-ḥukm) means the wisdom (al-ḥikmah), which is the Sunnah (the Prophetic way and tradition), or decisive judgment (faṣl al-qaḍāʾ). "And prophethood" is coordinated (ʿaṭf) on "yu'tiyahu." "Then he would say" is coordinated on "yu'tiyahu." "To the people, 'Be worshippers of me rather than of Allah.'" "But rather, he says, 'Be rabbāniyyīn.'"

The rabbānī (rabbāniyy, pl. rabbāniyyīn) is a noun ascribed to Rabb (the Lord), with the addition of the alif and nūn, and it refers to one who holds very firmly to the religion of Allah and to obedience to Him. When Ibn ʿAbbās died, Ibn al-Ḥanafiyyah said, "The rabbānī of this community has died." It is reported from al-Ḥasan that "rabbāniyyīn" means scholarly jurists (ʿulamāʾ fuqahāʾ). It is also said: teachers who teach (ʿulamāʾ muʿallimīn). They said: the rabbānī is the learned person who acts upon his knowledge.

"Because you used to teach the Book" (bi-mā kuntum tuʿallimūna al-kitāb). The Kufan and Syrian readers read it with the tashdīd removed (tukhfīf), so it is "tuʿallimūna" as a verb of teaching, meaning "others than you." "And because you used to study" (wa-bi-mā kuntum tadrusūn), i.e., you used to recite (taqraʾūn). The meaning is: by reason of your being learned, and by reason of your studying knowledge, rabbāniyyah, which is the strength of holding fast to obedience to Allah, was caused by knowledge and study. This is sufficient as evidence of the failure of the striving of one who exhausted himself and wore out his spirit in gathering knowledge, and then did not make it a means to action. He is like one who planted a beautiful tree which delights him with its appearance but does not benefit him with its fruit.

It is also said that the meaning of "tadrusūn" is "you teach it to the people," like His saying, ﴿that you recite it to the people﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 17:106]. So its meaning is the meaning of "tadrusūn" from tadrīs (teaching), like the reading of Ibn Jubayr.

(p-269)

**﴿And he would not command you﴾** is read in the accusative (*naṣb*), coordinated (*ʿaṭf*, conjunction of a term to a preceding one) with **﴿then say﴾**. Its interpretation is that you make the particle **"lā"** (*mazīda*, extra, non-semantic) in order to emphasise the sense of negation in His words **﴿It is not for a human﴾**. The meaning is: it is not for a human that God should give him prophecy and appoint him to call people to the exclusive worship of God and the abandonment of rivals, and then command people to become His servants, and command you **﴿to take the angels and the prophets as lords﴾**. This is like saying: "It is not for Zayd that I should honour him, and then he should humiliate me, and not show me respect."

The reading with the nominative (*rafʿ*) is by the **Ḥijāzī** (the reader of the Hijaz), Abū ʿAmr, and ʿAlī, on the basis of beginning a new sentence. The hamza in **﴿Would he command you to disbelief?﴾** is interrogative of denial (*li-l-inkār*). The pronoun in **"lā yaʾmurukum"** and **"a-yaʾmurukum"** refers to a human, or to God. His words **﴿after you have submitted﴾** indicate that those addressed were Muslims, and they are the ones who asked Him for permission to prostrate to him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 81:

﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets﴾ It is on its apparent meaning, that the covenant was taken from the prophets concerning this. Or the intended meaning is: the covenant of the sons of the prophets, who are the Children of Israel, with an elision of the mudaf (the omitted genitive-governed noun). The lam in ﴿that which I have given you of Scripture and wisdom﴾ is the lam of tawti'ah (the preparatory lam, introducing the oath), because the taking of a covenant carries the sense of making someone swear. The lam in ﴿you shall surely believe in him﴾ is the lam of the answer to the oath. The "ma" may be understood as containing the meaning of a conditional particle, in which case ﴿you shall surely believe in him﴾ serves as the answer to both the oath and the condition together; or it may be a relative pronoun, with the meaning: "that which I have given you, you shall surely believe in it."

﴿Then there came to you﴾ is coordinated with the relative clause, and the returning pronoun referring from it back to "ma" is omitted; the sense is: "Then there came to you with it ﴿a messenger confirming what is with you﴾, that is, confirming the Scripture that is with you,

﴿you shall surely believe in him﴾, in the Messenger, ﴿and you shall surely help him﴾, that is, the Messenger, who is Muhammad (ﷺ). (lamma ataytukum) — Hamzah (recited it). The "ma" is in the sense of "alladhi" (which), or it is a verbal-noun ma (masdariyyah), meaning: because of my giving you some of the Scripture (p-270) and wisdom, then because of the coming of a messenger confirming what is with you. The lam is for causation, meaning: Allah took their covenant that you shall surely believe in the Messenger and surely help him, for the sake of my having given you wisdom, and that the Messenger whom I command you to believe in and help is in agreement with you, not opposing you. (ataynakum) — Madani (recited it).

﴿He said﴾, that is, Allah: ﴿Do you acknowledge and take on this My burden?﴾ That is, do you accept My covenant. It is called isr (burden) because it is something that is bound and tied, that is, fastened and secured.

﴿They said: We acknowledge it. He said: Then bear witness﴾, so let some of you bear witness against others to the acknowledgment ﴿and I am with you among the witnesses﴾, I am with you in that, from your acknowledgment and your mutual witnessing. This is an emphasis upon them and a warning against retraction once they know that Allah and some of them bear witness against others. It is said that Allah said to the angels: "Bear witness."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 3, verse 82:

﴿Then whoever turns away after that﴾: after the covenant and the solemn affirmation, and breaks the pledge after having accepted it, and turns away from believing in the Prophet who is to come,

﴿those are the defiantly disobedient ones﴾: the rebellious among the disbelievers.

Al-Nasafi, *Madarik al-Tanzil*, on Surah 3, verse 83:

﴿Do they seek other than the religion of Allah?﴾ The interrogative hamza (*hamzat al-inkar*, the hamza of denial) entered upon the conjunctive *fa'* (*al-fa' al-'atifa*), joining one sentence to another. The meaning is: "Then those are the defiant ones (*al-fasiqun*). Do they seek other than the religion of Allah?" Then the hamza was placed between the two. It is also permissible to take it as coordinated with an implied element, whose estimate is: "Will they turn away, and seek other than the religion of Allah?" The object, which is "other than the religion of Allah," was placed before its verb, because it is more important, insofar as the denial that the hamza expresses is directed at that which is worshipped falsely. ﴿They seek, while to Him has submitted whoever is in the heavens﴾, the angels, ﴿and the earth﴾, humankind and the jinn, ﴿willingly﴾, by reflecting on the proofs and being fair to themselves, ﴿and unwillingly﴾, by the sword, or by witnessing the punishment, such as the lifting of the mountain over the Children of Israel, the drowning that overtook Pharaoh, and being on the brink of death. ﴿Then when they saw Our might, they said: "We believe in Allah alone"﴾ [Ghafir: 84]. *Ta'a* (willingly) and *karhan* (unwillingly) are in the accusative as circumstantial qualifiers (*'ala al-hal*), meaning: "obeying and compelled." ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾, so that He will recompense you for your deeds.

(*Yabghun*) and (*yurja'un*) with the *ya'* in both, Hafs; and with the *ta'* in the second and with the *jim* vowelled with a *fatha*, Abu 'Amr, because the ones who seek are those who turn away, while the ones who will be returned are all people. And with the *ta'* in both and the *jim* vowelled with a *fatha*, others than these two.

(p. 271)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 84:

﴿Say: "We believe in God and in what has been sent down to us.﴾ He (the Prophet ﷺ) was commanded to report on himself and on those with him concerning faith. Therefore the pronoun in "Say" is singular, while in "We believe" it is plural. Or, he was commanded to speak about himself in the way kings speak, out of honour from God for the rank of His Prophet. Here "unzila" (was sent down) is construed with the preposition ʿalā (on), denoting elevation, whereas in al-Baqara it is construed with ilā (to), denoting arrival, because both meanings are present: revelation descends from above and reaches the Messenger. So in one place one of the two meanings is given, and in another place the other. The author of al-Lubab said: The address in al-Baqara is to the community, due to His saying "Say" (plural, qūlū), so only "ilā" was appropriate, since the scriptures reach the prophets and their communities all together. Here He said "Say" (qul), which is an address to the Prophet ﷺ alone, not to his community, so the fitting preposition was "ʿalā", since the scriptures were sent down upon him, and the community has no share in it. There is room for consideration in this, because of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Believe in what has been sent down upon those who believed﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 72], and ﴿and what was sent down upon Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes﴾, the sons of Jacob, among whom there were prophets.

﴿And what was given to Moses, Jesus and the prophets﴾. In al-Baqara He repeated ﴿and what was given﴾, but did not repeat it here, because the mention of giving had already preceded, where He said: ﴿what I have given you﴾ (Āl ʿImrān: 81). ﴿From their Lord﴾, that is, from the presence of their Lord.

﴿We make no distinction between any of them﴾ in faith, as the Jews and Christians did, ﴿and to Him we are submitting﴾, that is, monotheists, sincerely dedicating ourselves to Him, not associating any partner with Him in our worship.

[Qur'an 3:85] "And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion" — meaning: monotheism (tawhid) and submitting one's face to God; or other than the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ). "As a religion" is a tamyiz (specification). "It will never be accepted from him, and he will be, in the Hereafter, among the losers" — i.e., among those who have fallen into loss.

It was revealed concerning a group who embraced Islam, then apostatized from Islam and joined (lahiqu) Makkah: ﴿How will Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their belief﴾. The waw in ﴿while they had testified that the Messenger is true﴾ is for the circumstantial state (li-l-hal), with a verb implied (qad), meaning: they disbelieved while they had testified that the Messenger, i.e., Muhammad, is true. Or it is for conjunction (li-l-'atf) upon what is in ﴿their belief﴾ of the meaning of a verb, because its meaning is: after they had believed. ﴿And clear proofs had come to them﴾, i.e., the evidences such as the Qur'an and all the other miracles. ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾, i.e., as long as they choose disbelief, or He does not guide them to the path of Paradise if they die as disbelievers.

﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ ("those," أُولَئِكَ) is a *mubtada'* (subject of a nominal sentence). ﴿جَزاؤُهُمْ﴾ ("their recompense," جَزاؤُهُمْ) is a second *mubtada'*, whose *khabar* (predicate, خَبَرُهُ) is ﴿أنَّ عَلَيْهِمْ لَعْنَةَ اللهِ﴾ ("that upon them is the curse of Allah"). Together, the second *mubtada'* and its *khabar* form the *khabar* of ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾. Alternatively, ﴿جَزاؤُهُمْ﴾ is a *badal al-ishtimal* (inclusive apposition, بَدَلُ الِاشْتِمالِ) of ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾, and ﴿أنَّ عَلَيْهِمْ لَعْنَةَ اللهِ﴾ is its *khabar*. The verse concludes with ﴿والمَلائِكَةِ والناسِ أجْمَعِينَ﴾ ("and of the angels and of mankind, all together").

﴿Abiding therein﴾ is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier, a grammatical state) of the *hā'* and *mīm* in "عَلَيْهِمْ" (upon them). ﴿Therein﴾ refers to the curse. ﴿The punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 89:

﴿Except those who repent after that﴾ — of the great disbelief and the apostasy,

﴿and make amends﴾ — for what they had corrupted, or enter into righteousness, ﴿for indeed Allah is Forgiving﴾ of their disbelief,

﴿Merciful﴾ toward them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 90:

It was revealed concerning the Jews: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ in Isa (ʿIsa) and the Injil (Gospel),

﴿after their belief﴾ in Musa (Musa) and the Tawrah (Torah), ﴿then increase in disbelief﴾ in Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an. Or, ﴿disbelieve﴾ in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) after they had been believers in him before his mission (mabʿath). ﴿Then increase in disbelief﴾ through their persistence in that and their attacking him at all times. Or it was revealed concerning those who apostatized and joined Makkah, and their increase in disbelief was that they said: "We will stay in Makkah and wait for Muhammad to be struck by the vicissitudes of fate (rayb al-manun)." ﴿Their repentance will never be accepted﴾, that is, their belief at the time of the punishment (al-basʾ), because they only repent at the moment of death. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then their belief did not benefit them when they saw Our punishment﴾ [Ghafir: 85]. ﴿And those are the astray.﴾

(p-273)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 91:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers — never will be accepted from any of them the earth filled with gold﴾ The fa' (the fa' of "fa-lan yuqbala," i.e. "so never will be accepted") indicates that the statement is constructed as a conditional and a consequent (shart wa jaza'), and that the cause of the impossibility of accepting the ransom is death upon disbelief. Omitting the fa' in what preceded indicates that the statement is a subject and predicate (mubtada' wa khabar), and there is no evidence in it for causation. ﴿Dhahaban﴾ is a tamyiz (specification). ﴿Even if he were to ransom himself with it﴾ means: ﴿never will be accepted from any of them﴾ a ransom, even if he ransomed himself with the earth filled with gold. The Prophet ﷺ said: "It will be said to the disbeliever on the Day of Resurrection: If you had the earth filled with gold, would you ransom yourself with it? He will say: Yes. It will be said to him: You were asked for something easier than that." It has been said: the waw is for emphasizing the negation.

﴿Those — for them is a painful punishment﴾ meaning painful (mu'lim). ﴿And they will have no helpers﴾ meaning those who assist, repelling the punishment.

﴿You will never attain righteousness﴾: you will not reach the reality of righteousness; or, you will not become righteous (abrar); or, you will not attain the righteousness of God, which is His reward.

﴿Until you spend from what you love﴾: until your spending is from the wealth you love and prefer. From al-Hasan: everyone who gives charity seeking the face of God, with something that he loves, even if it is a single date, is included in this verse. Al-Wasiti said: One reaches righteousness by spending some of what one loves, and reaches the Lord by renouncing both worlds. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: "You will never attain My righteousness through your righteousness, except through your righteousness toward your brothers." The summary is that there is no reaching the sought-after except by giving up the beloved. From Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz: he used to buy bales of sugar and give them in charity. It was said to him: Why do you not give charity with their price? He said: Because sugar is more beloved to me, so I wished to spend from what I love.

﴿And whatever you spend, indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾: that is, He is Knowing of everything you spend, and He will reward you according to it.

The first "min" (from) is partitive (li-l-tab'id, indicating a part), in accordance with the recitation (qira'a, a variant reading) of Abdullah: "until you spend part of what you love." The second "min" is explicative (li-l-tabyin, specifying the kind): whatever kind the spending is, whether good that you love, or bad that you dislike.

(p-274)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 93:

When "the Jews said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'You claim that you follow the religion of Ibrahim, yet you eat the flesh of camels and drink their milk.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'That was permissible for Ibrahim, so we make it permissible.' The Jews said: 'It has never ceased to be forbidden in the religion of Ibrahim and Nuh, peace be upon them both.' So it was revealed as a refutation of them: ﴿All food﴾" — meaning: the foods about which there is dispute, for some of them were already forbidden before that, such as carrion and blood,

﴿was lawful to the Children of Israel﴾, that is, lawful. It is a verbal noun (masdar), from "halla al-shay'" (the thing became lawful), *hillan*, and for this reason it is used uniformly for the masculine and feminine, the singular and the plural. God Most High said: ﴿They are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for them﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10], ﴿except what Israel forbade﴾, that is, Ya'qub (Jacob),

﴿upon himself before the Torah was sent down﴾. It is read with the lightened form (tatkhif) by Makki and Basri, and it refers to the flesh of camels and their milk, which were the most beloved foods to him. The meaning is: all foods had always been lawful to the Children of Israel before the Torah was sent down, except what Israel forbade upon himself. When the Torah was sent down to Musa, He forbade them in it the flesh of camels and their milk, due to Israel's prohibition of that upon himself. ﴿Say: Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful﴾. He was commanded to argue with them using their own Book, and to confound them with what it plainly states: that the prohibition of what was forbidden to them was a new prohibition, caused by their wrongdoing and transgression, not an ancient prohibition as they claim. So they did not dare to bring out the Torah, and they were confounded. In this there is a clear proof of the truthfulness of the Prophet ﷺ, and of the permissibility of abrogation (naskh), which they deny.

"Whoever fabricates a lie against Allah" — by claiming that this (i.e., the prohibited foods) was forbidden in the religion of Abraham and Noah, peace be upon them — "after that" — after the decisive proof had been established against them — "those are the wrongdoers" — the obstinate ones who do not deal justly with themselves and pay no heed to the clear proofs.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 95:

﴿Say: "Allah has spoken the truth"﴾ in His report that it was not forbidden. Therein is an implicit reproach of their lying, i.e., it is established that Allah the Exalted is truthful in what He has revealed, and you are the liars. ﴿Then follow the religion of Abraham﴾, and it is the religion of Islam upon which Muhammad (ﷺ) and those who believed with him are, so that you may be freed from Judaism (Yahudiyya), which has entangled you in the corruption of your religion and your worldly affairs, since it has compelled you to distort the Book of Allah to suit your purposes, and has obliged you to forbid the good things that Allah made lawful for Abraham and for those who followed him.

﴿Hanifan﴾ is a circumstantial state (hal) of Abraham, i.e., inclining away from the false religions.

﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾

The commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 96:

When the Jews said to the Muslims, "Our qibla (direction of prayer) is before your qibla," the verse came down: ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind﴾. The one who established it is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The meaning of Allah's establishing a House for mankind is that He made it a place of worship (mutaʿabbad) for them. It is as if He said: "Indeed, the first place of worship for mankind is the Kaʿba." In a hadith: "The Masjid al-Haram was established forty years before Bayt al-Maqdis." It has been said: the first to build it was Ibrahim. It has been said: it is the first House to be pilgrimed after the Flood. It has been said: it is the first house to appear upon the surface of the water at the creation of the heavens and the earth. It has been said: it is the first house that Adam, peace be upon him, built on earth. His saying ﴿established for mankind﴾ is in a position of genitive as an attribute of "a House," and the predicate is ﴿that which is at Bakka﴾, meaning: the House that is at Bakka. Bakka is a proper name for the Sacred City, and Makka and Bakka are two dialect forms for it. It has also been said: Makka is the city and Bakka is the site of the Masjid. It has also been said: its derivation is from bakka, meaning "he crowded him," due to the crowding of people in it; or because it "breaks" (tabukk) the necks of tyrants, i.e., it crushes them; no tyrant intended it except that Allah broke him.

﴿Blessed﴾: abundant in good, because of the reward and the expiation of sins that accrue to the pilgrims and the performers of umrah. ﴿And a guidance for the worlds﴾, because it is their qibla and place of worship. "Blessed" and "a guidance" are two circumstantial accusatives (hal) referring to the pronoun in "established."

﴿Therein are clear signs﴾: manifest markers that are not confused by anyone. ﴿The station of Ibrahim﴾ is an *'atf al-bayan* (apposition) to His words ﴿clear signs﴾. It is sound to explain a plural by a singular, because he alone is equivalent to many signs, given how evident his status is and how strongly he demonstrates the power of Allah the Exalted and the prophethood of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). This is seen in the impression of his foot on solid rock. Alternatively, it is because it contains several signs: the imprint of the foot on the hard rock is one sign; his sinking into it up to the ankles is another; the softening of part of the rock but not the rest is another; and his being preserved from the fate of the other prophets' signs (peace be upon them) is a sign specific to Ibrahim. Moreover, ﴿whoever enters it is safe﴾ is, in meaning, an apposition to "signs," even though it is an independent nominal sentence or a conditional sentence. This is because it indicates the safety of whoever enters it. It is as if it were said: "Therein are clear signs: the station of Ibrahim and the safety of whoever enters it." The two together are equivalent to the plural. It is also permissible to mention these two signs and omit mention of others, indicating that the signs are numerous and that there are many besides them, such as the crushing of the stones despite the number of those who throw them, and the prevention of birds from alighting upon it, and other things. Similar to this in omitting mention is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Three things of your world have been made dear to me: perfume, women, and the coolness of my eye in prayer." Here, "the coolness of my eye" is not one of the three; rather, it is the beginning of a new statement, because it is not of this world. The third item is left unstated, and it seems that the Prophet (ﷺ) omitted mention of the third as an indication that it was not part of his character to mention anything of this world, so he mentioned something that belongs to the religion.

It has been said regarding the cause of this trace that when the building of the Ka'bah was raised and Ibrahim (peace be upon him) became too weak to lift the stones, he stood on this stone, and his feet sank into it. It has also been said that he came as a visitor from Syria to Makkah, and Isma'il's wife (peace be upon him) said to him: "Dismount until you wash your head." He did not dismount, so she brought him this stone and placed it under his right side, and he placed his foot on it until she had washed the right side of his head. Then she moved it to his left side until she washed the other side, and so the traces of his two feet remained on it.

﴿Whoever enters it is safe﴾: the safety of whoever enters it is due to the supplication of Ibrahim (peace be upon him): ﴿My Lord, make this city secure﴾ [Ibrahim: 35]. A man who committed every crime and then sought refuge in the Haram would not be pursued. It is reported from 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him): "If I found the killer of al-Khattab within it, I would not touch him until he left it." Whoever deserves execution outside the sacred area, whether for retaliation, apostasy, or fornication, and then takes refuge in the Haram, will not be harmed, except that he will not be sheltered, fed, given drink, or sold to until he is compelled to leave. It has also been said that "safe" means safe from the Fire, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever dies in one of the two sanctuaries will be raised on the Day of Resurrection safe from the Fire." And from him (ﷺ): "Al-Hajun and al-Baqi' will be taken by their edges and scattered into Paradise; they are the cemeteries of Makkah and Madinah." And from him (ﷺ): "Whoever endures the heat of Makkah for an hour of the day, Hell will be removed from him a distance of two hundred years' journey."

﴿And for Allah is a pilgrimage to the House upon mankind﴾: that is, the obligation of Hajj has become established for them. The word *hajj* (in "hajj al-bayt") is read with a kasrah by the Kufans except Abu Bakr; it is a noun, and with a fatha it is a verbal noun. It has also been said that both are two dialects for the verbal noun of *hajja*. "Man" is in the genitive position, and it is a partial apposition (*badal al-ba'd min al-kull*) for ﴿mankind﴾. ﴿Who is able to make his way thereto﴾: the Prophet (ﷺ) explained "way" as provision and a mount. The pronoun in "ilayhi" refers to the House or to the Hajj; anything one can reach to attain a thing is a way to it. When the words of the Exalted were revealed, ﴿And for Allah is a pilgrimage to the House upon mankind﴾, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gathered the people of all religions, addressed them, and said: "Indeed Allah the Exalted has prescribed for you the Hajj, so perform it." One single community believed in it, namely the Muslims, while five communities rejected it, saying: "We do not believe in it, we do not pray toward it, and we do not perform it." So there was revealed: ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾, meaning: whoever denies the obligation of Hajj. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and 'Ata'. It is also permissible that it be from *kufran* (ingratitude), meaning: whoever does not give thanks for the blessings I have bestowed upon him, such as health of body and abundance of provision, and does not perform Hajj. ﴿Indeed, Allah is free from need of the worlds﴾: He is independent of them and of their obedience.

In this verse there are several kinds of emphasis and intensification. Among them: the use of the preposition *lam* (for) and *'ala* (upon), meaning that it is a binding right due to Allah upon the necks of people. Among them: the use of substitution (*ibdal*), which contains an indication of the intended meaning, its repetition, and because clarifying after vagueness and detailing after generality presents it in two different forms. Among them: his saying ﴿whoever disbelieves﴾ in place of "whoever does not perform Hajj," as a severe warning against those who abandon Hajj. Among them: the mention of independence (*istighna'*), which is evidence of abhorrence and wrath. Among them: his saying ﴿from the worlds﴾ although he did not say "from it"; and what it contains of indication of independence from it through proof, because whoever is independent of the worlds is necessarily independent of it as well. Moreover, it indicates complete independence, so it is more expressive of the greatness of the wrath that it describes.

Qur'anic quotation: "Say: O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of God, while God is Witness over what you do?"

The wāw here is the wāw of ḥāl (the circumstantial wāw, indicating that the following clause describes the circumstance). The meaning is: "Why do you disbelieve in the signs of God" — the signs that indicate the truthfulness of Muḥammad (ﷺ) — "while the circumstance is that God is Witness over your deeds, and so He will recompense you for them."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 99:

﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, why do you bar﴾ (tasudduna). Al-sadd means prevention, ﴿from the way of Allah those who believe﴾, from a true religion known to be the way of Allah that He commanded them to follow, which is Islam. They would use all their effort to prevent whoever wished to enter it. ﴿Seeking it﴾ (tabghunaha) means you seek it, and its position is an accusative of circumstance (nasb ʿala al-hal). ﴿Crookedness﴾ (ʿiwajan) means deviation and inclination away from the straight course and uprightness, by your altering the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from its proper form and the like. ﴿While you are witnesses﴾ that it is the way of Allah, which none bars from except one who is astray and leads others astray. ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ of barring from His way. This is a severe warning.

Then He forbade the believers from following these who turn people away from His path, by His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, if you obey a party of those who were given the Scripture, they will return you after your belief to be disbelievers.﴾ It was said: "Shas ibn Qays, a Jew, passed by a group of the Ansar from the Aws and the Khazraj in a gathering of theirs, where they were talking together. Their conversation and their harmony angered him, so he ordered a young Jew to remind them of the Day of Bu'ath, perhaps they would become angry. It was a day on which the Aws and the Khazraj had fought, and the victory on that day had belonged to the Aws. He did so, and the people quarreled at that point and said: 'The weapons! The weapons!' News of this reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and he went out to them with those of the Muhajirun and the Ansar who were with him and said: 'Do you call to the Jahiliyyah while I am among you, after Allah has honored you with Islam and united you?!' The people recognized that this was a stirring from Satan, so they threw down their weapons and embraced one another weeping, and then the verse was revealed."

How can you disbelieve, when the verses of Allah are recited to you and His Messenger is among you? The interrogative here conveys denial and wonder: from where could disbelief reach you?! "And the verses of Allah are recited to you" — while the verses of Allah, which are the Qur'an, the inimitable (al-Mu'jiz), are being recited to you through the tongue of the Messenger, fresh and tender,

"and among you is His Messenger" — the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is in your midst, admonishing you, exhorting you, and removing your doubts from you. "And whoever holds fast to Allah" — whoever adheres to His religion, or to His Book; or it is an exhortation to them to seek refuge in Him in repelling the evils and schemes of the disbelievers. "Then he has been guided to a straight path" — he has been directed to the true religion. Or: whoever makes his Lord a refuge and a resort at the time of doubts, He will protect him from doubts.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 102:

﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah as He should be feared﴾ — the required fear of Him, and what is due from it, which is performing what is obligatory and avoiding what is forbidden. It is related from ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud): it means that He is obeyed and not disobeyed, thanked and not denied, and remembered and not forgotten. Or it means that one is not swayed in (the matter of) Allah by the blame of any blamer, and that one upholds justice even against oneself, or one's sons, or one's father. It has also been said: a servant does not fear Allah as He should be feared until his tongue is kept in check. The word tuqat is from ittaqa (to fear/guard against), like tuwadah from ittaʾada (to be deliberate).

﴿And do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ — do not be in any state other than the state of Islam when death comes upon you.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on Surah 3, verse 103:

﴿And hold fast to the rope of Allah﴾ means: hold fast to the Qur'an, based on his (ﷺ) saying: "The Qur'an is the strong rope of Allah. Its wonders never end, and it does not wear out through much repetition. Whoever speaks by it speaks truly, whoever acts by it is guided aright, and whoever holds fast to it is guided to a straight path." ﴿All together﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring back to the pronoun of the addressees. It has also been said: hold fast to the *ijmāʿ* (consensus, the agreement) of the community (*ummah*). Its evidence is: ﴿and do not separate﴾, meaning: and do not become divided. That is, do not do what leads to division and what causes the collective unity to disappear. Or: do not separate from the truth by falling into disagreement among yourselves, as the Jews and Christians disagreed, or as you were divided in the Jahiliyya (the age of ignorance), when some of you fought against others.

﴿And remember the favour of Allah upon you, when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together, so that by His favour you became brothers﴾: In the Jahiliyya there was enmity and warfare among them, and He brought their hearts together through Islam, cast love into their hearts, and they became brothers. ﴿And you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire﴾: you were about to fall into the Fire of Hell because of the disbelief you were upon.

﴿Then He rescued you from it﴾ through Islam. This is a refutation of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist theological school which held that human beings, not God, bring about their own salvation from error), for in their view it is they who rescue themselves, not Allah the Exalted. The pronoun (in *minhā*, "from it") refers to the pit, or to the Fire, or to the brink. It is feminine because it is grammatically linked to the pit. The *shafā* of the pit means its edge, and its final radical is *waw* (the letter و), which is why its dual is *shafawān* (شَفَوانِ).

﴿Thus﴾, like this eloquent clarification, ﴿Allah makes clear to you His signs﴾, meaning: the Qur'an, which contains commands and prohibitions, promises and warnings. ﴿That you may be guided﴾: so that you may be upon the hope of guidance, or so that you may be guided by it to what is right and to what earns reward.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 104:

﴿And let there be among you a community who invite to good, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong﴾ "What is right" (al-ma'ruf) means what the Sharia and reason deem good, and "what is wrong" (al-munkar) means what the Sharia and reason deem ugly. Or: al-ma'ruf is what agrees with the Book and the Sunna, and al-munkar is what contradicts them. Or: al-ma'ruf is obedience, and al-munkar is disobedience. The call to good is general, covering the obligations, both the acts and the abstentions, and what is joined to it (enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong) is specific. The word "min" (among you) here is partitive (li-l-tab'id), because enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong are communal obligations (fard al-kifaya), and because only one who knows what is right and what is wrong, and who knows how to arrange the matter in its establishment, is fit for it. He begins with the easy, and if that does not benefit, he rises to the difficult. God the Exalted said: ﴿So make peace between them﴾ and then said: ﴿then fight﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9]. Or "min" is explicative (li-l-tabyin), meaning: "And be a community that enjoins," like His saying the Exalted: ﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind, enjoining what is right﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110]. ﴿And those are the successful﴾, meaning: they are the ones singled out for complete success. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong is the caliph (khalifa) of God on His earth, the caliph of His Messenger, and the caliph of His Book." And on the authority of Ali (may God be pleased with him): The best of jihad is enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 105:

﴿And do not be like those who became divided﴾ over enmity,

﴿and differed﴾ in the religion. They are the Jews and the Christians, for they differed, and some of them declared others to be disbelievers,

﴿after clear proofs had come to them﴾ which required agreement upon one word, which is the word of truth.

﴿And for them there is a great punishment﴾

The phrase ﴿يَوْمَ تَبْيَضُّ وُجُوهٌ﴾ is in the accusative by virtue of its being an adverb of time (ẓarf), governed either by the word "lahum" (for them), or by "ʿaẓīm" (a great [punishment]), or by "udhkurū" (remember), meaning: the faces of the believers.

﴿وَتَسْوَدُّ وُجُوهٌ﴾ means: the faces of the disbelievers. Whiteness comes from light, and blackness from darkness.

﴿فَأمّا الَّذِينَ اسْوَدَّتْ وُجُوهُهُمْ﴾ — it is said to them: ﴿أكَفَرْتُمْ﴾ (Did you disbelieve...?). The fa' (fa', "then") and the verb of saying (al-qawl) have both been omitted, because the meaning is known. The hamza (interrogative particle) is for reproach and for expressing astonishment at their condition.

﴿بَعْدَ إيمانِكُمْ﴾ (after your faith) refers to the Day of the Covenant (yawm al-mīthāq). Accordingly, what is meant by it is all the disbelievers; this is the view of Ubayy, and it is the apparent meaning. Or it refers to the apostates, or to the hypocrites, meaning: did you disbelieve inwardly after your faith outwardly? Or it refers to the People of the Book, whose disbelief after faith is their denial of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) after having acknowledged him before his coming.

﴿فَذُوقُوا العَذابَ بِما كُنْتُمْ تَكْفُرُونَ﴾ — "So taste the punishment because of what you used to disbelieve."

﴿As for those whose faces will be whitened, they will be in the mercy of Allah﴾: "fa-fi" means in His blessing, which is the everlasting reward. Then he resumed, saying: ﴿They will abide therein forever﴾, not departing from it, and not dying.

These are the verses of Allah, which We recite to you in truth (ﷺ is not part of this text) — 

Correction, translating exactly:

These are the signs of Allah (﴿تِلْكَ آياتُ اللهِ﴾), those revealed concerning the promise (al-wa'd), the threat (al-wa'id), and other matters, ﴿which We recite to you﴾ as things bound up with ﴿the truth﴾ and justice, concerning the recompense of the one who does good and the one who does evil. ﴿And Allah does not intend any injustice to the worlds﴾, meaning: He does not will to wrong His servants, so as to seize anyone without a crime, or to increase the punishment of a criminal, or to diminish the reward of one who does good.

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to Allah all matters are returned.﴾ So He recompenses the doer of good for his good, and the doer of evil for his evil. The reading (تَرْجِعُ), with the verb in the active form, is transmitted from al-Shami, Hamza, and Ali.

Kāna ('kāna') is an expression for the existence of a thing in a past time, in an indefinite manner. It does not indicate that the thing did not exist before, nor that its existence was suddenly interrupted. Among its uses is His saying, ﴿You were the best nation﴾. It is as if it were said: "You came into being as the best nation," or "You were the best nation in the knowledge of God," or "in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh) you were the best nation," or "you were mentioned among the nations before you as the best nation, described with this."

﴿Were brought forth﴾ means ﴿were made manifest﴾. The lam in ﴿for mankind﴾ is connected to ﴿were brought forth﴾.

﴿You enjoin what is right﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), in which it is explained why they are the best nation. This is like when you say: "Zayd is generous; he feeds people and clothes them." By mentioning feeding and clothing, you have shown the aspect of his generosity. ﴿What is right﴾ means faith and obedience to the Messenger. ﴿And you forbid what is wrong﴾ means disbelief and every prohibited thing. ﴿And you believe in God﴾ means and you persist in faith in Him. Or, it is because the waw (and) does not require sequence.

﴿If the People of the Book had believed﴾ in Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿it would have been better for them﴾. That is, faith would have been better for them than what they are in. They only preferred their religion over the religion of Islam out of love for leadership and for having followers among the common people. Had they believed, it would have been better for them than leadership, followers, and worldly pleasures, which are what they preferred the religion of falsehood for. In addition, they would have gained what they were promised for believing in it: the granting of their reward twice.

﴿Among them are believers﴾, such as ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his companions.

﴿And most of them are defiant transgressors﴾, those who persist stubbornly in disbelief.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 111:

﴿They will not harm you except with a little harm﴾, a harm limited to hurt caused by words from one who reviles the religion, or by a threat, or the like. (p. 283)

﴿And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you﴾, defeated, and they will not harm you with killing or capture.

﴿Then they will not be helped﴾, meaning they will have no support from anyone and will not be protected from you. In this there is reassurance for those among them who have embraced Islam, because they used to harm them by rebuke and threats. This is a new independent statement (ibtida' ikhbar), conjoined to the conditional clause (jumlat al-shart wa al-jaza', the protasis and apodosis), and it is not conjoined to "they will turn their backs to you." Had it been conjoined to that, it would have been said "then they will not be helped" in the past form of the verb (lā yunṣarū, in the jussive/subjunctive construction after lam). It was introduced as a new statement (istu'nifa) to indicate that God will not help them, whether they fight or do not fight. The sense of the sentence is: "I inform you that if they fight you, they will be routed; then I inform you that they will not be helped." The word "thumma" (then) here denotes sequence in rank, because the report that God will subject them to humiliation is greater than the report that they will turn their backs.

﴿Duribat﴾ (they were struck; i.e., imposed upon) ﴿ʿalayhimu l-dhillatu﴾ (humiliation was imposed upon them), namely upon the Jews.

﴿Ayna mā thuqifū﴾ (wherever they are found) ﴿illā bi-ḥablin mina Llāh﴾ (except with a rope from Allah). The phrase is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the bāʾ (with) is connected to a deleted element; its estimated sense is: "except as those who hold fast" or "who cling to a rope from Allah."

﴿Wa-ḥablin mina l-nās﴾ (and a rope from the people). The ḥabl (rope) here means covenant (ʿahd), protection (dhimmah). The meaning is: humiliation was imposed upon them in every state, except in the state of their holding fast to the rope of Allah and the rope of the people, meaning the protection (dhimmah) of Allah and the protection of the Muslims. That is, they have no honour at all except this one, which is their seeking refuge in protection (dhimmah) in return for the jizyah (poll tax) they accepted.

﴿Wa-bāʾū bi-ghaḍabin mina Llāh﴾ (and they returned with anger from Allah), which they deserved. ﴿Wa-ḍuribat ʿalayhimu l-maskanah﴾ (and destitution was imposed upon them), that is, poverty, as a punishment for them for their saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 181], or the fear of poverty alongside the existence of wealth. ﴿Dhālika bi-annahum kānū yakfurūna bi-āyāti Llāhi wa-yaqtulūna l-anbiyāʾa bi-ghayri ḥaqq﴾ (That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right). "Dhālika" (that) is a reference to what was mentioned of the imposition of humiliation, destitution, and returning with the anger of Allah; that is, that happened because of their disbelief in the signs of Allah and their killing of the prophets without right. Then He said: ﴿Dhālika bi-mā ʿaṣaw wa-kānū yaʿtadūn﴾ (That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress), that is, that disbelief and that killing occurred because of their disobedience to Allah and their transgression of His limits.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 113:

﴿They are not all alike.﴾ The People of the Book are not equal ﴿among the People of the Book﴾. This is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf) explaining His words ﴿They are not all alike﴾, just as His words ﴿enjoining what is right﴾ came as an explanation of His words ﴿you are the best nation﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 110]. ﴿A community standing (ummah qaʾimah)﴾: an upright, just community, from your saying "I straightened the stick (aqamtu al-ʿūd) so it stood (fa-qāma)", meaning it became straight (istaqāma). They are those among them who embraced Islam,

﴿reciting the signs of Allah﴾: the Qur'an,

﴿during the hours of the night (ānāʾ al-layl)﴾: its hours. Its singular is inan, like miʿan, or inwun, like qinwun, or iniyyun, like niḥyun (the forms of the word for "hour" as given by the grammarians).

﴿and they prostrate themselves﴾: they pray. It has been said: he means the ʿIshāʾ prayer, because the People of the Book do not perform it. It has also been said: he expressed their night vigil (tahajjud) by reciting the Qur'an during the hours of the night together with prostration.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 3, verse 114:

﴿They believe in Allah and the Last Day, and they enjoin what is right﴾ — by faith, and all the other gates of righteousness (*al-birr*).

﴿And they forbid what is wrong﴾ — from disbelief, and from what the Sharia (*al-Shar'*, sacred law) prohibits.

﴿And they hasten to good deeds﴾ — they rush toward them, fearing that the opportunity will pass. The words "they recite" (*yatlūna*) and "they believe" (*yu'minūna*) are in the nominative position as two descriptive clauses (*sifatān*) of "a community" (*ummah*), meaning: a standing community, reciting and believing. He described them with the distinctive features that were found among the Jews: reciting the verses of Allah during the night while prostrating; and belief in Allah, because their belief in Him was no true belief, given their association of 'Uzayr with Him and their disbelief in some of the books and messengers; and belief in the Last Day, because they described it contrary to its true nature; and enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, because they used to be compromisers (*mudāhinīn*); and hastening to good deeds, because they used to be slow to them, not desiring them. Hastening to good is an intense eagerness for it, since whoever desires a matter hastens to carry it out.

﴿And those are among the righteous﴾ — those described with what they have been described with — ﴿among the righteous﴾, that is, among the Muslims, or among the righteous whose states were made good in the sight of Allah, and He was pleased with them.

Qur'an 3:115: "And whatever good they do, it will never be denied them. And Allah is All-Knowing of the righteous."

(Qur'anic quotation: "And whatever good they do, it will never be denied them; and Allah is Knowing of the God-fearing.")

Al-Nasafi: ((And whatever good they do, it will never be denied them) is read with the yā' in both places (yaf'alū and yukfarūhu) by the Kufans except Abū Bakr, while Abū 'Amr has the choice (between yā' and tā'); the others read with the tā'. The verb yukfarūhu is transitive to two objects, although shakara ("to be thankful") and kafara ("to deny") are only transitive to one object, as in "shakara al-ni'mata" and "kafarahā" (he gave thanks for the blessing, he denied it), because it includes the sense of deprivation, as if it were said: "fa-lan tuḥramūhu" (you will never be deprived of it), i.e., "fa-lan tuḥramū jazā'ahu" (you will never be deprived of its reward). ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of the righteous﴾ is good news to the righteous of abundant reward.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 116:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, neither their wealth nor their children will avail them anything against Allah﴾ — i.e., from the punishment of Allah,

﴿And those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 117:

﴿The likeness of what they spend in this worldly life﴾ — in boasting, in acts of generosity, in seeking praise and a good reputation among people — or what they offer as a means of drawing near to God while they are in disbelief.

﴿Like the likeness of a wind﴾ — like the likeness of a wind that destroys, namely the tilth (al-harth), or the likeness of the destruction of what they spend is like the destruction by a wind ﴿in which is a frost﴾ — intense cold, according to Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. It is a subject and predicate in a position of genitive, as an attribute of "wind," like the verse: ﴿which smote the tilth of a people who had wronged themselves﴾ by disbelief ﴿and destroyed it﴾ as a punishment for their disbelief. ﴿Allah did not wrong them﴾ by destroying their tilth ﴿but they wronged themselves﴾ by committing what deserved punishment. Or the pronoun refers to the spenders, meaning: Allah did not wrong them by not accepting their expenditures, but they wronged themselves in that they did not bring them in a form fit for acceptance.

وَنَزَلَ نَهْيًا لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ عَنْ مُصافاةِ المُنافِقِينَ: It was revealed as a prohibition for the believers against befriending (musafah) the hypocrites. ﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لا تَتَّخِذُوا بِطانَةً﴾ [O you who believe, do not take intimate confidants]. بِطانَةُ الرَجُلِ ووَلِيجَتُهُ: خَصِيصِهِ، وصَفِيِّهِ: The bitana (inner circle, lining) of a man and his waliyja (confidant) are his special, intimate friend and chosen companion. شُبِّهَ بِبِطانَةِ الثَوْبِ، كَما يُقالُ: فُلانٌ شِعارِيٌّ (shi'ari, meaning close and intimate, like the undergarment next to the skin), وفي الحَدِيثِ: «"الأنْصارُ شِعارٌ، والناسُ دِثارٌ"». [It is likened to the lining of a garment, as one says: "So-and-so is shi'ari." And in the hadith: "The Ansar are the undergarment (shi'ar), and the people are the outer garment (di'thar)."] ﴿مِن دُونِكُمْ﴾ [from other than you]: مِن دُونِ أبْناءِ جِنْسِكُمْ، وهُمُ المُسْلِمُونَ، وهو صِفَةٌ لِبِطانَةٍ: meaning from other than your own kind, who are the Muslims. It is an adjective (sifah) modifying bitana. أيْ: (p-٢٨٦)بِطانَةً كائِنَةً مِن دُونِكم مُجاوِزَةً لَكم: That is, a bitana that is from outside you and beyond you. ﴿لا يَأْلُونَكم خَبالا﴾ [they do not fall short in corrupting you]: في مَوْضِعِ النَصْبِ صِفَةً لِبِطانَةٍ، يَعْنِي: لا يُقَصِّرُونَ في فَسادِ دِينِكم: It is in the accusative position as an adjective of bitana, meaning they do not fall short in corrupting your religion. يُقالُ: ألا في الأمْرِ يَأْلُو: إذا قَصَّرَ فِيهِ: One says alā fī al-amr ya'lū, meaning he fell short in the matter. والخَبالُ: الفَسادُ: Khabal means corruption. وانْتَصَبَ خَبالًا عَلى التَمْيِيزِ (tamyiz, a grammatical term meaning the specifying accusative): أوْ عَلى حَذْفِ فِي، أيْ: في خَبالِكم: Khabalan is in the accusative as a specification, or as an accusative after the deletion of fi (in), meaning in your corruption.

﴿وَدُّوا ما عَنِتُّمْ﴾ [they wish what distresses you]: أيْ: عَنَتَكُمْ، فَما: مَصْدَرِيَّةٌ (masdariyyah, meaning ma is a verbal-noun particle), والعَنَتُ: شِدَّةُ الضَرَرِ والمَشَقَّةُ، أيْ: تَمَنَّوْا أنْ يَضُرُّوكم في دِينِكم ودُنْياكم أشَدَّ الضَرَرِ وأبْلَغَهُ: That is, ʿanitakum, and ma is masdariyyah. ʿAnat means severe harm and hardship. That is, they wish to harm you in your religion and your worldly life with the greatest and most extreme harm. وهو مُسْتَأْنَفٌ عَلى وجْهِ التَعْلِيلِ لِلنَّهْيِ عَنِ اتِّخاذِهِمْ بِطانَةً: It is a new clause (isti'naf) giving the reason for the prohibition against taking them as bitana, كَقَوْلِهِ: ﴿قَدْ بَدَتِ البَغْضاءُ مِن أفْواهِهِمْ﴾ [hatred has already appeared from their mouths]، لِأنَّهم لا يَتَمالَكُونَ -مَعَ ضَبْطِهِمْ أنْفُسَهُمْ- أنْ يَنْفَلِتَ مِن ألْسِنَتِهِمْ ما يُعْلَمُ بِهِ بَعْضُهم لِلْمُسْلِمِينَ: as it is said elsewhere, because they cannot help, despite restraining themselves, but let slip from their tongues what reveals some of their hostility to the Muslims. ﴿وَما تُخْفِي صُدُورُهُمْ﴾ [and what their breasts conceal] مِنَ البُغْضِ لَكُمْ، ﴿أكْبَرُ﴾ [is greater] مِمّا بَدا: of hatred toward you, is greater than what has appeared.

﴿قَدْ بَيَّنّا لَكُمُ الآياتِ﴾ [We have certainly made the signs clear to you] الدالَّةَ عَلى وُجُوبِ الإخْلاصِ في الدِينِ، ومُوالاةِ أوْلِياءِ اللهِ، ومُعاداةِ أعْدائِهِ، ﴿إنْ كُنْتُمْ تَعْقِلُونَ﴾ [if you use your reason] ما بُيِّنَ لَكم: which indicate the obligation of sincerity in religion, loyalty to the friends of God, and enmity toward His enemies.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 119:

﴿Here you are, you are the ones⦆ "Ha" is used for attracting attention (tanbih), "antum" is the subject (mubtada'), and "ula'" is its predicate (khabar). That is: you are the ones who err in befriending the hypocrites among the People of the Book.

﴿You love them, but they do not love you﴾ This explains their error in befriending them, since they lavish their love upon people who harbour hatred. Alternatively, "ula'" is a relative pronoun (mawsul) whose relative clause (sila) is "you love them." The waw in ﴿and you believe in the Book, all of it﴾ is for the circumstantial state (waw al-hal), and its accusative case (intisab) derives from "they do not love you." That is: they do not love you, while you believe in their Book in its entirety, and yet they hate you. So why do you love them when they do not believe in any part of your Book? This contains severe reproach, because they are more steadfast in their falsehood than you are in your truth. It has also been said that "al-Kitab" here is generic (li-l-jins).

﴿When they meet you, they say, "We believe"﴾ They display the word of tawhid. ﴿And when they are alone﴾ they part from you, or some of them are alone with others.

﴿They bite their fingertips at you out of rage﴾ The one who is enraged or regretful is described by biting the fingertips, the finger-ends, and the thumbs.

﴿Say, "Die in your rage!"﴾ This is a curse upon them that their rage should increase until they perish from it. What is meant by the increase of rage is the increase of what enrages them of the strength of Islam and the honour of its people, and the humiliation and disgrace that they suffer because of that.

﴿Indeed, Allah knows what is in the breasts﴾ So He knows (p-287) what is in the breasts of the hypocrites of rage and hatred, and what occurs from them when some of them are alone with others. This is included in the content of what is spoken: that is, inform them of what they secretly do of biting their fingertips in rage when they are alone, and say to them: Indeed Allah knows what is more hidden than what you conceal among yourselves, namely the inner secrets of the breasts, so do not suppose that any of your secrets is hidden from Him. Or it is outside the content of what is spoken: that is, say that to them, O Muhammad, and do not be surprised at My informing you of what they conceal, for I know what is more hidden than that, namely what they have concealed in their breasts.

﴿If good touches you﴾: ease, abundance, spoils, and victory.

﴿Distresses them﴾: their being struck by it grieves them. ﴿And if evil befalls you﴾: the opposites of what we have mentioned. The word *massa* (touching) is used metaphorically (*mustaʿār*, a figurative transfer of meaning) from *iṣāba* (befalling), so the meaning is one. Do you not see His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If good befalls you, it distresses them, and if a misfortune befalls you﴾ [al-Tawba: 50]. ﴿They rejoice in it﴾: at its befalling them. ﴿And if you are patient﴾ toward their enmity ﴿and mindful of God﴾ regarding what you have been forbidden of their allegiance; or, ﴿and if you are patient﴾ with the obligations and hardships of religion, and "mindful" of God in avoiding His prohibitions. ﴿Their scheming will not harm you at all﴾: their plotting. You are within God's protection. This is an instruction from God and a guidance that enemy schemes be countered with patience and God-consciousness (taqwā). The wise have said: "If you want to humble one who envies you, increase in virtue within yourself."

﴿Lā yaḍurrukum﴾ (لا يَضِرْكُمْ) is read by Makki, Basri, and Nafiʿ, from *ḍāra yaḍīru*, meaning *ḍarra*, and it is clear. What is problematic is the reading of the others, because it is the response of the conditional (*jawāb al-shart*), and the response of the conditional is jussive (*majzūm*). It should therefore have been with a fatḥa on the rāʾ, like the reading of al-Mufaḍḍal from ʿĀṣim. However, the ḍamma on the rāʾ is for assimilation to the ḍamma of the ḍād, as in *mudda yā hādhā*. As for ﴿Indeed God is aware of what you do﴾ with the tāʾ (إنَّ اللهَ بِما تَعْمَلُونَ بِالتاءِ), it is easy, i.e., of patience, God-consciousness, and other things. ﴿Encompassing﴾ (*muḥīṭ*): then He will treat you with what you deserve. With the yāʾ (بِالياءِ), it refers to others, i.e., that He is aware of what they do in their enmity toward you, so He will punish them for it.

﴿And [remember] when you went out early in the morning from your household﴾. Remember, O Muhammad, when you set out in the morning from your household in Medina. What is meant is his departure from the chamber of ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, toward Uhud. ﴿Preparing the believers﴾, meaning settling them, and this is a ḥāl (grammatical circumstantial state). ﴿Positions for battle﴾, meaning places and stations on the right wing, the left wing, the center, the two flanks, and the rear guard. The phrase "لِلْقِتالِ" (for fighting) is connected to "تُبَوِّئُ" (tubawwi'u, "you settle"). ﴿And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾: All-Hearing of your words, and All-Knowing ("عَلِيمٌ") of your intentions and your inner thoughts.

It is narrated that the polytheists alighted at Uhud on Wednesday, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) consulted his Companions. He also summoned ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and consulted him. He said: "Remain in Medina. We have never gone out against an enemy without being struck by them, and they have never entered upon us without our striking them." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I saw in my dream cows being slaughtered around me, and I interpreted them as good. I saw a notch in the edge of my sword, and I interpreted it as a defeat. I saw that I had put my hand into a strong coat of mail, and I interpreted it as Medina." A group of people kept urging him toward martyrdom until he put on his coat of armour (لَأْمَة, la'mah). Then they regretted and said: "The matter is up to you, O Messenger of Allah." He (ﷺ) said: "It is not fitting for a Prophet to put on his armour and then take it off until he fights." He went out after the Friday prayer, and he arrived at the ravine (al-shiʿb) of Uhud on Saturday, in the middle of Shawwal.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 122:

﴿When two groups among you were about to lose heart﴾ is a substitution (badal) for ﴿when you set out early in the morning﴾, or the word "All-Knowing" (ʿalim) governs it in meaning. ﴿Two groups among you﴾ were two clans of the Ansar: Banu Salama of the Khazraj, and Banu Harithah of the Aws. The Prophet (ﷺ) had gone out to Uhud with a thousand men, while the polytheists numbered three thousand, and he had promised them victory if they remained steadfast. ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy withdrew with a third of the people, saying: "Why should we kill ourselves and our children?" The two clans then resolved to follow him, but Allah preserved them, and they went on with the Messenger of Allah. ﴿That you should lose heart﴾ means: "that you should lose heart," i.e., that you should become cowardly and weak. Fashal (failure of resolve) is cowardice and feebleness (khawar).

﴿And Allah is their Protector﴾: their Lover (muhibb), or their Helper (nasir), or the One who manages their affair (mutawalli amrihima). So why would they lose heart, and not put their trust in Allah? ﴿And in Allah let the believers put their trust﴾: He commanded them not to place their trust in anyone but Him, and not to entrust their affairs to anyone but Him. Jabir said: "By Allah, it would not please us that we had not resolved on what we resolved upon, since Allah has informed us that He is our Protector."

Then He reminded them of what makes trust in God obligatory, namely the victory He granted them at the Battle of Badr, when they were in a state of paucity and weakness. He said: ﴿And God had already helped you at Badr﴾. Badr is the name of a water-place between Makkah and Madinah. It was the property of a man called Badr, and so it was named after him. Or it is mentioned as "Badr" after Uhud, so as to combine patience (al-sabr) and gratitude (al-shukr). ﴿And you were weak﴾ because of the small number, for they were three hundred and some odd men (ten or more), while their enemy numbered about a thousand fighters, and because of the equipment, for they went out on water-camels (al-nawadih), with several men taking turns riding a single camel, and they had only one horse, whereas their enemy had a hundred horses, along with the armour and weaponry (al-shikkah wa al-shawkah). He used the plural of paucity, which is "adhillah" (weak), to indicate that, despite their weakness, they were few in number. ﴿So fear God﴾ by remaining steadfast alongside His Messenger, ﴿that perhaps you may be thankful﴾, by your piety, for the blessing of victory that God bestowed upon you.

﴿When you were saying to the believers﴾ is a *zarf* (a temporal adverbial complement) modifying *nasarakum* (God helped you), on the basis that he said this to them on the day of Badr. That is, God helped you at the time of this saying of yours. Alternatively, it is a second *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for *idh ghadawta* (when you set out), on the basis that he said it to them on the day of Uhud. ﴿Is it not enough for you that your Lord reinforce you with three thousand angels sent down?﴾ *Munazzilīn* is the reading of al-Shāmī (the Syrian reader), and *Munzilīn* is the reading of Abū Ḥayawa, meaning: sent down for the support. The meaning of ﴿Is it not enough for you﴾ is a denial that the reinforcement with three thousand angels would not suffice for them. *Lan*, which is used for emphasizing negation, is employed here to indicate that they, because of their small number, their weakness, and the large number and strength of their enemy, were like those who had despaired of victory.

Bala (بَلى) is an affirmation of what follows "lan" (لَنْ), meaning: the reinforcement with them suffices for you. So He made sufficiency obligatory. Then He said: ﴿If you are patient﴾ in the fighting, ﴿and you are mindful of God﴾ by not opposing the Messenger (ﷺ), ﴿and they come upon you﴾, meaning: the polytheists,

﴿immediately﴾ — the word here is min fawrihim hadha. Fawr (فَوْر) comes from fārat al-qidr (فارَتِ القِدْرُ), meaning when the pot boils over. The term was borrowed to mean speed, and then the state in which there is no delay and no turning aside for anything was called by it. So it is said: he left immediately (خَرَجَ مِن فَوْرِهِ), just as you say: from his very hour he did not tarry. From this is the statement of al-Karkhi (الكَرْخِيّ): "A command in absolute form requires immediacy, not postponement." The meaning is: if they come upon you from this very hour of theirs, ﴿your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels﴾ — in the state of their coming, their descent will not be delayed beyond their arrival. That is to say, God Most High hastens your victory and eases your conquest if you are patient and mindful of God.

(mussawwimin) (مُسَوِّمِينَ) with a kasra on the waw, read by Makki (مَكِّيّ), Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Sahl, means: marking themselves or their horses with a sign by which they are recognised in battle. Al-sawma (السُومَةُ) is the mark. On the authority of al-Dahhak: marked with white wool on the foreheads and tails of the mounts.

Ghayruhum (غَيْرُهُمْ) with a fatha on the waw, means: marked (مُعَلَّمِينَ). Al-Kalbi said: marked with yellow turbans hanging over their shoulders. The turban of al-Zubayr on the day of Badr was yellow, so the angels descended in that manner.

Qatada said: they first descended as a thousand, then they became three thousand, then five thousand.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 126:

﴿And Allah did not make it﴾: the pronoun refers to the reinforcement (imdad) that is indicated by ﴿that He should reinforce you﴾.

﴿except as good news for you﴾: that is, Allah did not make your reinforcement with the angels except as glad tidings for you that you would be given victory. ﴿And so that your hearts may be at rest through it﴾: just as the sakina (tranquillity) was for the Children of Israel a glad tiding of victory and an assurance for their hearts.

﴿And victory is only from Allah﴾: not from the fighters, nor from the angels. But that is among the things through which Allah strengthens the hope of victory and the desire for mercy.

﴿the Mighty﴾: the One who is not overcome in His judgments.

﴿the Wise﴾: the One who gives victory to His allies and tests them through striving against His enemies.

The lām in ﴿liyaqṭaʿa ṭarafan minal-ladhīna kafarū﴾ (﴿that He might cut off a part of those who disbelieved﴾) means: that a group of them be destroyed by killing and capture. This refers to what happened on the Day of Badr: seventy were killed and seventy taken captive from the chiefs of Quraysh. It is connected either to His words ﴿And Allah had already given you victory﴾, or to His words ﴿And victory is not except from Allah﴾, or to ﴿your Lord will reinforce you﴾, or to ﴿or He will subdue them﴾ or ﴿disgrace them﴾, and to infuriate them with defeat. The real meaning of al-kabt (subduing) is a severe weakness that strikes the heart, so that the face is struck down because of it. ﴿So they turn back frustrated﴾ means they return without having attained their aim.

﴿Laysa laka mina al-amri shay'un﴾ (You have no say at all in the matter). The ism of *laysa* (the subject of the verbal particle *laysa*) is "shay'un" (anything), and the khabar (predicate) is "laka" (for you). "Min al-amri" (of the matter) is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) modifying "shay'un," because it is a ṣifa (qualifier) that has been placed before its noun.

﴿Aw yatuba 'alayhim﴾ (or He turns to them in mercy) is an 'aṭf (conjunction) upon "li-yaqṭa'a ṭaraffan min al-ladhina kafaru aw yakbitahum" (that He may cut off a portion of those who disbelieved or subdue them). The clause "laysa laka mina al-amri shay'un" is an i'tiraḍ (parenthetical insertion) between the conjoined element and that to which it is conjoined. The meaning is: God, exalted is He, is the owner of their affair. So either He destroys them, or He defeats them, or He turns to them in mercy if they embrace Islam,

﴿aw yu'adhdhibahum﴾ (or He punishes them) if they persist in disbelief. You have no say in their affair. You are only a servant sent to warn them and to strive against them.
