It is narrated from al-Farrā' (the grammarian) that "aw" here means "ḥattā" (until), and it is narrated from Ibn 'Īsā that it means "illā an" (except that), as in your saying: "La-alzamannaka aw tu'ṭiyanī ḥaqqī" (I will certainly keep after you until you give me my right). That is: you have no say in their affair, except that God turns to them in mercy, so that you rejoice in their condition, or He punishes them, so that you take vengeance upon them. It has also been said: he (the Prophet) intended to invoke curses upon them, so God, exalted is He, forbade him, since He knew that among them there were those who would believe. ﴿Fa-innahum ẓālimūna﴾ (for they are wrongdoers) meaning: they deserve punishment.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 130:

﴿O you who have believed, do not consume usury, doubled and redoubled﴾ (مُضَعَّفَةً, muḍaʿʿafa) is the reading of Makki and Shami. This is a prohibition of usury (ribā), together with a rebuke for what they used to do of multiplying it. A man among them, when his debt reached its due date, would say: "Either you pay my right, or you increase it (turbī), and extend the term." ﴿And fear Allah﴾ regarding its consumption ﴿that you may prosper﴾.

﴿And fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers.﴾ Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say: "It is the most frightening verse in the Qur'an, since Allah threatened the believers with the Fire prepared for the disbelievers if they do not guard themselves against Him by avoiding His prohibitions. He has supplemented this threat with what follows it, linking the hope of the believers for His mercy to their steadfastness in obeying Him and obeying His Messenger, by His saying:"

Translation of the passage:

﴿And obey Allah and the Messenger, that you may receive mercy﴾. In this there is a refutation of the Murji'ah (the sect that deferred judgment on sins) in their saying: "No sin harms along with faith, and no one is punished in the Fire at all." According to us: those among the disobedient (ʿusat) who are not disbelievers may enter it (the Fire), but the final outcome of their affair is Paradise. And in Allah's mention, exalted is He, of "perhaps" (laʿalla) and "it may be" (ʿasā) in such contexts, although the people of tafsir have said that laʿalla and ʿasā from Allah are for certainty, there is what is not hidden from the one who knows (ʿārif) of the subtlety of the path of piety (taqwā), the difficulty of attaining the pleasure of Allah, and the rarity of reaching His mercy and reward.

(Sāri'ū) is read by Medina and Syria (as a variant reading). Whoever affirms the waw (wāw) connects it to what precedes it; whoever omits it begins a new sentence (isti'nāf). The meaning of hastening (musāra'a) toward forgiveness and Paradise is turning toward that which leads to them. Then it was said: it refers to the five daily prayers, or the first takbir (opening takbir), or obedience, or sincerity (ikhlāṣ), or repentance, or the Friday prayer and congregations.

﴿Its breadth is the heavens and the earth﴾: that is, its breadth is the breadth of the heavens and the earth, like His saying: ﴿Its breadth is like the breadth of heaven and earth﴾ [al-Ḥadīd: 21]. The intended meaning is describing it with vastness and expanse; it is compared to the widest thing people know of His creation and its expanse. He specified the breadth (ʿarḍ) because in common usage it is less than the length (ṭūl), for emphasis. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him both: "like seven heavens and seven earths, if some of them were joined to others." As for what is narrated: that Paradise is in the seventh heaven, or in the fourth heaven, its meaning is that it is in its direction, not that it is within it or in part of it, just as one says: "In the house there is a garden," even though it exceeds the house, because what is meant is that its door leads to it.

﴿It has been prepared﴾ (uʿiddat) is in a position of genitive as an attribute of Jannah also, meaning: a vast Garden prepared ﴿for the God-fearing﴾. The two verses indicate that Paradise and Hell are created. Then, "the God-fearing" (al-muttaqī) means: one who guards against shirk, as He said: ﴿and a Garden whose breadth is like the breadth of heaven and earth, prepared for those who believe in Allah and His messengers﴾ [al-Ḥadīd: 21]; or one who guards against sins. If the second is intended, then it is for them without punishment; and if the first is intended, it is also for them in the end. It may be pausing at it (waqf) if ﴿those who spend in ease and hardship﴾ is taken as a subject (mubtada'), with ﴿and those who, when they commit an indecency﴾ joined to it, and the predicate being ﴿those﴾ (ulā'ika). If it is taken as an attribute of the God-fearing, and ﴿and those who, when they commit an indecency﴾ is joined to it, meaning: it has been prepared for the God-fearing and the repentant, then there is no pause.

If you say: the verse indicates that Paradise is prepared for the God-fearing and the repentant (p-293) and not for the persistent ones, I say: it is possible that it is prepared for both, and then others enter it by the grace and pardon of Allah, just as one says: this feast has been prepared for the emir, and then his followers may eat it. Do you not see that He said: ﴿and fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 131], and then others than the disbelievers enter it by consensus?

It opens with mention of spending because it is the hardest thing on the self and the strongest indicator of sincerity; and because at that time the greatest of deeds was spending, due to the need for it in striving against the enemy and aiding the poor Muslims. It was said: what is meant is spending in all circumstances, because they are never free of a state of joy or of harm.

﴿And those who restrain (al-kāẓimīn) the anger (al-ghayẓ)﴾: those who withhold their anger from carrying out its effect. It is said: "kaẓama al-qirba" when he filled it and tied its mouth; and from it comes kaẓm al-ghayẓ, which is to hold back what is in oneself of it through patience and not let any trace of it appear. Al-ghayẓ is the blazing of the heart's heat from anger.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever restrains anger while he is able to carry it out, Allah fills his heart with security and faith."

﴿And those who pardon people﴾: that is, if someone wrongs them, they do not hold him accountable. It is reported: "A caller will call on the Day of Resurrection: Where are those whose reward was upon Allah? None will stand except those who pardoned." It is narrated from Ibn ʿUyayna that he related it to al-Rashīd, when he was angry with a man, and so he released him.

﴿And Allah loves the doers of good (al-muḥsinīn)﴾: the lām here is for the category (jins), so it includes every doer of good, and these mentioned are included under it; or it is for a specific reference (ʿahd), so it indicates these people. Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 135:

﴿Those who, when they commit an immorality﴾, an act of increased ugliness. It is permissible that "those who" (alladhina) be the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is "those" (ula'ika): ﴿or wrong themselves﴾. It has been said: "immorality" is the grave sin (al-kabira), and "wronging themselves" is the minor sin (al-saghira). Or: "immorality" is fornication (zina), and "wronging themselves" is kissing, touching, and the like.

﴿They remember Allah﴾ with their tongues, or with their hearts, so as to prompt them to repentance. ﴿And seek forgiveness for their sins﴾, so they repent of them, regretting their ugliness. It has been said: Iblis wept when this verse was revealed. ﴿And who forgives sins except Allah?﴾ "Man" (man) is the subject (mubtada'), and "yaghfiru" (forgives) is its predicate, and in it there is a pronoun referring back to "man". "Illa Allah" (except Allah) is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in "yaghfiru". The implied meaning is: "and no one forgives sins except Allah." This is a parenthetical sentence (jumla mu'tariḍa) between the conjoined (ma'tuf) and that to which it is conjoined (ma'tuf 'alayhi). In it there is a consolation for the souls of the servants, an encouragement to repentance, an incitement to it, a deterrent from despair and hopelessness, a statement of the vastness of His mercy and the nearness of His forgiveness to the penitent, and an indication that sins, however great, His pardon is greater and His generosity is more abundant.

﴿And they do not persist in what they have done﴾, they do not continue in their ugly deed. Iṣrar (persistence) means continuance. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "One who seeks forgiveness does not persist, even if he returns to it seventy times in a day." And it is narrated: "There is no major sin with seeking forgiveness, and no minor sin with persistence."

﴿While they know﴾: a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿and they do not persist﴾, meaning: "while they know" that they have done wrong, or ﴿while they know﴾ that none forgives their sins except Allah.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 136:

﴿Those﴾ who have been described,

﴿their reward is forgiveness from their Lord﴾ by His repentance (tawbah) ﴿and gardens﴾ by His mercy, ﴿beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein; and excellent is the reward of those who act﴾. The object of praise is omitted: that is, "and excellent is the reward of those who act that," meaning: the forgiveness and the gardens. It was revealed concerning a date-seller who said to a woman who wanted dates: "In my house there are better dates," so he brought her into his house, embraced her, and kissed her, and then he regretted it. Or it was revealed concerning an Ansari man whom a Thaqafi man had been left to take his place (during his absence) while the Prophet ﷺ had established brotherhood between them, during the absence on a military campaign (ghazwah). He came to his family to fulfil a need, saw her, and kissed her, then regretted it, so he wandered about the earth crying out, and Allah the Exalted sought to appease him (istaʿtabahu Allah).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 137:

﴿Indeed, there have passed﴾ (i.e., gone by) ﴿before you ways (sunan)﴾. He means: what Allah Most High established (sanna) concerning the afflictions He inflicted upon the nations that denied (the prophets). ﴿So travel through the earth and see what was the end of those who denied﴾, so that you may take warning from them.

This is the tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis) of al-Nasafi, Madarik al-Tanzil, on surah 3, verse 138.

﴿This﴾ means: the Qur'an, or what has been mentioned before it. ﴿Is a clarification (bayan) for mankind, and a guidance (huda)﴾ meaning: instruction (irshad). ﴿And an admonition (maw'itha)﴾ meaning: encouragement (targhib) and warning (tarhib). ﴿For those who are mindful (muttaqin)﴾ of shirk (associating partners with God).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 139:

﴿And do not weaken﴾ — ولا تَضْعُفُوا: do not become feeble in jihad (holy struggle) because of what afflicted you of defeat (al-hazima).

﴿And do not grieve﴾ — over what escaped you of the spoils (al-ghanima), or over those among you who were killed or wounded. It is a consolation from Allah to His Messenger and to the believers regarding what befell them on the Day of Uhud, and a strengthening of their hearts.

﴿And you will have the upper hand﴾ — and your condition is that you are higher than them and more victorious, because you inflicted upon them on the Day of Badr more than they inflicted upon you on the Day of Uhud. Or, "you will have the upper hand" means with victory and triumph in the end. It is a good tiding to them of superiority and dominance: ﴿And indeed Our soldiers, they will be the victorious﴾ [as-Saffat: 173]. Or ﴿And you will have the upper hand﴾ in standing, because your fighting is for Allah and for raising His word, while their fighting is for Satan and for raising the word of disbelief; or because your slain are in Paradise and their slain are in the Fire.

﴿If you are believers﴾ — this is connected to the prohibition, meaning: ﴿do not weaken﴾ if your faith is sound. That is, the soundness of faith necessitates strength of heart, trust in Allah's promise, and little concern for His enemies. Or it is connected to "the upper hand," meaning: if you are truly affirming what Allah promises you and gives you good news of, of victory.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 140:

﴿If a wound touches you, a similar wound has already touched the other people. And these days We alternate among people, so that Allah may know those who believe, and take martyrs from among you. And Allah does not love the wrongdoers.﴾

140 ﴿If a wound touches you﴾ — with a ḍamma on the qāf wherever it occurs, for Kūfī (ʿĀṣim's transmission) other than Ḥafṣ; and with a fatḥa on the qāf for the others. These are two dialectal forms, like ḍaʿf and ḍuʿf (weakness). It was said: with the fatḥa, it means the wound itself (al-jirāḥa), and with the ḍamma, its pain (alamuhā).

﴿a similar wound has already touched the other people﴾ — that is: if they inflicted [wounds] upon you on the day of Uhud, then you have inflicted [wounds] upon them on the day of Badr. Yet that did not weaken their hearts, nor did it prevent them from returning to fight with you. So you are more deserving of not becoming weak. ﴿And these days﴾ — ﴿tilka﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), ﴿al-ayyām﴾ is its attribute (ṣifa), and the predicate (khabar) is ﴿nudāwiluhā﴾.

﴿nudāwiluhā﴾ — We turn them around (nuṣarrifuhā),

﴿among people﴾ — that is: We turn among them the blessings and the calamities; We give to these people at one time and to those at another time, like the verse of poetry:

"One day against us, and one day for us,
and one day we are made to suffer, and one day we are gladdened."

﴿so that Allah may know those who believe﴾ — that is: We alternate them for various kinds of wisdom, and so that Allah may know the believers distinguished by patience and faith from others, just as He knew them before their existence. ﴿and take martyrs from among you﴾ — and so that He may honour some of you with martyrdom, meaning those who were martyred on the day of Uhud; or so that He may take from among you those who are fit to be witnesses over the nations on the Day of Resurrection, from His saying: ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾ [al-Baqara: 143]. ﴿And Allah does not love the wrongdoers﴾ — this is a parenthetical clause (i'tirāḍ) between one part of the causal explanation and another; its meaning: Allah does not love those who are not among these steadfast believers who strive in His way, namely the hypocrites and the disbelievers.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 141:

﴿And that Allah may purify those who believe﴾. At-tamhis (purification, refining): cleansing and clarifying.

﴿And destroy the disbelievers﴾, that is, annihilate them. The meaning is: if the turn of victory is for the believers, it is for distinction, for taking martyrs, and for purification; and if it is for the disbelievers, it is for their annihilation and the erasing of their traces.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 142:

﴿Or did you suppose that you would enter Paradise﴾ "Am" (or) here is munqati'ah (disjunctive), and the meaning of the hamzah (interrogative particle) in it is denial, i.e., "Do not suppose."

﴿And Allah has not yet known those of you who strove﴾ That is: "And you have not yet striven," because knowledge is connected to the object known, so the negation of knowledge was placed in the position of the negation of its object, since the object is non-existent by the non-existence of the knowledge. You say: "Allah does not know any good in so-and-so," meaning: there is no good in him for Allah to know it. "Lamma" (not yet) has the meaning of "lam" (not), except that it carries a kind of expectation, so it indicates the negation of striving in the past, and the expectation of it in the future. ﴿And [that] He may know the patient﴾ is in the subjunctive mood by the implied "an" (that), and the waw is in the sense of combining (the two verbs), like in the example "Do not eat fish and drink milk." Or it is in the jussive mood by conjunction with "yaʿlamu Allah" (Allah knows). The mim was given a vowel (harakah) because of the meeting of two sukun-marked letters, and the fatha was chosen because of the fatha preceding it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 143:

﴿And you had certainly wished for death before you met it.﴾ This was addressed to those who had not witnessed Badr. They used to wish to be present at a battle alongside the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so that they might attain the honor of martyrdom. These were the ones who pressed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to go out against the polytheists, although his opinion was to remain in Madinah. The meaning is: "You used to wish for death before you saw it and recognized its severity."

﴿Then you have certainly seen it while you were looking on.﴾ That is: you saw it face to face, witnessing it, when your brothers were killed before your eyes and you came close to being killed yourselves. This is a rebuke to them for their wishing for death, and for what they caused by their insistence upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) going out, then their fleeing from him. They wished for martyrdom only to attain the honor of the martyrs, without intending what it entailed of the victory of the disbelievers. This is like someone who drinks medicine prescribed by a Christian physician: his intention is to obtain healing, and it does not occur to him that in it there is a benefit conferred upon an enemy of Allah and a promotion of that physician's profession.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 144:

When Ibn Qami'a (ibn Qami'ah) struck the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with a stone and broke his incisor (rubaʿiyyah), he advanced intending to kill him. Musʿab ibn ʿUmayr, who was the bearer of the banner, defended him until Ibn Qami'a killed him, while thinking that he was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So he said: "I have killed Muhammad!" and went out crying aloud (it was said that it was Satan): "Verily Muhammad has been killed!" The news of his death spread among the people, and they turned away in retreat. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) began calling out: "Come to me, servants of Allah!" until a group of his Companions gathered around him. He rebuked them for their flight, and they said: "O Messenger of Allah, we would ransom you with our fathers and mothers! The news of your death reached us, so we turned and fled." Then ﴿Muhammad is but a Messenger; the Messengers have passed away before him﴾ was revealed, meaning: he will pass away as they passed away. And just as their followers remained holding fast to their religion after they had passed away, so you must hold fast to his religion after he has passed away, because the purpose of sending Messengers is the conveyance of the message and the establishment of proof, not their presence among their people. ﴿So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?﴾ The fa' (فَ) here links the conditional clause to the preceding clause with the sense of causation (التَّسْبِيبِ), and the hamzah (هَمْزَة) is for denouncing that they should make the passing away of the Messengers before him a cause for turning back on their heels after his destruction by death or killing, while they know that the passing away of the Messengers before him, and the continued adherence to their religion, should be made a cause for holding fast to the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ), not for turning away from it. Turning back on one's heels (al-inqilab ʿala al-ʿaqibayn) is a metaphor for apostasy or for flight. ﴿And whoever turns back on his heels, he will not harm Allah at all﴾, but he harms only himself. ﴿And Allah will reward the grateful﴾, those who did not turn back, and He named them grateful because they gave thanks for the blessing of Islam in what they did.

﴿وَما كانَ﴾ meaning: and it was not permissible ﴿لِنَفْسٍ أنْ تَمُوتَ إلا بِإذْنِ اللهِ﴾ meaning: for any soul to die except by the permission of Allah. That is, by His knowledge, or by His permitting the Angel of Death to take its soul. The meaning is that the death of souls cannot occur except by the will of Allah. It contains an exhortation to jihad (striving in the cause of Allah), an encouragement to meet the enemy, and an informing that caution does not avail, and that no one dies before the arrival of his term, even if he plunges into perils and storms the battlefields. ﴿كِتابًا﴾ meaning: a decree, is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used for emphasis (mu'akkid), because the meaning is: He decreed death as a decree ﴿مُؤَجَّلا﴾ meaning: fixed, having a specified term that is known and that cannot be advanced or delayed. ﴿وَمَن يُرِدْ﴾ meaning: and whoever desires, by his fighting, ﴿ثَوابَ الدُنْيا﴾ meaning: the reward of this world, that is, the spoils of war (ghanīmah). This is an allusion to those who were preoccupied with the spoils on the day of Uhud.

﴿نُؤْتِهِ مِنها﴾ meaning: We will give him of it, that is, of its reward. ﴿وَمَن يُرِدْ ثَوابَ الآخِرَةِ﴾ meaning: and whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter, that is, the elevation of the word of Allah and the rank in the Hereafter.

﴿نُؤْتِهِ مِنها وسَنَجْزِي الشاكِرِينَ﴾ meaning: We will give him of it, and We will reward the grateful. The word "al-jaza'" here is indefinite (mubham) in its magnitude, meaning a reward whose extent is not specified. It refers to those who were thankful for the blessing of Allah, so nothing distracted them from jihad.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 146:

﴿And how many a prophet﴾: its origin is ayyun (which) to which the kaf of comparison (ka) was attached, and it came to have the meaning of kam (how many), which is used for multiplication. Ka'ayyin, in the pattern of ka'in (kā'in), wherever it occurs, is read by Makki.

﴿There fought alongside him﴾: (qutila, "was killed") is read by Makki, Basri and Nafi'.

﴿alongside him﴾: is a circumstantial (ḥāl) clause referring to the pronoun in qutila, meaning: he was killed while there were with him ﴿multitudes of godly men, many﴾. Al-Ribbiyyun means al-Rabbaniyyun (the godly, those devoted to the Lord). It is also reported from al-Hasan with a damma on the ra', and from some others with a fatḥa. The fatḥa is according to analogy (qiyās), since it is a relative form derived from al-Rabb (the Lord), while the damma and kasra are alterations of the relative form.

﴿So they did not falter﴾: they did not weaken at the killing of their prophet ﴿for what befell them in the way of Allah, nor did they weaken﴾ in jihad after him ﴿nor did they submit﴾ nor did they yield to their enemy. This is an allusion to the weakness that afflicted them when the rumour of the killing of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spread, and to their submission to them when they wished to seek the support of Ibn Ubayy in asking for safe conduct from Abu Sufyan.

﴿And Allah loves the patient﴾: in the jihad against the disbelievers.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 147:

﴿And their saying was only that they said: "Our Lord, forgive us our sins﴾, meaning: their saying was none other than this statement, which consists in attributing the sins to themselves, despite their being godly (rabbaniyyun), out of humility before them (hadman laha).

﴿and our excesses in our affair﴾, meaning: our exceeding the bounds of servitude ('ubudiyyah).

﴿And make firm our feet﴾ in the fighting.

﴿And help us against the disbelieving people﴾ with victory. He placed the supplication for forgiveness of sins before the request for the firming of feet in the places of war and for support against the enemies, because it is closer to being answered, owing to what it contains of submission (khudu') and humble entreaty (istikanah).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 148:

﴿So Allah gave them the reward of this world﴾, i.e., victory, triumph, and spoils of war.

﴿And the good reward of the Hereafter﴾: forgiveness and Paradise. The word "good" (ḥusn) is singled out to indicate His favour and His precedence, and that this is what He counts as valuable.

﴿And Allah loves the doers of good﴾, i.e., they are doers of good, and Allah loves them.

O you who have believed, if you obey those who disbelieved, they will return you on your heels [i.e., they will bring you back] (يُرْجِعُوكم إلى الشَرِّ, "they will bring you back to evil"), and you will turn back as losers.

It was said: this is general, applying to all the disbelievers, and it is incumbent upon the believers to keep away from them (يُجانِبُوهُمْ) and not to obey them in anything, lest they draw them (يَسْتَجِرُّوهم) into agreeing with them.

And it is related from al-Suddi: "If you submit (تَسْتَكِينُوا) to Abu Sufyan and his companions, and seek safe-conduct from them (تَسْتَأْمِنُوهُمْ), they will return you to their religion."

And Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it was revealed concerning the saying of the hypocrites to the believers at the time of the defeat: "Return to your brothers, and enter into their religion."
Allah is your Protector (mawlakum), meaning your Helper (nasirukum), so be content to have no need of the help of anyone else. "And He is the best of helpers."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 151:

﴿We shall cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved﴾ (al-Ru'b) is read by Ibn 'Amir (Shami) and 'Asim (Ali). Both are two dialects (lughatan). It was said: God cast fear into the hearts of the polytheists on the Day of Uhud, so they fled to Makkah without any cause, though they had strength and dominance.

﴿because they associated with God﴾ (bi-ma ashraku bi-llah), i.e., because of their association (bi-sabab ishrakihim). That is: the cause of God casting terror into their hearts was their associating with Him ﴿that for which He had sent down no authority﴾ (ma lam yunazzil bihi sultanan), namely gods for whose association God had sent down no proof. He did not mean that there is a proof which would descend upon them, because association (shirk) cannot be supported by any proof. Rather, what is intended is the negation of proof and of its descent altogether, like the saying of the poet:

"And you do not see the lizard (dabb) therein burrowing"

i.e., there is no lizard there that would burrow; he did not mean that there is a lizard there which does not burrow. ﴿Their refuge is﴾ their place of return ﴿the Fire, and wretched is the abode of the wrongdoers﴾: the Fire; the object of the dispraise is omitted (fa-al-makhsus bi-l-dhamm mahdhuf).

"When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned to Madina with his Companions, some of his Companions said: 'How has this befallen us, when Allah promised us victory?!' Then there was revealed: ﴿And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you﴾, i.e., He made it true, ﴿when you were killing them with His permission﴾, i.e., you were slaughtering them in a devastating slaughter. And on the authority of Ibn 'Isa: "hassahu" means he eliminated its sensation (hiss) by killing.

﴿by His permission﴾, i.e., by His command and His knowledge. ﴿Until, when you lost courage﴾, i.e., became cowardly,

﴿and disputed concerning the matter﴾, i.e., you differed, ﴿and disobeyed﴾ the command of your Prophet by abandoning your position and busying yourselves with the spoils of war.

﴿after He had shown you what you love﴾, i.e., victory and the subjugation of the disbelievers. The complement of "idha" is omitted, its implied sense being: ﴿until, when you lost courage﴾, He withheld His help from you. It is also permissible that the meaning be: Allah fulfilled His promise to you up until the time of your cowardice. (p-301) ﴿Among you are those who desire this world﴾, i.e., the spoils of war; and they are those who abandoned their position in pursuit of the spoils.

It is narrated that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ placed Uhud behind his back, faced Madina, and stationed the archers at the mountain, ordering them to hold their ground in their place and not leave it, whether the state was in favour of the Muslims or against them. When the polytheists advanced, the archers began shooting at their horses, while the rest struck them with swords, until they were routed, and the Muslims were pursuing them, killing them. When they lost courage and disputed, some of them said: 'The polytheists have been defeated; why do we remain here? Enter the camp of the Muslims and take the spoils with your brothers.' Others said: 'Do not disobey the command of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.'" Among those who held firm in their place was 'Abdullah ibn Jubayr, the commander of the archers, along with a group of fewer than ten, and they are those referred to by His words: ﴿and among you are those who desire the Hereafter﴾. Then the polytheists charged back at the archers, killed 'Abdullah ibn Jubayr, turned upon the Muslims until they routed them, and killed whomever they killed. This is His words: ﴿Then He turned you away from them﴾, i.e., He withdrew His aid from you, so they overpowered you, ﴿that He might test you﴾, to examine your patience in calamities and your steadfastness in them. Its real meaning is that He dealt with you as one who tests, for He recompenses what the servant does, not what He knows of him. ﴿And He has certainly pardoned you﴾, when you repented of having disobeyed the command of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. ﴿And Allah is Bountiful to the believers﴾, by pardoning them and accepting their repentance; or He is bountiful to them in all circumstances, whether they are given the upper hand or it is turned against them, for trial is a mercy just as victory is a mercy.

The phrase ﴿when you were climbing﴾ is in the accusative case (*intaṣaba*, grammatically governed). It means "you were going far" (*tubalighūna*) in going into the surface of the earth (*ṣa'īd al-arḍ*). *Al-iṣʿād* is going into the surface of the earth, and *al-ibʿād* is going far into it, by your fleeing, or by His saying ﴿that He might test you﴾, or by an implied ﴿remember﴾.

﴿And you did not turn back for anyone﴾: you did not look back. This is an expression for the extreme of their defeat and fear of their enemy. ﴿While the Messenger was calling you﴾: he was saying, "To me, servants of God! I am the Messenger of God! Whoever turns back, for him is Paradise." The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). ﴿In your rear﴾: in your rear-guard and your other, later group, which is the one that lagged behind. It is said, "I came at the end of the people and their last (*ukhrāhum*)," just as you say "at their beginning and their first (*ūlāhum*)," with the meaning of their vanguard and their first group.

﴿So He rewarded you﴾ is coordinated (*ʿaṭf*) upon ﴿He turned you away﴾, meaning: so God requited you ﴿with grief﴾ when He turned you away from them, and tested you.

﴿With grief﴾: because of a grief you caused the Messenger of God (ﷺ) by your disobedience to his command. Or it means a doubled grief, grief after grief, and grief joined to grief, from the distress caused by what was spread about the killing of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), the wounding, the slaughter, the victory of the polytheists, and the loss of the spoils and the victory.

﴿So that you would not grieve over what escaped you﴾: so that you would train yourselves to swallow griefs, so that afterwards you would not grieve over any benefit that was lost. ﴿Nor over what befell you﴾: nor over any harm that struck you. ﴿And God is Aware of what you do﴾: He knows your deeds, and nothing of your actions is hidden from Him. This is an encouragement to obedience and a warning against disobedience.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 154:

﴿Then after the distress He sent down upon you security, drowsiness that overcame a group of you.﴾ Allah sent down security upon the believers and removed from them the fear that had been upon them, so that they dozed off and sleep overcame them. "On the authority of Abu Talha: drowsiness overtook us while we were in our battle lines, and the sword would fall from one of our hands and he would take it, then it would fall and he would take it again." Al-amana (security) means al-amn (safety). "Nu'asan" (drowsiness) is a badal (substitution, in apposition) for amanatan, or it is the object (maf'ul bihi), and "amanatan" is a ḥal (circumstantial accusative, a state) of it, placed before it, like the example "I saw a rider, a man." The underlying sense is: He sent down upon you drowsiness accompanied by security, since drowsiness is not itself security. It is also permissible for "amanatan" to be a maf'ul lahu (object of purpose), or a ḥal from the addressees in the sense of "possessors of security," or that it is the plural of "amin" (secure), like "barr" and "barara." ﴿Yaghsha﴾ means: al-nu'as (drowsiness). The reading "tughsha" with a ta' and imala (vowel inclination) is that of Hamza and Ali, meaning: al-amana (security).

﴿A group of you﴾ means the people of truthfulness and certainty.

﴿And another group﴾ means the hypocrites, ﴿whom their own selves had made anxious﴾: nothing concerned them except concern for their own selves and their deliverance, not concern for the religion, nor concern for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims, may Allah be pleased with them.

﴿They harbour thoughts about Allah that are not the truth﴾: this is in the position of a masdar (verbal noun), meaning: they think about Allah other than the true thought that ought to be held about Him, which is that He would not give victory to Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿The thought of the Jahiliyya﴾ is a badal from it. The intended meaning is: the thought specific to the jahili (pre-Islamic ignorant) creed, or the thought of the people of the Jahiliyya, that is, only the polytheists who are ignorant of Allah would think such a thought. ﴿They say: Do we have any share in the affair?﴾ meaning: Do we, the community of Muslims, have any share at all in the command of Allah? They mean victory and dominance over the enemy.

﴿Say: Indeed the affair﴾ i.e. victory and dominance ﴿is entirely for Allah﴾ and for His allies, the believers. ﴿And indeed Our hosts, they are the victorious﴾ [al-Saffat: 173]. "Kulluhu" (entirely) is an emphasis for "al-amr" (the affair), and "lillah" (for Allah) is the predicate of "inna." "Kulluhu" is in the nominative as a mubtada' (subject), and "lillah" is its predicate, and the whole sentence is the predicate of "inna."

﴿They conceal within themselves what they do not disclose to you﴾, out of fear of the sword. ﴿They say﴾ within themselves, or some of them say to others, denying your words to them: ﴿Indeed the affair is entirely for Allah.﴾ ﴿If we had any share in the affair, we would not have been slain here﴾: meaning, if the matter were as Muhammad said, that the affair belongs entirely to Allah and to His allies, and that they are the victorious, we would never have been defeated, and none of the Muslims who were killed in this battle would have been killed.

﴿Whom their own selves had made anxious﴾ is an attribute of a group. "Yazunnun" (they harbour thoughts) is the predicate of a group, or another attribute, or a ḥal, meaning: their own selves had made them anxious while they were harbouring thoughts. "Yaqulun" (they say) is a badal from "yazunnun." "Yukhfun" (they conceal) is a ḥal from "yaqulun." And ﴿Say: Indeed the affair is entirely for Allah﴾ is an i'tiraḍ (parenthetical interjection) between the ḥal and the one it qualifies (dhu al-ḥal). "Yaqulun" is a badal from "yukhfun," or an isti'naf (new, resumptive sentence).

﴿Say: Even if you had been in your houses﴾, meaning: whoever Allah knew would be killed in this battle, and whose fate He had written in the Preserved Tablet, there was no escape from its occurrence, even if you had remained in your houses.

﴿Those for whom death had been decreed would have gone forth﴾ from among you ﴿to their places of death﴾: their places of falling at Uhud, so that what Allah knew would come to pass might happen. The meaning is: Allah wrote in the Tablet the killing of those among the believers who would be killed, and He also wrote that they would be the victorious, because He knew that the final outcome lies in their victory, that the religion of Islam would prevail over all religions, and that what afflicts them at some times is a purification for them. ﴿And that Allah might test what is in your breasts and purify what is in your hearts﴾: to test the sincerity that is in the breasts of the believers and to purify what is in their hearts of the whisperings of Satan. He did this, or He did this for many benefits, and for the sake of the trial and the purification.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾: of its hidden things.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 155:

﴿Indeed, those of you who turned away﴾ fled (infahamu), ﴿on the day the two hosts met﴾ the host of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the host of Abu Sufyan, for battle at Uhud. ﴿It was only Satan who caused them to slip﴾ he called them to the slip (al-zilla) and drove them to it.

﴿because of some of what they had earned﴾ by their leaving the position (al-markaz) in which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had ordered them to remain steadfast. The attribution to Satan is gentle and brings them near, while the explanation by their earning is admonition and discipline. The companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) turned away from him on the day of Uhud, except for thirteen men, among them: Abu Bakr, Ali, Talha, Ibn Awf, and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas; the rest were from the Ansar.

﴿And Allah has certainly pardoned them﴾ He overlooked them (tajawaza 'anhum). ﴿Indeed Allah is Forgiving﴾ and Merciful toward sins,

﴿Forbearing﴾ He does not hasten with punishment.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 156:

﴿O you who have believed, do not be like those who disbelieved﴾ — like Ibn Ubayy and his companions,

﴿and who say of their brothers﴾ — i.e., concerning their brothers by lineage, or in hypocrisy (nifaq).

﴿when they travel through the land﴾ — they journeyed in it for trade or other purposes.

﴿or were raiders﴾ — plural of ghazin (ghāzin, one who goes on a raid), like ʿafin and ʿufFan (ʿufṣan, the plural of ʿāfin, one who is pardoned/forgiving), and death or killing befell them.

﴿If they had been with us, they would not have died or been killed,﴾ — the lam here is connected to "do not be" (lā takūnū), meaning: do not be like these people in uttering that statement and believing in it, so that God may make that a regret in their hearts specifically, and may protect your hearts from it. Or it is connected to "they say" (qālū), meaning: they said that and believed it, so that it would be a regret in their hearts. Ḥasra (regret) is remorse over the loss of what is loved.

﴿And God gives life and causes death﴾ — a refutation of their statement that fighting cuts short the appointed terms of life; that is, the matter is in His hand: He may give life to the traveler and the fighter, and cause death to (p-305) the one who stays home and the one who sits back.

﴿And God is Seer of what you do﴾ — so He will recompense you for your deeds. (yaʿmalūna, "they do") is read by Ibn Kathir (Makki), Hamza, and ʿAlī, meaning: those who disbelieved.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 157:

﴿And if you are killed in the way of Allah or you die﴾ "(mutum)" and its pattern with a kasra [on the mim] is [recited by] Nafi', and the Kufans except ʿAsim. Ḥafs followed them, except in this surah, as if he intended harmony between it and "qutiltum" (you are killed). Others [recite it] with a damma on the mim throughout the Qur'an. So the damma is from māta yamūtu (to die), and the kasra is from māta yamātu (to die), like khāfa yakhāfu (to fear): just as you say khiftu (I feared), you say mittu (I died).

﴿Surely forgiveness from Allah and mercy are better than what they amass﴾ "mā" is in the sense of "alladhī" (that which), and the returning pronoun is omitted. Ḥafs [recites] with the ya' (yajmaʿūna, "they amass," with the third-person prefix).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 158:

﴿And if you die or are killed, surely to God you will be gathered﴾. Surely to the Merciful, the One of vast mercy, the Rewarder, the One of great reward, you will be gathered. The placing of the name of God in this position, with its being placed first and the lam being attached to the particle joined to it, is a matter that needs no proof. "Forgiveness" (laMaghfiratun) is the response to the oath, and it stands in place of the response to the condition. Likewise, ﴿surely to God you will be gathered﴾. He first refuted the disbelievers in their claim that whoever of their brothers travelled or went on a raid, had he been in Medina, would not have died, and He forbade the Muslims from that, because it is the cause of withdrawing from jihad. Then He said to them: And if there befalls you what you fear of destruction by death or killing in the way of God, then what you attain of forgiveness and mercy through death in the way of God is better than what you gather of the worldly life, because the worldly life is the provision for the return, and when the servant reaches the goal he has no need of provision.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 159:

﴿Then it was by a mercy from Allah that you were gentle with them.﴾ "Ma" (مَا) is added here for emphasis and to indicate that his gentleness toward them came about only through a mercy from Allah. The meaning of "mercy" is that He steadied his heart (رَبْطُهُ عَلى جَأْشِهِ) and granted him success (تَوْفِيقُهُ) in gentleness and kindness toward them.

﴿And had you been harsh (فَظًّا) — coarse (جافِيًا) — hard-hearted (غَلِيظَ القَلْبِ), qasiyah (قاسِيَهُ)﴾ ﴿they would have scattered from around you﴾, meaning they would have dispersed away from you until no one from among them remained around you. ﴿So pardon them﴾ for what they did on the Day of Uhud that concerned you specifically, ﴿and ask forgiveness for them﴾ regarding what concerns the right of Allah, completing the compassion toward them.

﴿And consult them in the matter﴾, that is, in the matter of war and the like, concerning what no revelation has come down to you about, to console their souls, refresh their hearts, and raise their status, and so that your community may follow you in it. In a hadith: "No people ever consulted among themselves except that they were guided to the most rightful course of their affair." And on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him: "I have never seen anyone who consulted more than the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

The meaning of "shawartu fulanan" (شاوَرْتُ فُلانًا) is: I displayed what I had of opinion and what he had of opinion. "Sharat al-dabbah" (شَرَتِ الدابَّةُ) means the animal displayed its speed in running, and "shirtu al-'asal" (شِرْتُ العَسَلَ) means I took the honey from its sources. In this is evidence for the permissibility of ijtihad (independent legal reasoning, ijtihad) and a demonstration that qiyas (analogical reasoning) is a valid proof.

﴿So when you have resolved (فَإذا عَزَمْتَ)﴾, that is, when you have settled your opinion upon something after consultation, ﴿then put your trust in Allah﴾ in carrying out your affair toward what is most rightful, not in the consultation itself. ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who rely (upon Him)﴾. Tawakkul (التَوَكُّلُ) is reliance upon Allah and committing one's affairs to Him. Dhu al-Nun said: "Tawakkul is the casting off of lords and the severing of means."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 3, verse 160:

﴿If Allah helps you﴾, as He helped you on the day of Badr, ﴿then none can overcome you﴾, meaning no one will overcome you. Only the one who disowns his own strength and power and holds fast to his Lord and His might attains the help of Allah.

﴿And if He forsakes you﴾, as He forsook you on the day of Uhud, ﴿who is there that can help you after Him?﴾ After His forsaking, which is the withholding of aid. Or it may be from your saying: "So-and-so has no one who does him good after him," meaning when he has passed him by. This is a reminder that the whole matter belongs to Allah, and of the obligation of *tawakkul* (reliance upon Allah). ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾ The believers should single out their Lord for reliance and for committing their affairs to Him (*tafwid*, entrusting). He taught them that there is no helper besides Him, and because their faith requires that.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 161:

﴿It is not for a Prophet to deceive (yaghull)﴾. Makki, Abu ʿAmr, Hafs and ʿAsim [read it as yaghull], meaning: he betrays. [Reading it] with a dammah on the yaʾ and a fatha on the ghayn, the others [read it as yughall], from ghalla shay'an min al-maghnam ghululan, and aghalla ighlalan (to take something from the spoils secretly, i.e., to embezzle, ghulul), when he takes it in secret. It is also said: aghallahu means when he finds him to be a ghall (one who embezzles). The meaning is: it is not proper for him to do that, i.e., prophethood is incompatible with embezzlement. The same applies to the one who reads it in the passive form (yughall), which refers back to this meaning, because its meaning is: it is not proper for him to be found embezzling, and one is not found embezzling unless he is a ghall. It is related that a red woollen cloak was lost on the day of Badr from what was taken from the polytheists, and some of the hypocrites said: "Perhaps the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took it." So the verse was revealed: ﴿And whoever embezzles will bring what he embezzled on the Day of Resurrection﴾, meaning: he will come with the very thing he embezzled, carrying it on his back, as has come in the hadith, or he will come bearing its burden and its sin. ﴿Then every soul will be paid in full what it has earned﴾, meaning: it will be given its recompense in full. He did not say "then what he earned will be paid in full" so that it would connect with his saying "yaghull", rather a general term was used so that every earner, whether an embezzler or otherwise, would be included under it. Thus it connects in meaning, and it is more eloquent, because when the embezzler knows that every earner of good or evil is recompensed and paid his due, he knows that he cannot escape from among them, along with the enormity of what he has earned. ﴿And they will not be wronged﴾, meaning: the recompense of each is according to the measure of his earnings.

﴿Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah﴾, i.e., the pleasure of Allah. It was said: they are the Emigrants (*muhajirun*) and the Helpers (*ansar*). ﴿Like one who has incurred wrath from Allah﴾, and they are the hypocrites and the disbelievers. ﴿Their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination﴾, the place of return.

(p-٣٠٨)

﴿They are of varying ranks in the sight of Allah﴾ They differ from one another just as ranks differ, or they are people of ranks. The meaning is the difference between the stations of those who are rewarded among them and the stations of those who are punished, and the difference between reward and punishment.

﴿And Allah is All-Seeing of what they do﴾ He is knowing of their deeds and their ranks, so He will recompense them according to their reckoning.

Allah has certainly bestowed His favor upon the believers: upon those of their people who believed along with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He singled out the believers among them, because they are the ones who benefit from his mission.

﴿when He raised among them a Messenger from among themselves﴾: from their own kind, an Arab like them, or from the descendants of Ishmael (Isma'il), just as they themselves are his descendants. The favor in this lies in the fact that, since he was [one] from them, the language was one, so it was easy for them to take what they were obliged to take from him. They were also acquainted with his circumstances in truthfulness and trustworthiness, and this was closer to their affirming him. It was also an honor for them that he was one of them. In the recitation of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) it is read as "مِن أنْفَسِهِمْ" (from their nafs), meaning: from their most noble.

﴿He recites to them His verses﴾: that is, the Qur'an, after they had been a people of ignorance (jahiliyyah), in whose ears nothing of revelation had ever reached.

﴿and purifies them﴾: He cleanses them through faith from the filth of disbelief and transgression, or He takes from them zakat (obligatory alms-tax).

﴿and teaches them the Book and wisdom﴾: the Qur'an and the Sunnah (the Prophet's sayings and practice, as a technical term in the Islamic sciences). ﴿And indeed they had been before﴾: before the mission of the Messenger (ﷺ).

﴿in clear error﴾: in blindness and ignorance.

﴿clear﴾: manifest, with no doubt about it. The إنْ here is a lightened form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy إنَّ (inna), and the اللامُ is a distinguishing lam (lam al-farqah) that separates it from the negating إنْ (in al-nafiyah). The sense is: indeed the matter and the reality was that they had been, before this, in manifest error.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 165:

﴿When a calamity afflicted you﴾ — he means: what befell them on the Day of Uhud, the killing of seventy of them, ﴿though you had inflicted twice as much﴾ on the Day of Badr: the killing of seventy and the capture of seventy. It is in the nominative position as a qualifier of ﴿calamity﴾. ﴿You said, "From where is this?"﴾ — from where is this? ﴿Say, "It is from yourselves."﴾ — because of your choosing to go out of Madinah, or because of your abandoning the post. "Lamma" is in the accusative case governed by "qultum," and "asabatkum" is in the genitive position through the "lamma" being annexed to it; its implied sense is: did you say when it afflicted you? And ﴿from where is this﴾ is in the accusative because it is the object of speech. The hamza is for confirmation and reproach. The conjunction "wa" has joined this sentence to what preceded of the story of Uhud, from His words: ﴿And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you﴾; or it has joined it to an elided element, as if it were said: Did you do such and such, and say at that time such and such? ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾ — He is capable of granting victory and of withholding it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 3, verse 166:

﴿وَما أصابَكُمْ﴾ "ما" (*ma*) is in the sense of "that which" (الَّذِي, *alladhi*), and it is a *mubtada'* (the nominal subject of the sentence).

﴿يَوْمَ التَقى الجَمْعانِ﴾ The two hosts are your host and the host of the polytheists at Uhud. The *khabar* (predicate) is ﴿فَبِإذْنِ اللهِ﴾: it occurred by the permission of God, that is, by His knowledge and decree. ﴿وَلِيَعْلَمَ المُؤْمِنِينَ﴾

﴿And that He might make evident those who believe﴾ ﴿and that He might make evident those who were hypocrites﴾ — and this was (certainly to happen), so that the believers and the hypocrites would be distinguished, and so that the faith of these and the hypocrisy of those would become manifest. ﴿And it was said to them﴾ — to the hypocrites — and this is an independent statement. ﴿"Come, fight in the way of Allah"﴾ — that is, "Strive for the sake of the Hereafter as the believers fight." ﴿"Or defend"﴾ — that is, "Fight in defence of yourselves, your families and your property, if you will not fight for the Hereafter." It has also been said: ﴿"or defend"﴾ the enemy by increasing the number of the fighters with your numbers, if you will not fight, because a large host is among the things that frighten the enemy. ﴿They said, "If we knew there would be fighting, we would certainly follow you."﴾ — that is, "If we knew what could properly be called fighting, we would certainly follow you." They mean: what you are engaged in is due to the error of your opinion; it is nothing, and no one would call the like of it "fighting"; it is merely casting oneself into destruction.

﴿They were nearer to disbelief that day than to faith﴾ — meaning: they used to make a show of faith before that, and no sign of their disbelief had appeared from them; but when they withdrew from the army of the believers and said what they said, they distanced themselves by that from the faith that was attributed to them, and drew near to disbelief. Or: they were nearer in support to the people of disbelief than to the people of faith, because their reducing the number of the believers by withdrawing is a strengthening of the polytheists. ﴿They say with their mouths what is not in their hearts﴾ — that is, they display the opposite of what they conceal of (p-310) faith and otherwise; and the restriction to "with their mouths" is for emphasis and to negate metaphor. ﴿And Allah knows best what they conceal﴾ — of hypocrisy.

﴿Those who said﴾ That is, Ibn Ubayy and his companions. The phrase ﴿الَّذِينَ قالُوا﴾ (alladhina qalu) may be in the nominative, as in "they are the ones who said" (hum alladhina qalu), or it may be a substitution (ibdal) for the wa of "yaktumuna" (they conceal). It may also be in the accusative with an implied verb, "I mean" (a'ni), or it may be an apposition (badal) of "alladhina nafaqu" (those who were hypocrites). It may also be in the genitive as an apposition of the pronoun in "afwahihim" (their mouths) or "qulubihim" (their hearts). ﴿to their brothers﴾ means on account of their brothers, who were of the same kind as the hypocrites and were killed on the day of Uhud. ﴿and sat back﴾ means they said, while they had remained seated and held back from fighting.

﴿If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed.﴾ If our brothers had obeyed us in what we ordered them, namely to withdraw from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and to remain seated, and had agreed with us in this, they would not have been killed, just as we were not killed.

﴿Say: Then avert death from yourselves, if you are truthful.﴾ That is, caution averts the decree (al-qadar), so take your precaution against death. Or its meaning is: say, if you are truthful in claiming that you found a way to avert being killed, namely by sitting back from fighting, then strive to find a way to avert death. It is reported that on the day they uttered this saying, seventy hypocrites died.

Al-Nasafi, Madarik al-Tanzil, on surah 3, verse 169:

It was revealed concerning the martyrs of Uhud. (And do not think) — read by al-Shami, Hamzah, ʿAli and ʿAsim; others read it with a kasra on the sīn (tahsibanna, "do not think" in the form with a kasra) — the address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to every person. ﴿Those who were killed﴾ (qutilu, "were killed", with the doubled tāʾ) — read by al-Shami.

﴿in the way of Allah, dead. Nay, they are alive﴾: nay, they are alive ﴿with their Lord﴾, brought near to Him, holding a high station with Him, ﴿and are provided for﴾ in the same way that the rest of the living are provided for, eating and drinking. This is an emphasis on their being alive, and a description of their condition, in which they enjoy the provision of Allah.

**Al-Nasafi, *Madarik al-Tanzil*, on Surah 3, verse 170:**

﴿Rejoicing﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) referring to the pronoun in ﴿they are provided for﴾. ﴿In what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾ means the success (*tawfīq*) in martyrdom, and what it brought them of honor and of being preferred over others by being living ones brought near, with the provision of Paradise and its delights granted to them in advance. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When your brothers were struck at Uhud, Allah placed their souls in the bodies of green birds that roam in the rivers of Paradise, eat from its fruits, and take refuge in golden lanterns suspended in the shade of the Throne." It has been said that this provision is in Paradise on the Day of Resurrection, but this is weak, because then the specification would serve no purpose. ﴿And they rejoice at those﴾ — their brothers, the fighters in the cause of Allah — ﴿who have not yet joined them﴾, meaning those who have not been killed and so have not joined them, ﴿from behind them﴾. The meaning is those who remain behind them after them, though they have already preceded them. Or ﴿have not yet joined them﴾ means they have not attained their virtue and rank. ﴿No fear will be upon them﴾ is a substitution (*badal*) for "those." The meaning is: they rejoice at what has become clear to them concerning the state of those whom they left behind among the believers, namely that they will be raised on the Day of Resurrection secure. Allah gave them this glad tidings, so they rejoice in it. In mentioning the state of the martyrs and their rejoicing over those left behind is an incitement to those who remain after them to be earnest in jihad and eager to attain the ranks of the martyrs. ﴿Nor will they grieve﴾.

﴿They rejoice in favour from Allah and bounty﴾ They are gladdened by what Allah has bestowed upon them, and by the increase in honour that He has graciously added to them.

﴿And that Allah﴾ is in coordination (ʿaṭf) with "the favour and the bounty." As for (إنَّ اللهَ), ʿAlī reads it with a kasra (إنَّ), on the basis of resumption (istiʾnāf), a new independent sentence, and on the basis that the clause is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ). ﴿Certainly, Allah does not waste the reward of the believers﴾, but rather He bestows it on them in full.

﴿Alladhina istajabu lillahi wa'l-Rasul﴾ (Those who answered God and the Messenger). This is a mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence). Its khabar (predicate) is ﴿lilladhina ahsanu﴾ (for those who did good). Alternatively, it is a sifah (qualifier) of "the believers," or it is in the accusative as a mark of praise (nasb 'ala'l-madh). ﴿Min ba'di ma asabahumu'l-qarh﴾ (after the wound had befallen them), where al-qarh means the wound (al-jurh).

It was narrated that when Abu Sufyan and his companions turned back from Uhud, they reached al-Ruha and regretted it and resolved to return. The news of this reached the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he wished to frighten them and to show them his strength and that of his companions. So the Prophet (ﷺ) called his companions to go out in pursuit of Abu Sufyan. He went out on Sunday from Medina with seventy men until they reached Hamra' al-Asad, which is eight miles from Medina, and his companions were still suffering from their wounds. God cast terror into the hearts of the polytheists (p-312), and they went away. Then this was revealed: ﴿Lilladhina ahsanu minhum wa'ttaqaw﴾ (for those among them who did good and were mindful of God).

"Min" here is for specification (li'l-tabyin), and similar to it is His saying: ﴿God has promised those among them who believed and did righteous deeds forgiveness﴾ [al-Fath: 29], because all of those who answered God and the Messenger did good and were mindful of God, not only some of them. ﴿An unfolding great reward﴾ in the Hereafter.

﴿Those to whom the people said﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿those who responded﴾. ﴿Indeed, the people have gathered against you﴾. It is related that "Abu Sufyan called out as he was departing from Uhud: 'O Muhammad, our appointment is at the Badr season next year.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'If Allah wills.' When the following year came, Abu Sufyan set out with the people of Makkah, but Allah cast terror into his heart, and it occurred to him to turn back. He met Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud al-Ashja'i, who had come to perform 'umrah, and said: 'O Nu'aym, I had promised Muhammad that we would meet at the Badr season, but it has occurred to me to turn back and not go. Go to Madinah and dissuade them, and I will give you ten camels.' Nu'aym set out and found the Muslims preparing, and said to them: 'Do you intend to go out when they have gathered against you?! By Allah, not one of you will escape!' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'By Allah, I will go out even if no one goes out with me.' So he went out with seventy riders, and they were saying: ﴿Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs﴾, until they reached Badr and remained there for eight nights. They had merchandise with them, which they sold, and they gained profit. Then they returned to Madinah safe and laden with gain, and there was no fighting. Abu Sufyan returned to Makkah." So the people of Makkah named his army the "Army of Sawiq" and said: "You only went out to eat sawiq (parched grain)." The first ﴿the people﴾ is Nu'aym, and it is a collective term used for the singular, or he had followers who dissuaded in the same manner as his dissuasion. The second is Abu Sufyan and his companions.

﴿So fear them﴾: i.e., be afraid of them. ﴿So it increased them﴾: i.e., the statement, which is ﴿Indeed, the people have gathered against you, so fear them﴾, or the saying, or Nu'aym.

﴿In faith﴾: insight and certainty.

﴿And they said: Allah is sufficient for us﴾: Allah is sufficient for us, i.e., He who suffices us is Allah. It is said: "ahsabahu al-shay'" when it sufficed him; it has the meaning of al-muhsib (the one who suffices). The evidence is that you say: "This is a man who is ḥasbuka (sufficient for you)," describing an indefinite noun with it, because its annexation is not genuine, since it has the meaning of the active participle. ﴿And He is the best Disposer of affairs﴾: and the best one to whom affairs are entrusted is He.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 174:

﴿So they returned with a blessing from Allah﴾, which is safety and the enemy's fear of them.

﴿And bounty﴾, which is the profit in trade, so they gained two dirhams for every dirham.

﴿No harm touched them﴾: they met with nothing that would distress them from the plotting of the enemy. This is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "انْقَلَبُوا" (inqalabu, "they returned"), and likewise "بِنِعْمَةٍ" (bi-ni'mah, "with a blessing"). The implied sense is: they returned from Badr, enjoying favour, free from any harm.

﴿And they followed the pleasure of Allah﴾ by their boldness and their going out toward the enemy after his discouragement, and it is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "انْقَلَبُوا". ﴿And Allah is the Possessor of great bounty﴾, for He had graciously granted them success in what they did.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 175:

﴿Indeed, that is the Shaytan﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of "dhalikum" (that), i.e., ﴿Indeed, that [one] who frightens you﴾ is ﴿the Shaytan﴾, and he is Nu'aym, ﴿who frightens his allies﴾, i.e., the hypocrites. This is a resumed sentence (jumla musta'nafa) explaining his being a devil (shaytana). Or ﴿the Shaytan﴾ is an adjective (sifa) of the demonstrative (ism al-ishara), and ﴿frightens﴾ is the predicate (khabar). ﴿So do not fear them﴾, i.e., his allies, ﴿but fear Me, if you are believers﴾, because faith requires that the servant prefer the fear of God over the fear of others. And "wakhafuni" (fear Me), in both pausal and continuous recitation, is read by Sahl and Ya'qub, and Abu 'Amr agreed with them in continuous recitation.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 176:

﴿And let them not grieve you﴾ (yuhzinuka). In the whole Qur'an, Nafi' reads it as yuhzinuka (with damma on the yaʾ and kasra on the zay), except in Surat al-Anbiya', ﴿They will not be grieved by the greatest terror﴾ [al-Anbiya': 103]. ﴿Those who hasten into disbelief﴾. That is: "Do not let them grieve you out of fear that they may harm you." Do you not see His saying: ﴿Indeed, they will never harm Allah at all﴾, meaning: the friends of Allah? That is: by their hastening into disbelief they harm none but themselves, and the harm of that does not return to anyone else. Then He explained how its harm returns upon them by His saying: ﴿Allah intends not to give them any share in the Hereafter﴾, meaning: any portion of reward,

﴿and for them is a great punishment﴾ instead of reward. And that is the most extreme harm a person can do to himself. The verse indicates the will of Allah regarding disbelief (p-314) and sins, because His intending that they have no reward in the Hereafter cannot be without His intending their disbelief and their sins.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 177:

﴿Indeed, those who have exchanged disbelief for faith﴾ That is: they substituted it for it. ﴿They will not harm Allah at all﴾ Shay'an is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: any harm at all. The first verse is about those among the ones who stayed behind (al-mukhallafin) who practiced hypocrisy, or who apostatized from Islam; the second is about all the disbelievers. Or the reverse. ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾

﴿Wa-la yahsabanna﴾ The three that follow it, with the *ba'* of *yahsabannahum* vowelled with a *damma*, are read with *ya'* (the third person) by Makki and Abu 'Amr. All of them are read with *ta'* (the second person) by Hamza, and all of them with *ya'* by Madani and Shami, except *fa-la tahsabannahum* [Al 'Imran: 188], which is read with *ta'*. The rest read the first two with *ya'* and the last two with *ta'*.

﴿Alladhina kafaru﴾: For those who read with *ya'*, it is in the nominative case, meaning: "And let not the disbelievers suppose." *Inna* together with its noun and predicate, in His words ﴿that what We grant them respite for is better for their souls﴾, occupies the position of the two objects of *yahsabanna*, and the implied meaning is: "And let not those who disbelieved suppose that Our granting them respite is good for themselves." The *ma* is a verbal (*masdariyya*) particle. By the rule of orthographic science (*'ilm al-khatt*, the science of Arabic script), it should have been written separately, but in the *imam* (the standard 'Uthmanic codex) it was written joined, so this does not contradict it. For those who read with *ta'*, it is in the accusative case, meaning: "And do not suppose the disbelievers." ﴿That what We grant them respite for is better for them﴾ is an apposition (*badal*) to "the disbelievers," meaning: "And do not suppose that what We grant to the disbelievers is good for them." *Anna* with what follows it in its clause stands in place of the two objects. *Al-imla'* (granting respite) for them means: giving them time and prolonging their lives.

﴿Innama numli lahum liyazdadu ithman﴾: This *ma* should be written joined, because it is a *kaffa* (a particle that restrains the governing particle) and is distinct from the first *ma*. This is a resumed sentence (*jumla mustaʼnafa*) giving the reason for the sentence before it, as if it were said: "What is the matter with them that they do not reckon the respite to be good for them?" Then it is said: ﴿We only grant them respite so that they may increase in sin﴾. The verse is an argument for us against the Mu'tazila in the two questions of *al-aslah* (what is most beneficial for the servant) and the willing of sins. ﴿And for them is a humiliating punishment.﴾

The lam in ﴿Allah would not leave the believers in the state you are in﴾ indicates the emphasis of the negation, concerning the mixing of sincere believers with hypocrites (p. 315). ﴿Until He distinguishes the wicked from the good﴾: until He separates the hypocrite from the sincere believer. The verb (yumayyaza), in the passive form, is read by Hamzah and ʿAli. The address in "antum" (you) is to those who affirm belief, both the sincere and the hypocrites, as if it were said: Allah would not leave the sincere among you in the condition you are in, with some of you mixed up with others, until He distinguishes them from you through revelation to His Prophet and his informing of your states.

﴿And Allah would not let you know the unseen﴾: and Allah would not grant any of you knowledge of the hidden matters. So do not imagine, when the Messenger informs of a man's hypocrisy and of another's sincerity, that he knows what is in the hearts with Allah's knowledge, so as to report their disbelief or their faith. ﴿But Allah chooses from His messengers whom He wills﴾: that is, but Allah sends a Messenger, reveals to him, and informs him that in the unseen such-and-such is the case, that so-and-so has hypocrisy in his heart, and so-and-so has sincerity in his heart. He knows this from the direction of Allah's informing, not from himself. This verse is a proof against the Batiniyya (an esoteric sect), who claim that knowledge of this kind belongs to their imam. If they do not affirm prophethood for him, they have opposed the explicit text by ascribing knowledge of the unseen to non-messengers; and if they do affirm prophethood for him, they have opposed another text, namely His saying: ﴿and the Seal of the Prophets﴾ [al-Ahzab: 40]. ﴿So believe in Allah and His messengers﴾ with the quality of sincerity.

﴿And if you believe and fear Allah﴾, by abandoning hypocrisy, ﴿then for you is a great reward﴾ in the Hereafter.

Revealed concerning those who withhold zakat: ﴿And let not those who are niggardly with what Allah has given them of His bounty think that it is good for them﴾. Whoever reads it with the (ta') (second-person form) supposes an omitted genitive (mudaf mahdhuf), i.e., "and let not you think the stinginess of the stingy [is good]." Here "huwa" is a separator (fasl, a pronoun of separation that marks the predicate). And ﴿khayran lahum﴾ is the second object (maf'ul thani). Likewise for whoever reads it with the (ya') (third-person form), and who takes the subject of "yahsabanna" to be the pronoun of the Messenger of Allah, or the pronoun of someone unspecified. Whoever takes its subject to be "alladhina yabkhaluna" (those who are niggardly), the implied construction is: ﴿And let not those who are niggardly﴾ [think] their stinginess ﴿it is good for them﴾, where "huwa" is a separator and "khayran lahum" is the second object.

﴿Rather, it is evil for them﴾, i.e., the stinginess.

﴿Rather, it is evil for them﴾ because their wealth will leave them, while the burden of stinginess remains upon them. ﴿They will have what they were niggardly with hung around their necks on the Day of Resurrection﴾ is an explanation of His saying ﴿rather, it is evil for them﴾; i.e., He will make the wealth they withheld from what is right into a collar around their necks, as came in the hadith: "Whoever withholds the zakat of his property, his property will become a male, bald-headed serpent with two fangs; it will be collared around his neck, and it will seize him and drive him to the Fire." And ﴿To Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth﴾: and to Him belongs what is in them, of what their people inherit, of wealth and other things. So why are they niggardly toward Him with His own dominion, and do not spend it in the way of Allah?! The original form of "mirath" is "miwrath," and the waw was changed into a ya' because the letter before it is kasra.

﴿And Allah is All-Aware of what you do﴾. Read with the ya' by Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr; the ta' (you) is in the manner of iltifat (a shift of person), and it is more forceful in warning; the ya' follows the apparent sense.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 181:

﴿Indeed, Allah has heard the statement of those who said, "Indeed, Allah is poor, and we are rich."﴾ The Jews said this when they heard His saying, ﴿Who is it that would loan Allah a good loan?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245], and they said: "The god of Muhammad is asking to borrow from us; so we are then rich and He is poor." The meaning of Allah's hearing it is that it was not hidden from Him, and that He prepared for them a sufficient punishment (kifa', i.e. a recompense that suffices them).

﴿We will record what they have said.﴾ We will command the guardian angels (al-hafazah) to write down what they have said in the records (al-sahA'if), or We will preserve it, since the book (al-kitab) is something created to preserve what is in it, so it is named by it metaphorically. The "ma" here is verbal-masdariyyah (i.e. it forms a verbal noun with the verb), or it means "alladhi" (that which).

﴿And their killing of the prophets without right﴾ is conjoined to "ma" (i.e. it is in the accusative/genitive sense of what they said). He placed their killing of the prophets alongside it as its companion, as an indication that the two are brothers in gravity, and that one who killed the prophets would not be deemed unlikely to dare to utter a statement like this. ﴿And We will say﴾ to them on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿Taste the punishment of the burning.﴾ That is: the punishment of the Fire, just as you made the Muslims taste distress (al-ghusas). Al-Dahhak said: "The keepers of Hell will say that to them."

It is attributed to Allah Most High because it is by His command, as in His saying, "We will record" (sanaktub), "it will be recorded" (sa-yuktab), "and their killing" (wa-qatlahum), and Hamzah recites it so.

﴿That﴾ refers to the punishment mentioned earlier, ﴿because of what your hands have sent forth﴾, i.e., that punishment is because of the disbelief and sins you sent forth. The attribution to the hands is because most deeds are done with the hands, so every deed is treated as if it were done with the hands, by way of *taghlīb* (a figurative usage in which the predominant part stands for the whole). It is also because one who commands a thing is called its doer, so mentioning the hands serves *taḥqīq* (emphasis and confirmation), meaning that it is the act of the people themselves and not of someone else acting on their command.

﴿And that Allah is not unjust to the servants﴾, meaning that Allah does not wrong His servants, so He does not punish them without a crime.

﴿Those who said﴾ is in the genitive case (*jarr*) as an apposition (*badal*) to ﴿those who said﴾ [in the previous verse], or in the accusative (*naṣb*) by implying ﴿I mean﴾ (*a'nī*), or in the nominative (*raf'*) by implying ﴿they﴾ (*hum*). ﴿God has enjoined upon us﴾: He commanded us in the Torah (*al-Tawrah*) and charged us with it.

﴿That we should not believe﴾: ﴿*bi-allā nu'mina*﴾ (بِأَلَّا نُؤْمِنَ).

﴿To a messenger until he brings us an offering which the fire devours﴾: that is, he offers an offering, and a fire descends from heaven and consumes it. ﴿If you bring us that, we will confirm you.﴾ This is a false claim and a fabrication against God, because the fire's consuming of the offering is a cause of belief in the messenger who brings it, by virtue of it being a miracle; so it and all other miracles are alike.

﴿Say: Messengers before me have certainly come to you with the clear proofs﴾, meaning the miracles other than the offering, ﴿and with what you have said﴾, that is, with the offering. The meaning is: your forefathers, whose religion you follow and with whose deeds you are content, came with it.

﴿Why then did you kill them?﴾ That is: if your refusal to believe is for this reason, why did you not believe in those who brought it? And why did you kill them? ﴿If you are truthful﴾ in your saying: we only delay belief for this.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 184:

﴿If they deny you, [O Muhammad], then messengers before you were denied as well.﴾ If the Jews deny you, then do not let it dismay you, for the nations have done the same to their prophets. ﴿They came with the clear proofs﴾ (al-bayyinat), the evident miracles, ﴿and the scriptures﴾ (al-zubur), the books, plural of zabur, from zabr, which means writing. (wa-bi-l-zubur) is read by the people of Syria (Shami).

﴿And the Book﴾ (al-kitab), its genus, ﴿giving light﴾ (al-munir), the illuminating. It was said: both are one in origin. They are mentioned separately only because the two descriptions differ. So the zabur is a book containing restraining wisdoms, and the Book giving light is the guiding Book.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 185:

(p-318) ﴿Every soul﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate (khabar) is ﴿shall taste death﴾. The subject was permitted to be indefinite (nakira) because of the generality it contains. The meaning is: let their denial of you not grieve you, for the return of all creation is to Me, so I will recompense them for their denial and recompense you for your patience. This is His saying: ﴿And you will only be paid your full wages on the Day of Resurrection﴾, meaning: you will be given the reward of your deeds in full on the Day of Resurrection, for the world is not the abode of recompense.

﴿Whoever is drawn away﴾ from the Fire, i.e. is kept far from it (zuhziha: distanced; al-zahzahah means removal far away), ﴿and is admitted to the Garden, has indeed triumphed﴾, meaning he has attained good. It has been said: he has attained absolute triumph. It has also been said: triumph (al-fawz) is the attainment of what is loved and the distance from what is disliked.

﴿And the life of this world is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion﴾. He likened the world to a commodity that is passed off with deception upon the buyer, who is misled until he purchases it, and then its defect and worthlessness become clear to him. The Shaytan (devil) is the one who deceives and misleads (al-mudallis al-gharur). It is reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: this applies only to one who prefers it over the Hereafter; as for one who seeks the Hereafter, then it is "a provision for a time" (matā' balāgh). And it is reported from al-Hasan: it is like the greenery of plants and the play of girls, having no lasting substance.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 186:

﴿Surely you will be tested﴾ — by Allah, surely you will be tested, i.e., you will be examined ﴿in your possessions﴾ through spending in the way of Allah, and through what befalls them of calamities.

﴿and in your selves﴾ through being killed, taken captive, wounded, and what comes upon them of various kinds of fears and calamities. This verse is evidence that the self (nafs) is the perceptible body, without the additional meaning that is false, as some of the people of kalam (kalam, scholastic theology) and the philosophers have said. So it is in "Sharh al-Ta'wilat" (Sharh al-Ta'wilat, a commentary on Nasafi's own work). ﴿And you will surely hear from those who were given the Scripture before you﴾, meaning: the Jews and the Christians.

﴿and from those who associate partners with Allah, much hurt﴾, such as reviling the religion, obstructing whoever wishes to believe, condemning whoever has believed, and the like.

﴿But if you are patient﴾ over their harm ﴿and fear Allah﴾, opposing the command of Allah, ﴿then indeed that﴾ — indeed patience and taqwa ﴿are of the steadfast matters (ʿazm al-umur)﴾, i.e., of the matters that must be resolved upon, which are obligatory to resolve upon. The believers were addressed with this so that they would prepare their selves to endure what hardships they will meet and to be patient with them, so that when they encounter them, while they are prepared, the hardship will not overwhelm them as it overwhelms one who is struck by hardship suddenly, so that he denies it and his self recoils from it. (p-319)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 187:

﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Book﴾ — remember the time when Allah took the covenant from the People of the Book ﴿that you shall make it clear to the people and not conceal it﴾ from the people.
