It is read with the ta' (tubayyinunnahu, "you shall make it clear," second person), in keeping with the narration of their direct address, like His saying: ﴿And We decreed for the Children of Israel in the Book that you will surely cause corruption﴾ [al-Isra' 17:4]. It is read with the ya' (yubayyinunnahu, third person) by Makki, Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr, because they are referred to in the third person, and the pronoun refers to the Book, emphasizing upon them the obligation of making the Book clear and the prohibition of concealing it.

﴿So they cast it behind their backs﴾ — so they cast away the covenant and its emphasis upon them, meaning: they did not heed it and did not pay attention to it. Casting behind the back is an idiom for discarding and disregarding. This is evidence that it is obligatory upon the scholars to make the truth clear to the people, what they know of it, and not to conceal any part of it for a corrupt purpose, such as facilitating matters for the oppressors, pleasing their souls, gaining some benefit, averting some harm, or stinginess with knowledge. And in a hadith: "Whoever conceals knowledge from its people, Allah will bridle him with a bridle of fire." ﴿And they sold it for a small price﴾ — a fleeting gain — ﴿How evil is what they purchase﴾.

The address in ﴿لا تَحْسَبَنَّ﴾ (Do not think) is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The first object (maf'ul) is ﴿الَّذِينَ يَفْرَحُونَ﴾ (those who rejoice), and the second is ﴿بِمَفازَةٍ﴾ (safe from). His words ﴿فَلا تَحْسَبَنَّهُمْ﴾ (do not think them) are an emphasis (ta'kid). Its implied sense is: "Do not think them to be triumphant (fa'izin) ﴿بِما أتَوْا﴾ (in what they did)," meaning "in what they did." This is the reading of Ubayy (Ubayy ibn Ka'b). Jā'a (came) and atā (came/brought) are used with the meaning of fa'ala (did).

﴿إنَّهُ كانَ وعْدُهُ مَأْتِيًّا﴾ (Indeed, His promise has always been fulfilled) [Maryam: 61]. ﴿لَقَدْ جِئْتِ شَيْئًا فَرِيًّا﴾ (You have certainly brought something unprecedented) [Maryam: 27]. Al-Nakha'i (al-Nakha'i) recited ﴿بِما آتَوْا﴾ (in what they gave), meaning "in what they gave."

﴿وَيُحِبُّونَ أنْ يُحْمَدُوا بِما لَمْ يَفْعَلُوا فَلا تَحْسَبَنَّهم بِمَفازَةٍ مِنَ العَذابِ﴾ (and they love to be praised for what they did not do, so do not think them safe from the punishment) means "in a place of safety from it." ﴿وَلَهم عَذابٌ ألِيمٌ﴾ (and for them is a painful punishment) means "painful."

(p-320) It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked the Jews about something that was in the Torah, but they concealed the truth, informed him of the opposite, and showed him that they had been truthful with him. They sought his praise and rejoiced in what they had done through their deception. So Allah informed His Messenger of this and consoled him with what He revealed of their threat. That is: do not think that the Jews who rejoice in what they did of their deception toward you, and love that you praise them for what they did not do, namely informing you truthfully about what you asked them, are safe from the punishment. It is said that they are the hypocrites, who rejoice in what they did by showing faith to the Muslims and reaching their aims through it, and who seek praise from them through a faith they did not truly hold. This contains a warning for whoever does a good deed and rejoices in it with the joy of self-admiration, and loves that people praise him for what is not in him.

﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾: so He owns their affair. And in it is a refutation of those who said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is poor﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 181]. ﴿And Allah is over all things competent﴾: so He is able to punish them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 190:

﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of the night and the day, there are signs﴾ — clear proofs pointing to a Creator who is eternal, all-knowing, wise, and powerful.

﴿for those of understanding (ulul-albab)﴾ — for the one whose intellect is freed from desire, as the kernel is freed from the husk. Such a person sees that an accident (ʿaraḍ) that has come into being within substances (jawahir) indicates that the substances have come into being, because a substance is never free of a newly arising accident, and whatever is not free of what has come into being is itself come into being. Then their coming into being points to the one who brought them into being, and He is eternal; otherwise He would need another originator, and so on to infinity. The excellence of His workmanship points to His knowledge, its perfection points to His wisdom, and its permanence points to His power. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Woe to the one who recites it and does not reflect upon it." It is related concerning this that among the Children of Israel there was a man who, when he had worshipped God for thirty years, a cloud would shade him. A youth worshipped Him, but the cloud did not shade him. His mother said to him: "Perhaps some lapse has occurred from you during your period?" He said: "I do not recall any." She said: "Perhaps you once looked at the sky and did not take heed?" He said: "Perhaps." She said: "You were not afflicted except through that."

﴿Those who﴾ is in the genitive case as a qualifier (*naʿt*, descriptive adjective) of *ulī* ("possessors of"), or in the accusative by an implied *aʿnī* ("I mean"), or in the nominative by an implied *hum* ("they are").

﴿remember God﴾ means they pray. ﴿Standing﴾ means standing while able, ﴿and sitting﴾ means sitting.

﴿And on their sides﴾ means lying down when unable. *Qiyāman* and *quʿūdan* are circumstantial accusatives (*ḥāl*, a term for the accusative of state) referring back to the subject pronoun in *yadhkurūna* ("they remember"). *ʿAlā junūbihim* is also a circumstantial phrase. Alternatively, the meaning is that they remember God in every state, since a person is never free of these conditions. In a hadith: "Whoever wishes to graze in the gardens of Paradise, let him increase his remembrance of God."

﴿And they reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ and what the invention of these great bodies indicates, and the perfection of their making, and what has been arranged within them, the wonders of which human minds are unable fully to grasp. This indicates the greatness of the Creator and the majesty of His dominion. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "While a man was lying on his bed, he raised his head, looked at the stars and the sky, and said: 'I testify that You are a Lord and a Creator. O God, forgive me.' God looked at him and forgave him." He (ﷺ) also said: "There is no worship like reflection." It has been said: reflection removes heedlessness, produces fear of God in the heart, and nothing polishes hearts like sorrows, nor is anything illuminated like reflection.

﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾. That is, they say this, and it is in the position of a circumstantial clause: they reflect while saying it. The meaning is that You did not create it in vain, without wisdom; rather You created it for a great wisdom, which is that You made it dwellings for those who are accountable and proofs for them of Your knowledge. Here "this" points to the creation, understood as the created thing, or to the heavens and the earth, since they carry the sense of created things, as if it were said: "You did not create this wondrous creation in vain."

﴿Glory be to You﴾: exalting You above being described as creating in vain. This is a parenthetical interjection (*iʿtirāḍ*).

﴿So protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾. The *fa* (so) has entered to convey the sense of a conditional, its implied sense being: "Since we have exalted You, then protect us."

(p-٣٢٢)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 192:

﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You cause to enter the Fire – You have certainly disgraced him.﴾ (It means) humiliated him, or destroyed him, or exposed him. The People of the Threat (ahl al-wa'id, those who hold that grave sinners are punished eternally) argued from this verse, together with His saying: ﴿On the Day when Allah will not disgrace the Prophet and those who believed with him﴾ [al-Tahrim: 8], that whoever enters the Fire is not a believer and will abide in it forever. We say: Jabir said: "The disgracing of a believer is his disciplining, and indeed there is a greater disgrace above that."

﴿But for the wrongdoers﴾ The lam here indicates those who enter the Fire, and what is meant is the disbelievers.

﴿there will be no helpers﴾ from helpers and intercessors who would intercede for them as they do for the believers.

"O our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith" (Q 3:193).

Tells you: "I heard a man say such-and-such." You make the verb fall on "the man" and delete what was heard, because you have described him by what he says, and that description has made the mention of it unnecessary. Without the description, it would be necessary to mention it. It may also be said: "I heard the speech of so-and-so." The caller (al-Munadi) is the Messenger (ﷺ), or the Qur'an.

﴿Calling to faith﴾: for the sake of faith in God. In this there is an exaltation of the status of the caller, since there is no caller greater than one who calls to faith.

﴿That believe﴾: meaning, "that you believe," or, "i.e., believe."

﴿In your Lord, so we believed﴾: Shaykh Abu Mansur, may God have mercy on him, said: In this is evidence for the invalidity of making an exception (istithna') in faith.

﴿Our Lord, forgive us our sins﴾: our major sins (kaba'ir); ﴿and remove from us our misdeeds﴾: our minor sins (saghair); ﴿and take us in death with the righteous﴾: singled out for their companionship, counted among their number. Al-abrar (the righteous): those who hold firmly to the Sunnah, plural of barr or barr (bārr), like rabb and arbab, and sahib and ashab.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 194:

﴿Our Lord, and give us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾ That is: concerning the confirmation of Your messengers; or, what You promised us revealed upon Your messengers; or, upon the tongues of Your messengers. "ʿalā" (upon) is connected to "waʿadtanā" (You promised us). The promised thing is the reward, or victory over the enemies. They asked for the fulfilment of what Allah promised — and Allah does not break His promise — because its meaning is: a request for success in that which preserves for them the means of fulfilling the promise. Or the intent is: make us among those for whom the promise is, since the promise does not specify who they are. Or the intent is: keep us firm upon that which brings us to Your reward, supported by His saying: ﴿And do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection﴾ (p-323). Or it is a display of submission and humble supplication. ﴿Indeed, You do not break the promise﴾: "al-mīʿād" is a verbal noun with the meaning of "al-waʿd" (the promise).

﴿So their Lord answered them﴾: meaning, He responded. It is said: *istajaba lahu* and *istajabahu* (both mean "he answered him").

﴿That﴾: *bi-anni* (that), ﴿I will not allow to be lost the work of any worker among you﴾. The phrase ﴿of any worker among you﴾ is a qualifier of *'amil* (worker). ﴿Male or female﴾ is an explanation of *'amil*. ﴿You are of one another﴾: the male is from the female and the female from the male; all of you are the children of Adam. Or it means that some of you are from others in support and in religion. This is a parenthetical sentence (*jumla mu'tarida*), by which the partnership of women with men is shown in what God promised His worship­pers who act righteously.

From Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him: "Whoever is struck by a matter and says five times, 'Our Lord...' [the supplication], Allah will save him from what he fears and give him what he wants." He recited the verses: ﴿Then those who emigrated﴾. *Alladhina* (those who) is the subject (*mubtada'*, the topic of the sentence), and it is a detailed description of the work of the worker among them, as a way of honouring them. As if he said: "Those who did these noble and excellent deeds, namely emigrating from their homelands, fleeing to God with their religion to where they can be safe in it." Thus emigration exists at the end of time just as it existed at the beginning of Islam.

﴿And were expelled from their homes﴾ in which they were born and raised, ﴿and were harmed in My way﴾ by insult, beating, and the plundering of wealth. He means: the way of the religion.

﴿And fought and were killed﴾, and fought the polytheists and were martyred. (*Wa-qutilu* with the doubled *qaf*, i.e., *quttilu*) is read by Makki and Shami. (*Wa-qutilu wa-qatalu*, with the order reversed) is read by Hamza and Ali. This indicates that the conjunction *wa* (and) does not necessarily imply sequence. The predicate is ﴿Surely I will remove from them their misdeeds and surely I will admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾, and it is the answer to an implied oath. ﴿As a reward﴾ is in the position of an emphatic verbal noun (*masdar mu'akkid*), meaning: a granting of reward (*ithaba*), or a recompense (*tathwiban*).

﴿From the presence of Allah﴾, because His saying "I will surely remove from them... and surely admit them" carries the meaning of "I will surely reward them". ﴿And with Allah is the best of rewards﴾: that is, it is specific to Him, and no one other than Him has power over it.

It is related that a group of the believers said: "The enemies of God are in what we see of prosperity, while we have perished from hunger." So there was revealed: ﴿Let not the going about of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you﴾. The address is to every individual, or it is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and what is meant by it is someone other than him; or, because the leader and foremost of a people is addressed with something, his address stands in place of addressing all of them, so it is as if it were said: "Let it not deceive you." Or, because the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was not deceived by their condition, he was emphatically commanded to remain as he was and to hold firm to his obligation, like His saying: ﴿So do not be a supporter of the disbelievers﴾ [al-Qasas: 86], and ﴿And do not be among the polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 14]. This, in prohibition, is the counterpart of His saying in command: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatihah: 6], and ﴿O you who have believed, believe﴾ [al-Nisa': 136].

Qur'an 3:197 — Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil)

﴿A brief enjoyment﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada'), i.e., "their moving about in the lands is a brief enjoyment." He meant: its brevity in comparison with what they have missed of the bliss of the Hereafter, or in comparison with the reward that Allah has prepared for the believers. Or he meant that it is brief in itself, because it comes to an end, and everything that passes away is brief.

﴿Then their refuge is Hell, and what an evil resting-place﴾: and evil is what they have prepared for themselves as a resting-place.

﴿But those who have been mindful of their Lord﴾ from associating partners with Him (shirk), ﴿for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever, as a welcome gift (nuzul)﴾.

The *nuzul* and *nuzl* (النُّزُلُ والنُّزْلُ) are what is prepared for one who arrives as a guest. It is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier) of *jannāt* (gardens), since the gardens are specified by this description. The agent of the *ḥāl* is the *lām* in *lahum* (لَهُمْ). Alternatively, it is an emphatic verbal noun (*maṣdar mu'akkid*), as if it were said: a provision (*rizqan*) or a gift (*'aṭā'an*).

﴿From the presence of Allah﴾: this is a qualifier (ṣifah) of it. ﴿And what is with Allah is better for the righteous﴾: it is of the abundant and lasting, better than what the wicked enjoy of the little and transient.

(*Lakin*, لَكِنْ) with the shaddah (*lakinna*, لَكِنَّ) means it adds (*yazīd*). It is used for *istidrāk* (a corrective or contrasting turn), meaning: there is no permanence to their enjoyment, but that [lasting reward] belongs to those who were mindful of their Lord.

It was revealed concerning Ibn Salam and others among the Muslims of the People of the Book, or concerning forty people from Najran, thirty-two from Abyssinia, and eight from Rome, who had been upon the religion of Jesus, peace be upon him, and then embraced Islam. ﴿And among the People of the Book are those who believe in God﴾. The lam al-ibtida' (the emphatic lam, a particle of emphasis placed at the start of a clause) entered upon the subject of inna, to separate the adverbial element between them. ﴿and what has been sent down to you﴾, namely from the Qur'an (p-325) ﴿and what has been sent down to them﴾, namely from the two Scriptures. ﴿humbly submitting to God﴾ is a hal (circumstantial clause describing the state of the subject) of the subject of yu'minu, because "man yu'minu" carries the meaning of the plural.

﴿They do not sell the signs of God for a small price﴾, as those of their rabbis and elders who did not embrace Islam do. This is a hal following another hal, meaning: not purchasing.

﴿For them is their reward with their Lord﴾, that is, the reward that belongs specifically to them, which is what they were promised in His saying: ﴿They will be given their reward twice﴾. ﴿Indeed God is swift in reckoning﴾, because His knowledge takes effect over everything.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 200:

﴿O you who believe, be patient﴾ in the religion and its obligations. Al-Junayd, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Patience (sabr) is restraining the self from what is disliked, by negating anxiety (jaza').

﴿And be steadfast﴾ against the enemies of Allah in jihad, meaning: outdo them in patience under the hardships of war, and do not be less patient and steadfast than they are. ﴿And guard your frontiers﴾ and remain stationed in the border regions (thughur), guarding them with your horses, watching and prepared for raiding.

﴿And fear Allah, that you may prosper﴾. Falah (prosperity) is remaining with what is loved after being freed from what is disliked. "La'alla" (perhaps/that you may) here indicates the uncertainty of the outcome, lest they rely on hopes instead of advancing deeds. It was also said: be patient in My love, be steadfast in My blessings, and guard yourselves in My service;

﴿that you may prosper﴾, that you may attain nearness to Me.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "Recite the two bright ones: al-Baqarah and Aal 'Imran, for they will come on the Day of Resurrection as if they were two clouds, or two shades, or two flocks of birds in ranks, pleading on behalf of their companions." And Allah knows best what is correct, and to Him is the return and the final destination.
